full_text:
Kalif Raymond's Bears coaches and teammates rave about his speed and blocking ability. Kamil Krzaczynski / Imagn Images
LAKE FOREST, Ill. — The quickest way to elicit a grin from anyone on the Chicago Bears is to ask about Kalif Raymond.
Mundane news conferences suddenly get a jolt of energy. Players tired from a long practice light up at the topic of “‘Lif,” the 5-foot-9, 32-year-old wide receiver and returner signed this past March.
“Man, Kalif is amazing,” receiver Luther Burden III said this summer. “He’s really like a coach out there. He’s a great guy on and off the field. You can learn from him. His release package is sick. He’s a great guy and he’s out the roof. Kalif is a great leader for the team; he’s the guy, man.”
Jahdae Walker, who might’ve been the presumed No. 3 receiver had the Bears not signed Raymond, was asked about competing with the veteran whom “everyone seems to love.”
“Yeah, but I mean, I love Raymond, too,” he said.
Here’s a player who’s been with the team for only five months. He hasn’t had more than 300 yards receiving since 2023. But he’s established himself as a Hall of Famer in work ethic and vibes.
“This guy is the most selfless player I’ve ever been around,” coach Ben Johnson told The Athletic .
It’s Raymond’s third consecutive interview after practice in early August, and his energy hasn’t waned. He lights up at the potential of quarterback Caleb Williams, what it means to be part of this team and his reunion with Johnson .
“I have such love, respect and admiration for Ben,” Raymond said, “so compliments from him and criticism from him mean twice as much to me just because I know who he is and I know where he’s coming from.”
When Johnson was Detroit’s passing game coordinator in 2021, Raymond had 576 receiving yards and four touchdowns. He had 369 yards in the five previous seasons combined. Then, when Johnson took over as play caller in 2022, Raymond had 616 yards, followed by 489 in 2023.
In training camp, he has been the recipient of some of the Bears’ most explosive plays, with his speed on display daily. This is someone whose signing may have been a bit of an afterthought as the No. 3 receiver in an offense that figures to use multiple tight ends often.
But never doubt Kalif Raymond. His teammates have all marveled at his on-field abilities.
“Just watching film on him every day, he just looks the same. You don’t know what he’s doing,” Burden said. “You don’t know if he’s snapping up (or) breaking in because he’s just running at you so fast and he’s so little.”
For receiver Rome Odunze, it’s been the “nuance of things in his routes.”
“He has the speed to run by folks, but he also has the craftiness to get in and out of breaks and veteran moves when it comes to the top of his routes and different things that we like to look at,” he said.
No one can talk about Raymond’s skill set without mentioning his calling card: speed.
“Fast, talking about gas,” quarterbacks coach J.T. Barrett said. “You got a burner and then with that, he’s going to be smart. He knows the different positions and where he’s supposed to be when you need him to be there. So that trust in order to let the ball go early and knowing he’s gonna be in the right spot, I think that means so much to the quarterback.”
We saw that in Cincinnati. Raymond was running a deep over route from right to left, and Williams floated a high-arcing pass to a spot, placing it right in the arms of his newest wideout.
Raymond endeared himself to Williams in OTAs, not with his 22-mph burners but with how he lifted his quarterback after a rough practice.
“I wasn’t having the best practice,” Williams said in June, “so I got really frustrated and Kalif came up to me and said, ‘Everybody is looking at you.’ That really resonated for me because that’s been something from my first year to now, I want to be as stoic as possible, good, bad or indifferent.”
Later in that joint practice, he found Raymond for a touchdown in the corner of the end zone.
“I know he’s a special player,” Williams said. “I’ve been on the opposite side of the ball from him, and I’ve seen him from the sideline and how explosive he is. Then being able to get him here and his knowledge is really important, one, for the wide receiver room, but him and I when we’re talking, we’re talking ball and talking about what we could’ve done here, what we could’ve done here.
“When we get to the season, it’ll show up because those small moments, those small talks, that open communication that I always talk about is going to show up, and it always does.”
Ask around about Raymond, and two traits come up often, and neither is catching a pass or returning a punt.
“Blocking,” said guard Jonah Jackson, who played with Raymond in Detroit.
Yes, the 5-9, 160-pounder can block.
“He was special in space in punt return and catching the ball, but even more special when he was an insert on duo or plays where he had to go down and lay the hammer on a safety,” Jackson said. “That’s tough to do in Year 12. Some guys lose that ability to want to go block.”
Raymond views his stature as an advantage and uses a basketball analogy to explain.
“If somebody’s going for a layup, you’re on defense, if he’s 6-foot-4, you probably gonna move out of the way. But if he’s 5-8, you’re gonna try to block it and send it to the other side of the court, because he’s shorter,” he said. “So in my head, I think everybody’s looking at me like that. I’m like, ‘OK, that’s OK, but you don’t quit before I do because I’m about to throw my whole existence into you.'”
Then there’s the clearout, a deep route that’s a decoy to stretch the defense deep. Raymond doesn’t just go through the motions when he’s asked to do it.
Raymond puts himself in the shoes of the player running the dagger route or whoever is breaking across the field, more shallow than the clearout.
“You’re not just running a clearout just to run,” Raymond said. “You are legitimately getting your guy open.”
To Barrett, it’s a great example to the young receivers in the room.
“It also teaches the young guys like, ‘Hey, this is part of being a receiver,'” he said. “Like, ‘Hey, it might not be my play on this one,’ but you see him raging down the field like that and be like, ‘Oh, we got to get this guy the ball because he’s helping his guys get open.'”
And Raymond knows with Williams at quarterback, a simple “clearout” could suddenly become an option.
“If he does decide to throw it and I’m on a clearout, you bet your butt I’m ready to catch it, just in case,” he said with a laugh. “The game’s about percentages, and it may be 1 percent, but 1 percent is enough for me.”
When the Bears drafted LSU wide receiver Zavion Thomas in the third round, a speedster who can return kicks, Johnson had a task for him.
“We have a guy named Kalif. I want you to follow him around,” Johnson told him. “I want you to do everything that he does.”
“So that’s what I’ve been doing,” Thomas said. “I’ve been staying on his hip.”
Special teams coordinator Richard Hightower raved about his first meeting with Raymond, a two-time second-team All-Pro returner who still wanted to learn.
“He came right to my office,” Hightower said, “and said, ‘Hey, Coach, I’m looking for the extra 1 percent. So how do we do JUGS here in pre-practice and post-practice? Can I get with the equipment guy? Can I talk to him about that? And I like to do a lot, a lot more, you know.'”
Walker prides himself on getting to practice extra early to work with the JUGS machine and catch passes. Raymond does it before and after practice.
But when Raymond goes above and beyond to get his reps in, he’s not doing it just for himself. He’s looking to be an example for his younger teammates.
“He has zero ‘It’s about me,'” Johnson said. “It’s always about the team and how I can help. I think it’s easy to see that he’s different. He’s a special person.”

full_text:
Receiver Dominic Lovett saw limited snaps last season as a rookie. Where does he fit as the Lions prepare to finalize their roster? Justin Casterline / Getty Images
NFL cutdown day is set for Sunday, Aug. 30, and teams have until 6 p.m. ET to finalize their rosters. On the heels of their final preseason game versus the Colts on Saturday, it’ll be a quick turnaround for the Lions. It makes this final week of practice an important one.
Before roster hopefuls make one final push, here’s a look at where we believe things stand for Dan Campbell, Brad Holmes and the Detroit Lions.
The case for keeping Dobbs over Altmyer is a matter of preference. The Lions typically like an experienced backup to assist Goff on game days and in practice during the week — an extension of the coaching staff. Dobbs is that guy. He’s played for offensive coordinator Drew Petzing, has known Goff for 15 years and is one of the smartest QBs in the league. The case for keeping Altmyer is that he’s been here since OTAs, doesn’t make turnover-worthy throws and can be very accurate when he has time to process.
That said, his pocket feel needs improvement, and he’s never played a regular-season snap. You could make the argument that another team will claim him if the Lions waive him, but only one QB was claimed after cutdown day last year, and that was an experienced backup in Tommy DeVito. Not sure teams will be clamoring to add Altmyer if he’s cut, so the Lions could keep him on the practice squad. Dobbs, meanwhile, could have options elsewhere.
Reserves: Isiah Pacheco, Sione Vaki, Jacob Saylors
Cut: Jabari Small, Trayveon Williams, Raheem Blackshear
Williams had some nice runs in the Washington game, but it might be too late for him to leave an impression here. Gibbs, Pacheco, Vaki and Saylors feel like the final group. Pacheco’s MCL sprain might be worth monitoring, but the Lions seem to think he’ll be ready for Week 1.
Starters: Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jameson Williams, Isaac TeSlaa
Reserves: Greg Dortch, Tay Martin
Cut: Dominic Lovett, Tarik Black, Cedrick Wilson Jr., Malik Cunningham, Tom Kennedy, Lucky Jackson
I went back and forth between five and six receivers, and between the names here. The top four are all locks, but everything after that is murky. Wilson is dealing with a knee injury and Campbell said he’s concerned about it. Martin has earned serious praise from Campbell and special teams coordinator Dave Fipp. I’m going with five and giving the final nod to Martin over Lovett.
Reserves: Brock Wright, Tyler Conklin, Jackson Meeks
Cut: Thomas Gordon, Zach Horton, Miles Kitselman
This room goes from three to four after a hip injury to LaPorta . The Lions are hoping that resting LaPorta will help his availability for Week 1, but Campbell acknowledged he’s not sure if LaPorta will be ready. If that’s the case, I’d expect the Lions to roster four tight ends, with Meeks being the final addition. Meeks just missed my last roster projection, and after a strong preseason performance on both special teams and as a pass catcher, he earns a spot. The Lions like his development after moving him from receiver to TE last season. The fact that he can still play some receiver adds to his value (and makes the idea of five WRs easier to swallow).
Starters (right to left): Blake Miller, Tate Ratledge, Juice Scruggs, Christian Mahogany, Penei Sewell
Reserves: Ben Bartch, Larry Borom, Miles Frazier, Seth McLaughlin
Cut: Mason Miller, Melvin Priestly, Michael Niese, Devin Cochran, Colby Sorsdal
No real changes here. It’s going to be tough for another lineman to work his way into the mix at this point. I’m not sure Frazier has done enough to make the roster, but I see the Lions keeping him as a developmental guard/tackle. Bartch was expected to compete for the starting left guard job, but he was slow to return from a foot injury and is now in concussion protocol. You can safely pencil in Mahogany as a starter.
“That window is shrinking right now,” Campbell said of Bartch’s chances to win the left guard battle. “So, the most important thing is for him to get to where he feels right again and to where he can go. He’s healthy, he feels good and he can start practicing, and then we’ll see. But no, I mean, I think that window is closing quickly.”
Starters: Aidan Hutchinson, Tyleik Williams, Alim McNeill, Tyler Lacy
Reserves: D.J. Wonnum, Derrick Moore, Ahmed Hassanein, Levi Onwuzurike, Skyler Gill-Howard, Ben Stille
Cut: Chris Smith, Eric O’Neill, Payton Turner, Mekhi Wingo, Anthony Lucas, Tyre West, Myles Adams
The defensive line room is almost set. Hutchinson, Williams, McNeill and Lacy have been the first group trotted out since OTAs. Wonnum, Moore and even Hassanein offer a mix of skills in the edge room, and Onwuzurike and Gill-Howard offer pass-rush juice in the interior. Will the Lions go with nine or 10 here? If they go with 10, I’m keeping an eye on Stille. He arrived a bit later, but he’s left an impact in practice and was playing with several starters against Washington. He reminds me of John Cominsky a bit, offering big end/DT capabilities. O’Neill has had a good preseason, too, but he hasn’t been elevated with the first-team defense like Stille, which was my deciding factor.
Starters: Jack Campbell, Derrick Barnes, Devin White
Reserves: Malcolm Rodriguez, Trevor Nowaske
IR to return: Jimmy Rolder
Cut: Damone Clark, Erick Hunter, Joe Bachie, Troy Reeder, Amen Ogbongbemiga
In years past, the Lions have kept six linebackers on their 53-man roster. I’m going with five, but only because it’s hard to get a feel for Rolder’s status. Campbell initially said Rolder would be out “a while,” but it appears Rolder is ahead of schedule and could return to practice by the end of the month or early September. Still, because the Lions have two IR-to-return spots, they could use one on Rolder, allowing him to fully heal and then work him back into the mix. They have a number of capable linebackers who they could add to the practice squad and elevate while Rolder is out. Bachie has caught my eye.
Starters: D.J. Reed, Rock Ya-Sin, Christian Izien (nickel)
Reserves: Nick Whiteside, Ennis Rakestraw Jr., Keith Abney II (nickel), Roger McCreary, Khalil Dorsey
Cut: Aamaris Brown, Ryan Cooper Jr., Ekow Boye-Doe
Cornerback feels pretty unsettled, and eight feels a bit aggressive. If you consider Izien a safety, then think of it as seven corners and four safeties. But Reed and Ya-Sin are locks as outside corners, Dorsey is a special teams lock, Rakestraw is a second-round investment and Abney shows real promise. Whiteside has had a consistent camp — more so than McCreary — so I have him in. McCreary could go either way, but if the Lions want veteran depth, they’ll keep him.
Starters: Chuck Clark, Avonte Maddox
PUP: Kerby Joseph, Brian Branch
Safety is less of a need if Branch is ready by the end of September. Even if he’s still shaking off the rust, he can help this defense. Joseph is more of a wild card, but if he’s on a similar timeline as Branch, he could return by late September/early October. Clark and Maddox are smart veterans who should be able to hold down the fort until the starters return. Harper started games for this unit last year and provides depth, and Izien can also move from nickel to safety in a pinch.
Starters: Jack Fox (punter), Jake Bates (kicker), Hogan Hatten (long snapper)
No change here. This trio is locked in.

title: Patriots 53-man roster projection: Where things stand with one week until cutdown day New England has less than a week — and its final preseason game against the Browns — before cutting its roster down to 53 players. Chad Graff
summary: Patriots 53-man roster projection: Where things stand with one week until cutdown day New England has less than a week — and its final preseason game against the Browns — before cutting its roster down to 53 players. Chad Graff
full_text:
The Patriots are preparing for their final preseason game on Thursday against the Browns in Cleveland. Maddie Meyer / Getty Images
With the New England Patriots resting most of their starters this preseason, we’ve gotten an extended look at the players on the roster bubble. That’s by design. Coach Mike Vrabel said Saturday night after his team’s 24-21 win over the Philadelphia Eagles that he doesn’t feel this roster is very deep, so he doesn’t want to risk starters getting injured.
So expect another week with a lot of reps for backups as attention turns to the preseason finale on Thursday night in Cleveland. The Pats will have only two practices before then. That matchup against the Browns will be a final chance for players to make an impression.
So entering the last week before roster cuts are due Aug. 30, here’s how we see things shaking out.
In: Drake Maye, Tommy DeVito, Behren Morton
Morton made things fun against the Eagles, showcasing his punting ability in addition to playing quarterback in the second half. Morton was also a kicker and punter during his high school days in Texas, so maybe he can convince Vrabel to let him try an extra point on Thursday. Either way, look for a lot of snaps for Morton in the finale.
In: Rhamondre Stevenson, TreVeyon Henderson, Reggie Gilliam, Lan Larison
Out: Jam Miller, Hassan Haskins, JaMycal Hasty
I was tempted to keep only two running backs, considering the team could simply use practice-squad elevations for at least the first two weeks of the season. That’s a possibility, especially if Thursday is a quiet game for Larison. But Vrabel liked the way Larison ran in the second half of Saturday’s game, calling it a “gritty, tough performance.” Thursday’s game will still be important for this competition, but Larison may have done enough against the Eagles to be on the right side of the roster bubble.
In: A.J. Brown, Romeo Doubs, Kayshon Boutte, Mack Hollins, DeMario Douglas, Kyle Williams, Efton Chism
Out: Kyle Dixon, Nick DeGennaro, Cameron Dorner, Kobe Prentice, Tejhaun Palmer
The Patriots seemed to be trending toward keeping seven wide receivers entering Saturday’s game, and that likely solidified it. Chism was impressive and showed he deserves a spot as Douglas’ backup, and Williams caught a 69-yard touchdown that overshadowed some earlier mishaps and highlighted his potential.
In: Hunter Henry, Eli Raridon, Tanner Arkin
Out: Jack Westover, CJ Dippre
Westover has been plenty versatile for the Pats, but they need a true blocker in that No. 3 tight end job, and that’s where Arkin has a big advantage. That said, it’ll be interesting to see whether offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels uses Arkin or Caleb Lomu during the regular season when they want a jumbo tight end in short-yardage situations.
In: Will Campbell, Alijah Vera-Tucker, Jared Wilson, Mike Onwenu, Morgan Moses, Caleb Lomu, Marcus Bryant, Dametrious Crownover, Greg Van Roten
Out: James Hudson III, Mehki Butler, Lorenz Metz, Jacob Rizy, JonDarius Morgan, Darrian Dalcourt, Joe Michalski
The drawback here is that without Brown, there’s no true backup center. But the Patriots likely think they could get Rizy onto the practice squad and activate him when needed. Hudson struggled against the Eagles and may have lost his spot even with the lack of depth at guard — though if Bryant’s ankle injury is serious, it could put Hudson back on the team.
Van Roten provides some much-needed insurance on the interior of the O-line, having started 17 games in each of the last three seasons. For the Pats to avoid the worst-case scenario, they need Wilson to stay healthy and play well.
In: Dre’Mont Jones, Milton Williams, Christian Barmore, Gabe Jacas, Elijah Ponder, Cory Durden, Joshua Farmer, Eric Gregory, Quintayvious Hutchins
Out: Bradyn Swinson, Leonard Taylor III, Jeremiah Pharms Jr., Jesse Luketa, Xavier Holmes, Isaiah Iton, Casey Rogers
Injured: Harold Landry III
Landry still hasn’t practiced all offseason, and it’s now fair to ask whether he’ll open the season on the PUP list, which would force him to miss the first four games. Either way, his absence will test the New England edge rushers. Jacas had some nice moments against the Eagles, but he also had a roughing-the-passer penalty that negated an interception. The big decision may come down to Hutchins or Swinson. When Vrabel talks about a lack of depth, this is one of several areas he’s likely referring to.
In: Robert Spillane, Christian Elliss, K.J. Britt, Namdi Obiazor, Chad Muma
Out: Amari Gainer, Riley Wilson, Khalil Jacobs
The depth here isn’t great either, and it was an issue during joint practices with the Eagles. If Muma and others in this group struggle again this week, perhaps the Patriots will turn to the waiver wire in search of reinforcements.
In: Christian Gonzalez, Carlton Davis III, Marcus Jones, Kindle Vildor, Charles Woods, Karon Prunty
Out: Kobee Minor, Marcellas Dial Jr., Brandon Crossley, Channing Canada, Kenneth Harris
Vildor entered the Eagles game on the roster bubble and was probably the team’s best cornerback. Canada still has an outside chance of making the team and could leapfrog Prunty. It’ll be worth monitoring how each of them plays on Thursday.
In: Kevin Byard, Craig Woodson, Dell Pettus, John Saunders Jr.
Out: Mike Brown, Peter Manuma, Eric Butler
Schooler remains on the PUP list and hasn’t practiced this summer. He’s a big loss to the team’s special teams, but also its safety depth. Saunders keeps making plays in practice and may have earned a roster spot in the last week. Brown had an interception in joint practices against the Eagles, but it may not be enough to beat out Saunders.
In: Andy Borregales, Bryce Baringer, Julian Ashby
An uneventful game for Borregales on Saturday night was a welcome sight after he missed three field goals in the preseason opener.

An improbable Super Bowl run wasn’t enough to earn the New England Patriots the status as “favorites” to win the AFC East. Instead, the rights to that title belong to the Buffalo Bills, whose -136 odds at DraftKings give them a 53 percent implied probability to win the division.

full_text:
Drake Maye and the New England Patriots sit second behind Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills on the AFC East oddsboard. Bryan M. Bennett / Getty Images
An improbable Super Bowl run wasn’t enough to earn the New England Patriots the status as “favorites” to win the AFC East. Instead, the rights to that title belong to the Buffalo Bills, whose -136 odds at DraftKings give them a 53 percent implied probability to win the division.
Meanwhile, the Patriots are +125, a legitimate contender but getting underdog status compared to the Bills. Meanwhile, the New York Jets (+1900) and Miami Dolphins (+4000) are long shots.
Austin Mock, The Athletic ‘s predictive analyst, is projecting a similar forecast. Let’s dive into what his model projects for every AFC East team’s season — and unpack why the Bills are ahead of the Patriots in terms of expectations.
We have to start with the fact the Patriots were a tad overrated in 2025. Sure, they ran through the AFC to finish 14-3 with a Super Bowl appearance, but they played an incredibly soft schedule. It ranked dead last in the league, almost a full win easier than the next team, and about a win-and-a-half easier than average. That’s going to come back to Earth as they play the 20th-ranked schedule.
That said, the Patriots did spend the offseason getting better, especially on offense. They struggled against quality competition last season, having averaged fewer than 17 points in their four playoff games against good defenses. Then they went out and traded for a true WR1 in A.J. Brown, added another pass catcher in Romeo Doubs and boosted the offensive line by signing Alijah Vera-Tucker — that’s three moves to directly address the offensive issues they dealt with in the playoffs.
The Patriots recognized an inefficiency and addressed it. The problem is that the Bills still have Josh Allen. And that’s a sizable edge.
It’s possible that Drake Maye takes another step forward and blossoms into the elite echelon of quarterbacks, but the data doesn’t support that yet. Now, I do think the Bills have a bit of a house of cards as their roster is built heavily around Allen’s arm and legs. And given the additions the Patriots made this offseason, I do think they have a higher ceiling. But we are dealing with averages across thousands of simulations and Allen is a more proven commodity than Maye.
The Patriots are right on the heels of the Bills, but until I see more out of the offense, Buffalo gets the nod as the division favorite for the time being.

full_text:
Philadelphia Eagles backup QB Andy Dalton could be on the roster bubble as cutdown day inches closer. Maddie Meyer / Getty Images
The clock is ticking on roster decisions around the NFL. The Philadelphia Eagles must cut their roster from 91 to 53 by Aug 30 at 6 p.m. ET, and all that’s left to evaluate are the final practices of training camp during the next four days and Friday’s preseason finale.
There’s also the possibility of a Howie Roseman trade — this was the week the Eagles acquired Jahan Dotson in 2024 — that could shake up the roster.
With one additional week of information and evaluation, The Athletic ’s Zach Berman and Brooks Kubena took their third swing at projecting the 53-man roster. (Here’s the first version and second version .)
Kubena (3): Jalen Hurts, Tanner McKee, Cole Payton
The Eagles hedged their bets on the backup job by acquiring Andy Dalton in the offseason. The arrangement inherently limited the training camp reps that could be split between Dalton and Tanner McKee. Still, there was no guarantee McKee would adapt to a very different system from what he’d experienced at Stanford. But McKee showed progress when given more opportunity against the New England Patriots. He was more decisive with his hot reads under pressure. He led a successful five-play, two-minute drill by taking advantage of illusory “short” routes that turned into long gains.
He said more of the playbook was accessed than against the Baltimore Ravens, but the short game seemed to be an emphasis; McKee did not attempt a pass of 10-plus air yards until 6:18 left in the fourth quarter — and he threw just two. McKee’s seven drives suggest he can advance under OC Sean Mannion if given more time to do so. The Eagles can part with Dalton — by trade, if possible — knowing he at the very least served as motivation for McKee.
Berman (3): Jalen Hurts, Tanner McKee, Cole Payton
These three have been my pick since the start of the summer, and Andy Dalton has not done enough to change that. I still think the Eagles would try to trade one of Dalton or McKee. The clock is ticking. Could Roseman carry four on the initial 53-man roster to hold a bluff?
Kubena (3): Saquon Barkley, Tank Bigsby, Will Shipley
Carson Steele just made it very hard for the Eagles to stash him on their practice squad. The hurdling Steele played like all the other 31 teams were watching — and, indeed, their pro scouting departments were. Steele, an undrafted rookie in 2024, will be subject to waivers if the Eagles cut him. I can’t see him making the roster in this crowded position group, and he has not been practicing as an H-back in training camp, suggesting the Eagles wouldn’t file him under the “tight end/fullback” category.
This happens in training camp. Steele’s preseason appearances are essentially job interviews with other teams. He’ll have another one in the preseason finale on Friday against the Cincinnati Bengals.
Berman (3): Saquon Barkley, Tank Bigsby, Will Shipley
This is a quality trio. Barkley is one of the best running backs in the NFL; Bigsby is one of the better No. 2 running backs. If Shipley is third on the depth chart, that’s a good depth chart. The Eagles could stash a veteran such as Dameon Pierce on the practice squad for injury insurance.
Kubena (6): DeVonta Smith, Dontayvion Wicks, Hollywood Brown, Elijah Moore, Makai Lemon, Darius Cooper
I go back and forth on this position group. Last time , I removed Moore. But it doesn’t seem prudent to cut the only wideout who has consistently showcased explosiveness as a deep-ball threat. Moore caught another bomb for a touchdown in joint practices with the Patriots. I think this comes down to the Eagles’ relationship with Moore. His one-year, $1.3 million contract is not guaranteed.
They can persuade him to stick around town as a vested veteran with the understanding that he’d temporarily join the practice squad until another spot opens (or they make use of their in-season elevations). Makai Lemon, who returned to practice last week, under limitations with his hamstring injury, will need time to learn this system before he can be relied upon to make an impact.
Berman (5): DeVonta Smith, Dontayvion Wicks, Makai Lemon, Darius Cooper, Hollywood Brown
Brown has $5 million guaranteed and should be on the roster unless he’s traded. I struggled with the Moore decision, but figured he’s a practice squad candidate for the initial roster, considering he’s a vested veteran without a significant financial obligation. They can elevate him for Week 1 and see how the roster looks thereafter.
Kubena (3): Dallas Goedert, Johnny Mundt, Eli Stowers
Same group as before. The remaining preseason time appears to be a battle for who the Eagles stash on their practice squad. Consider the snap counts against the Patriots: Stone Smartt (25), Cam Latu (22), E.J. Jenkins (21). These are players that, as practice squad elevations, can offer support as blockers.
Berman (4): Dallas Goedert, Johnny Mundt, Eli Stowers, Cameron Latu
This is the discrepancy between Brooks’ 53 and mine, and I don’t write it with much conviction. If the Eagles are going to play with as many heavy packages as I expect, they need depth at tight end. Latu, who also carries value on special teams and as a potential fullback, earned a roster spot last season and would be subject to waivers if he doesn’t make the initial roster. That’s why I put him on here, although I could see Roseman swinging a deal for a tight end or even scanning the waiver wire.
Kubena (10): Lane Johnson, Jordan Mailata, Markel Bell, Fred Johnson, Cam Jurgens, Landon Dickerson, Tyler Steen, Drew Kendall, Willie Lampkin, Micah Morris
The spoken confidence of Sirianni and Mannion about their offensive line depth showed up on film. Lampkin was impressive against the Patriots. Kendall assisted Lampkin on a powerful double-team that paved the way for Will Shipley’s touchdown run. Bell consistently moved people in the run game. Kendall and Bell have both taken reps with the first-team rotation in training camp. Lampkin’s play warrants some first-team looks in the final week of the preseason.
Berman (10): Jordan Mailata, Landon Dickerson, Cam Jurgens, Tyler Steen, Lane Johnson, Fred Johnson, Markel Bell, Drew Kendall, Willie Lampkin, Micah Morris
One of the best developments of the summer has been the progress of the young reserves. Bell, Kendall, Lampkin and Morris have all shown encouraging signs. Bell’s emergence as a potential swing tackle could make Fred Johnson expendable. I still have him on here, but could he be floated as a trade candidate? That would allow the Eagles to further develop Myles Hinton or Cameron Williams, although neither has pushed his way on the right side of this 53 yet.
Kubena (6): Jalen Carter, Jordan Davis, Moro Ojomo, Byron Young, Ty Robinson, Uar Bernard
To borrow defensive coordinator Vic Fangio’s phrasing, Ty Robinson is no longer on life support. He has three sacks in two preseason games and has proven he belongs on an NFL roster. The main question here is if the Eagles think Bernard will pass through the waiver wire. I still do not think Roseman will take the risk. Bernard logged his first two tackles of the preseason against the Patriots.
Berman (6): Jalen Carter, Jordan Davis, Moro Ojomo, Byron Young, Ty Robinson, Uar Bernard
This group is taking shape, with the first five locks. My position on Bernard is unchanged — I believe the Eagles view this as a multi-year investment and would be less inclined to expose him to waivers for another team to assume the experiment. Gabe Hall and Zion Wilson are two players worthy of consideration. They would be prime practice squad candidates if they go unclaimed.
Kubena (6): Jonathan Greenard, Jalyx Hunt, Nolan Smith, Arnold Ebiketie, A.J. Epenesa, Joshua Weru
I am keeping Weru — the Eagles’ other developmental D-lineman from the International Pathway Program. The former member of the Kenyan national rugby team recorded his first sack of the preseason.…

title: Cardinals Say Josh Sweat Could Practice This Week
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals' preseason is nearly over, though outside linebacker Josh Sweat's prep for the 2026 season could just be beginning.
Sweat hasn't practiced at all for the Cardinals in 2026. Not in voluntary team activities, mandatory minicamp or training camp. Sweat was placed on the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list at the beginning of camp and has not played in any of Arizona's three preseason games.
We're roughly three weeks away from Arizona's season opener in Los Angeles. There's hope Sweat will have plenty of practices under his belt — and when speaking with reporters after last night's preseason battle against Dallas, Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur was asked if Sweat could potentially return this week.
“This coming week? Yeah. Josh is doing good," LaFleur said.
“We want all these guys, whether they're injured, they got injured a week ago or obviously in Sweat's case just getting them out there for that first time. We want all those guys back.
"Like I always say with the guys that are edge rushers, they rush the quarterback. It's a little different than the rhythm and timing of a quarterback and (wide) receiver—I’m just being real about it. It's one thing with rhythm, timing and working in combination with an offensive line. It's another thing when you know you are in that stance on third down and you're finding your point.
"(There is) no doubt in my mind (that if) you want to get better at football, you have to be out there in football. There is a little difference in my opinion. Not everyone would agree with me on that.”
The Cardinals have one more preseason game this coming Friday against the Green Bay Packers, though Arizona will hold a joint practice beforehand with Green Bay and likely won't play their starters.
After this week, they'll have a week off before game week arrives for Week 1 against the Chargers.
Whether Sweat, who is protecting a knee injury, will be physically ready to handle a full workload during a game remains to be seen. The Cardinals insist he is working out on his own and in meetings, though it's plausible Sweat could be on a pitch count to begin the year. Arizona rotates their outside linebackers often anyways.
"Josh is making good progress. Josh is getting closer every day," Cardinals general manager Monti Ossenfort said back on Aug. 10. "I think Josh is going to be out there in due time to get ready for the season opener, and we're excited to get him out there and get him going."
The Cardinals have one day of practice on Monday before traveling to Green Bay on Tuesday.

title: Arizona Cardinals Injury Report Following Preseason Week 2 Loss vs Cowboys
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals are happy to get back to Tempe for corrections after a eye-opening 34-13 loss to the Dallas Cowboys in preseason Week 2 action.
The Cardinals emerged with a few bumps and bruises from action at State Farm Stadium, which head coach Mike LaFleur addressed with reporters after the loss.
"(P) Blake Gillikin ended up having a groin (injury), he'll get an MRI tomorrow. ‘Rabbit’ (S Dadrion Taylor-Demerson) with ribs, (WR) Xavier Weaver with a ‘hammy’ (hamstring), (CB) Kei’Trel Clark ended up having a hip (injury), (S) Wydett Williams Jr. and (CB) Kalen King are both getting evaluated for concussions," he said to begin his post-game press conference.
Gillikin, who missed much of 2025 with a back injury, suffered the injury pre-game, which forced Chad Ryland into punting duties for the night.
“(It was) just a groin (injury) when he was warming up. Again, I'll probably have more information in two days," LaFleur said on Gillikin, who is one of the better punters in the league when healthy.
"Obviously in the preseason, I didn't even ask him. If this were Week 1, ‘could you-’, you know, what does it matter?”
LaFleur is unsure if Taylor-Demerson's injury is serious after he went to the ground following a collision.
“I can't answer that right now. I don't think so, but I'll have a better understanding of that tomorrow and then when I'm with you guys in two days," he said. The Cardinals have an off day today before returning to work on Monday.
Weaver was in a yellow non-contact jersey earlier this week during practice while Clark, Williams and King all practiced fine before picking up their injuries.
Williams brought the boom for a big hit during last night's game.
What a hit by Wydett Williams Jr. 😳 DALvsAZ on @nflnetwork Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/W1V4kDuXdI
We even got an update on Sweat, who remains on the PUP list and has yet to step foot on a practice field for the Cardinals in 2026.
“This coming week? Yeah. Josh is doing good," said LaFleur when asked if Sweat could return.
“We want all these guys, whether they're injured, they got injured a week ago or obviously in Sweat's case just getting them out there for that first time. We want all those guys back. Like I always say with the guys that are edge rushers, they rush the quarterback. It's a little different than the rhythm and timing of a quarterback and (wide) receiver.
"I’m just being real about it. It's one thing with rhythm, timing and working in combination with an offensive line. It's another thing when you know you are in that stance on third down and you're finding your point. (There is) no doubt in my mind (that if) you want to get better at football, you have to be out there in football. There is a little difference in my opinion. Not everyone would agree with me on that.”

title: 8 Winners and Losers From Cardinals' Ugly Loss to Cowboys
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals put another preseason game in the books, and it was one to forget.
The Dallas Cowboys marched into State Farm Stadium and easily handled the Cardinals in 34-13 fashion. The two sides mostly rested their starters as one more preseason game looms before final roster cuts arrive.
In spite of the loss, there were still some noticeable winners to pair with some forgettable performances from Saturday.
Eight winners/losers from the Cardinals' loss against Dallas:
Leota has climbed up the Cardinals' outside linebacker depth chart during training camp and very well could have earned himself a roster spot last night. Leota registered a sack with two tackles for a loss and five total tackles — second-highest on the team.
"I thought from my eyes—I have to go back and watch this tape obviously (but) I thought from my eyes (that) this was the most productive he was through the three preseason games," Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur said after the game .
Leota has been a consistent winner for the Cardinals in the last few weeks. Last night only drove that home further.
The Cardinals only played a select group of starters against Dallas with majority resting — so anybody who got some run last night, it wasn't exactly for good reason.
Robinson was in that mix, and it's a fairly glaring endorsement on how the Cardinals' coaching staff views him at this moment in time.
"You can get a lot done in practice, but sometimes the live bullets, not having a script and all that kind of stuff (helps players grow). There are a few guys on the defensive side that we want to get out there in that kind of heightened competitive environment and see what they can do. Not ruling out anything for next week either," LaFleur said on playing Robinson.
Robinson logged one tackle, and the former first-round pick has again yet to make an impact during live action football.
Perhaps one of last night's biggest winners was a player who didn't even suit up.
Knight did not play, as the Cardinals opted to rest their running back — a player who is on the bubble of making the team's final 53-man roster, and his nonparticipation is a great sign of him making the team.
"I think you guys saw that in the first game when we were in Canton, and even last year knowing his running style. (We) just wanted to make sure that we were taking care of him at this point and kind of where we're at in the running back room," LaFleur said when asked about Knight not playing.
Knight feels like a good bet to make the team.
The Cardinals have been begging for somebody in their outside linebacker room to step up, with hopes of Ojulari fully bouncing back from an injury suffered ahead of the 2024 season.
That's yet to happen, and Ojulari has been getting consistently heavy run during preseason games. The combination of extensive looks with minimal production against third-string players simply has not mixed well for Ojulari's chances of making the team – especially with Leota's rise.
Ojulari did have three tackles last night, though he's still unable to reach the quarterback.
The race for Arizona's final receiver spot has been highly competitive through camp and preseason with things mostly being a two-man sprint to the finish between Jalen Brooks and Ihmir Smith-Marsette.
Fehoko didn't leapfrog anybody, though his team-leading 42 receiving yards on two catches was indeed a bright spot for a Cardinals squad that didn't see much of that.
This catch by Simi Fehoko 🔥 DALvsAZ on @nflnetwork Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/mhgVNDjpUr
Fehoko's special teams prowess should also keep him heavily in the mix for a roster spot. On a night where somebody needed to step up, Fehoko certainly did.
It's only preseason, but Rallis is being picked apart by people online after another forgettable outing on the defensive side of the ball.
While a mix of starters played, mostly role players and backups took the field — and fans have simply not been happy with the overall defensive product, which has been copy-and-paste this entire preseason.
The Cardinals' defense was expected to be different after Jonathan Gannon was fired. Thus far, it's been anything but a polished product under Rallis' watch in either run or pass defense.
Sharar's chances of making the roster, thanks to his status as a late-round pick and depth in the inside linebacker's room, will mostly come on special teams and his ability to make an impact there.
Sharar, a specialist at Iowa with over 500 snaps in that phase, has proved to be a playmaker on special teams, and last night was no different after setting the tone on the opening kickoff.
karson sharar is a special teams DEMON 👀 pic.twitter.com/LbF4goVkOX
That's exactly how you make an NFL roster as a Day 3 pick.
The Cardinals, consistently, have had issues with pre-snap penalties this preseason. Officials told reporters they'd be calling games more tightly to prepare teams for the regular season, which is fine, though Arizona's mishaps are mostly happening before the ball is even snapped.
Last night, the Cardinals had eight penalties for 63 yards, and LaFleur clearly was not happy with the operation.
"It’s sometimes a lack of focus. Sometimes (it’s) just other guys being in there that haven't been put in these situations. There are no excuses for it," LaFleur said.
"You guys are going to talk about it more because I'm always going to talk about it. Obviously, you guys are going to be looking for it a little bit more too. I wasn't happy with how we did against Las Vegas. You look at the totality of it, most people would say we were pretty clean that game. Well, not to our standard. If we have one, that's one too many.”

title: 5 Biggest Things Cardinals HC Mike LaFleur Said After Eye-Opening Cowboys Loss
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals were throttled in 34-13 fashion against the Dallas Cowboys, a loss that — even with it being preseason — is sure to generate plenty of talking points entering their final week of preseason ball.
Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur met with reporters after the game. Here's the five biggest things he said:
"I told the guys I thought it was just a culmination of our week. We had a sloppy week of practice. I don't think we've practiced really well over the last week since Las Vegas. I think there have been individuals that have practiced well. I think there have been times where we've done some good things, but overall, it was not good enough. I thought tonight was a summary of that week in general.”
“This coming week? Yeah. Josh is doing good.
“We want all these guys, whether they're injured, they got injured a week ago or obviously in Sweat's case just getting them out there for that first time. We want all those guys back. Like I always say with the guys that are edge rushers, they rush the quarterback. It's a little different than the rhythm and timing of a quarterback and (wide) receiver—I’m just being real about it. It's one thing with rhythm, timing and working in combination with an offensive line. It's another thing when you know you are in that stance on third down and you're finding your point. (There is) no doubt in my mind (that if) you want to get better at football, you have to be out there in football. There is a little difference in my opinion. Not everyone would agree with me on that.”
“He kept the ball in play. I thought he did a good job. The interception was unfortunate because it wasn't a ‘PI’ (pass interference) either—it was a zoning backer with incidental contact on (WR) Simi (Fehoko). Simi almost kept his balance as he was taking a hitch to rip it to an open spot in the soft zone; I thought that would've been a first down on third-and-12. Even to get ourselves in that situation on third-and-17, use the hard count to get the five (yards) there. I said, ‘Hey, you're going to use that hard count. I'll give you a shot to get the first down here.’ That was one of his favorite plays going into it. I like where he ripped it (but) it was just unfortunate that he obviously fell there.”
“I thought Eku did a good job tonight from what I saw. You just said it right there—there has been a lot of good stuff that we've seen throughout camp. I thought from my eyes—I have to go back and watch this tape obviously (but) I thought from my eyes (that) this was the most productive he was through the three preseason games. We'll go back and look at the tape to see if we can confirm that.”
“Yeah, (there is) some good stuff to build on, and we just thought we needed to get a little bit more time with him in real football. That was the reason to get him out there.
“Just the complete package. Like I say with a lot of these guys, (it’s) ‘time on task, value received.’ You can get a lot done in practice, but sometimes the live bullets, not having a script and all that kind of stuff (helps players grow). There are a few guys on the defensive side that we want to get out there in that kind of heightened competitive environment and see what they can do. Not ruling out anything for next week either.”

title: Three Bold Predictions For Cowboys vs Cardinals in Preseason Week 2
full_text:
The Arizona Cardinals and Dallas Cowboys will be kicking off shortly at State Farm Stadium for Week 2 preseason action.
The Cardinals are hoping to give the Red Sea a show for their only home preseason battle of 2026, though the likes of Jacoby Brissett and other starting players won't be suiting up in Arizona. The same will go for the Cowboys, too.
With majority of backups playing , there's bound to space for eye-opening plays to happen — let's throw out some bold predictions for tonight:
This is shaping up to be a massive night in terms of offensive production.
The Arizona Cardinals and Dallas Cowboys both are capable of putting up points thanks to Mike LaFleur and Brian Schottenheimer. With majority of starters not playing for either side, that can lead to some sloppy defense from the Cardinals and Cowboys, respectively.
The result? Points galore, with two strong offensive minds in LaFleur/Schottenheimer running the show. It's preseason. It's vanilla. We get it — though the execution offensively mixed with poor defense leaves the door wide open for plenty of fireworks.
The Cardinals have firmly established their intentions (and ability) to run the ball, and run it well. Arizona, especially with Gardner Minshew and Kedon Slovis, will again look towards their bread and butter to keep the chains moving.
Knight's had an incredibly strong camp and has averaged five yards per carry across Arizona's two preseason games — though he's been unable to find the end zone.
With no Jeremiyah Love and likely no Tyler Allgeier or James Conner, Knight figures to get plenty of reps against Dallas. If he receivers similar opportunities, it could be a big night for Knight.
The Cardinals haven't had a truly electric return game in years, and while that could be the case with Devin Duvernay, it's likely we may not see him tonight.
If we don't, Arizona will deploy Ihmir Smith-Marsette — the backup receiver who is battling for a roster spot and effectively is their No. 2 return man behind Duvernay.
Smith-Marsette is a fast player with long strides, and with opportunities to impact both punt and kick return, he just needs a sliver of daylight to break one loose.
Tonight, we're calling our shot. Smith-Marsette might not house one for a touchdown, but he's a big play waiting to happen.

title: 5 Overlooked Cardinals With the Most to Gain vs. Cowboys
full_text:
The Arizona Cardinals are set to enter tonight's preseason matchup against the Dallas Cowboys with little starters set to take the field.
Head coach Mike LaFleur informed reporters earlier this week only a mix of guys likely to make major contributions will take the field . Exactly who those players are remains to be seen.
Yet that opens the door for hefty playing time for Arizona's backups, players who range from potential role players to bottom of the floor depth guys. With plenty of green grass available tonight, here's five overlooked Cardinals who have the most to gain.
After the injury to second-round pick Chase Bisontis, Gaines has a clear opportunity ahead of him to solidify himself as the immediate fill-in to practically all three interior spots along the Cardinals' offensive line.
Gaines has been running with the second team unit as a center but also has versatility to play both left and right guard. Hayden Conner is shaping up to be his only competition there alongside either Oli Udoh or Matt Pryor.
With a strong performance tonight, Gaines can leave no doubt on who Arizona should turn to if the Cardinals need an interior replacement.
Knight's one of the more heavily debated roster spots , as the Cardinals may or may not keep a fourth running back. With Trey Benson still sidelined with injuries, Knight clearly is over him in terms of roster chances.
Now, it boils down to Knight justifying his spot in the final 53, and that can be done in two ways: offensively and special teams. Not only does Knight need to run the ball well against Dallas, he also needs to prove he can contribute to special teams if he's going to stay up and avoid waivers or the practice squad.
If Knight can do both against the Cowboys, he might very well secure his spot.
We included both players on this list, as we couldn't choose just one. Brooks and Smith-Marsette are the top two leaders in the clubhouse for Arizona's WR6 spot — if they decide to keep a sixth receiver.
Some of that will boil down to roster manipulation and other areas of need, though Brooks and Smith-Marsette both have had respectively good training camp and preseason outings — strong enough to warrant a roster spot.
Brooks is thought to have pole position in the race, though Smith-Marsette also has special teams value as a return man. It's a multi-dimensional battle between those two and fighting against other players who are on the bubble as well.
BJ Ojulari simply hasn't found the form from his rookie season, which has seen the outside linebacker fall somewhat out of favor with the Cardinals' coaching staff. That's opened the door for Eku Leota.
Leota is one of the more surprising names who could make the team, especially given how stacked the room is with returning veterans ahead of him. However, he's had a strong training camp and has earned some first-team snaps with starters.
It's clear the Cardinals are searching for some sort of secondary option opposite of Josh Sweat. Can Leota keep climbing up the roster? A strong performance tonight won't put his name in concrete, though the scale would certainly tip in his favor.

title: Gardner Minshew Could Change His Cardinals Future vs. Cowboys
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals play host to the Dallas Cowboys today, marking what could very well be the final preseason outing of quarterback Gardner Minshew.
Minshew, second-string to starting quarterback Jacoby Brissett, is set to play roughly the first half of tonight's battle at State Farm Stadium according to head coach Mike LaFleur . Kedon Slovis will anchor the second half.
There's typically not much value in preseason games beyond roster evaluation and shaking some rust off, though for Minshew, it could potentially be a defining moment of his Cardinals tenure — and beyond.
Minshew signed as a free agent this offseason on a one-year contract to be the secondary option in the room behind Brissett. Minshew's placement in the pecking order as a backup wasn't up for debate, though the arrival of third-round pick Carson Beck changed the outlook entirely.
Beck — as we previously discussed — will need every opportunity available in either preseason or regular season for the Cardinals to evaluate the rookie passer ahead of next offseason, where the organization could very well entertain another option at football's most important position.
Beck isn't playing tonight due to a ribs injury, though the overall sentiment remains: The Cardinals, whenever possible, will want to see their rookie quarterback.
That leaves Minshew in a precarious position — he's obviously the backup to Brissett while Arizona's front office will need to see Beck in action, leaving the former Pro Bowl passer in somewhat of a purgatory.
Yet uncertainty can bring opportunity, and if Minshew can play well tonight against Dallas, that just might change the outlook of his future in Arizona.
Minshew, by all accounts, would be the most likely trade candidate out of Arizona's quarterback room. Teams typically don't carry three quarterbacks on the active roster, though the organization is essentially forced to do so.
Every year, teams around the trade deadline are looking to rescue their room in some form or fashion. Whether it be replacing a recently injured starter to rescue a playoff push or simply supplementing depth, you'll typically see plenty of buzz and chatter around quarterback moves.
Minshew, thanks to his prior resume, cheap contract and outlook in Arizona, projects as a likely candidate to be moved if/when teams come calling.
When teams begin to explore options, they'll be looking at the most recent film — which will likely be Minshew's performance tonight against Dallas.
A good performance against the Cowboys won't immediately boost his trade value, and a poor outing won't instantly diminish interest from other organizations.
He performed well in Las Vegas, and if he can carry some of that success over tonight, that might just seal his fate as a potential trade target around the league later down the road.

title: 5 Biggest Questions Cardinals Need Answered vs. Cowboys
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals play host to the Dallas Cowboys today for preseason game No. 3 on 2026's schedule.
The Cardinals return to State Farm Stadium for the first time since ending training camp for their lone exhibition battle, as three of their total four preseason games are on the road.
Here's the five biggest things we're watching for when action begins at 7:00 PM AZ time.
The Cardinals' running back depth chart is established, at least at the top. Jeremiyah Love and Tyler Allgeier are 1A and 1B while James Conner figures to be the third back - when healthy.
Bam Knight has an opportunity to firmly establish himself among Arizona's pecking order as RB4, and if the Cardinals do indeed decide to keep four players at the spot, a strong performance from Knight (especially with Trey Benson still out due to injury) can really swing the pendulum in his favor.
That's not just speaking offensively, as he'll need to perform well as a special teams asset to justify his presence on the final 53-man roster.
Similar to running back, the Cardinals' receiver's room will have some tough decisions to be made. All of Marvin Harrison Jr., Michael Wilson and Kendrick Bourne are firmly established while Devin Duvernay and Reggie Virgil are considered to be safe, too.
If the Cardinals want a sixth receiver, that leaves one spot with numerous guys playing well at the moment. All of Jalen Brooks, Ihmir Smith-Marsette and Simi Fehoko are battling for what's considered to be the final receiver spot.
Similar to Knight, special teams will also play a factor in any of the aforementioned players making the roster. Brooks has been gaining momentum lately for the job after Smith-Marsette was training camp's early leader in the clubhouse.
Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur said some starters will play while others won't. We know Jacoby Brissett won't participate, though most others (not related to injury at least) are still up in the air.
Who plays could be particularly telling, as it won't exactly be a glaring endorsement on those who will find themselves on the field for either depth chart or overall roster reasons.
Pay attention to whatever big names are playing tonight, it could be more meaningful than you think – especially with starters very likely not participating in next week's finale against Green Bay.
Darius Robinson and BJ Ojulari both entered the desert as high draft picks with potential that's been unfulfilled thus far. A mix of injuries and inability to impact the quarterback have held back the defensive end and outside linebacker, respectively.
Robinson and Ojulari both failed to impress last week in Las Vegas. Robinson again has had a strong training camp but didn't make noise against the Raiders while Ojulari, playing in both of Arizona's preseason battles thus far, hasn't quite been able to find his rookie season form.
One (if not both) needs to step up against the Cowboys to show some sign of progress ahead of their respective 2026 seasons. Back to back underwhelming performances won't cut it for either side.
The Cardinals' front seven needs somebody to emerge, and Robinson/Ojulari are near the top of that list.
Garrett Williams was activated off the PUP list this week, giving the Cardinals a much-needed boost in the secondary. Williams will man slot corner duties while also getting run in base sets opposite of Will Johnson.
Yet how will Arizona deploy its third cornerback when using Williams in the slot for 11 personnel matching? All of Denzel Burke, Starling Thomas, Max Melton, Sean Murphy-Bunting, Elijah Jones, and Kei'Trel Clark are battling for not only playing time, but also roster spots in yet another competitive room.
There hasn't quite been any standout performances thus far. If the Cardinals can get somebody — anybody — to elevate their game against the Cowboys, that might just help clear up the picture in some form or fashion.

title: Jack Strand Shines at QB for Atlanta Falcons Despite Limited Practice
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons ' biggest questions this season revolve around the quarterback position. Who will be the starter? Can Tua Tagovailoa or Michael Penix Jr. stay healthy for an entire season? Can either of them be the long-term answer for the Falcons after struggling in 2025?
While those questions remain unanswered, the Falcons find themselves near the bottom of any kind of power rankings, even future power rankings that try to look four seasons down the road.
While the focus has been on Tagovailoa and Penix, the Falcons got an unlikely boost from undrafted free agent Jack Strand in Saturday's convincing 34-6 win over the Indianapolis Colts.
The Falcons spent last week in Indianapolis and had a pair of joint practices with the Colts that included the bulk of the first-team reps. With Tagovailoa and Penix splitting the opportunities, there was little work for Strand as he watched.
When he got his chance on Saturday against the Colts' second and third team, he shined. At 6'5 and 240 pounds with a strong arm and quick release, Strand has stood out since being signed by the Falcons out of Minnesota State University Moorhead (MSUM).
On Saturday, he kicked it up a notch.
Strand was 12 of 17 for 212 yards and a touchdown. He added another 16-yard rushing touchdown. At one point, Strand was 8/8 for 155 yards, a touchdown, and a perfect 158.3 passer rating.
. @AtlantaFalcons QB Jack Strand throws for 212 yards and scores 2 touchdowns in Preseason Week 2 🔥 pic.twitter.com/FVGq6WtkyV
Head coach Kevin Stefanski was impressed with not just Strand's performance, but his maturity in being able to learn and then thrive, despite being a spectator most of the week in practice.
"I think any quarterback gets great mental work when they're not out there," Stefanski said after the game on Saturday. "Jack didn't have a ton of reps in those joint practices, but he's getting every rep, both when he's watching it the first time and then when he's paying attention to the meeting room.
"He's getting that mental rep. So, he's somebody that can get better that way, which I think is a great attribute for young players, period. Certainly, at the quarterback position, I think you can apply a lot of those lessons learned. I saw that tonight from Jack.”
Having success against the Colts' reserves is a far cry from facing the Broncos' first-team defense in the Falcons' first preseason game, but Strand and the rest of the offense could only play who was put in front of them.
Atlanta outgained the Colts 461 yards to 164. They were 9 of 17 on third down compared to 1 of 11 for Indianapolis.
While Strand was the star of the show, the Falcons also got good play in the first half from Cooper Rush who was an efficient 10 of 11 passing for 86 yards.
“I thought the quarterback position, in total, both those guys made good decisions," Stefanski said. "I thought there were some unique looks that we got in the game that we really haven't seen a ton of, if you will, in the last week or so, and I thought they both saw it clearly. The ball went where the ball was supposed to go the majority of the time.”
The ball went into the end zone four times, and kicker Nick Folk added a pair of 50+ yard field goals for good measure.
Coaches often talk about complementary football, and the Falcons showed what that looked like on Saturday. Offense, defense, and special teams came together for a dominating win . Sure, it's just preseason, but there haven't been enough of those games in Atlanta in any season lately.
The Falcons only kept two quarterbacks last year on their initial 53-man roster , but at this point, it will be a shock if Strand isn't on the team after roster cutdowns next Sunday.

title: 3 Winners and 3 Losers From Falcons' Dominant Win Over Colts
full_text:
The Atlanta Falco ns needed a response after a disappointing preseason opener and delivered one Saturday.
Atlanta dominated the Indianapolis Colts 34-6, showing considerably more energy and physicality after spending the week in Indianapolis for two joint practices. The victory also provided another important opportunity for players competing for roster spots to make their final impressions before cut day arrives.
With several position battles still unsettled, here are three winners and three losers from Atlanta's preseason victory.
Goodson continues to make his case for a roster spot.
The running back was one of Atlanta's most explosive offensive players Saturday, breaking loose for a 49-yard touchdown and providing the type of big-play ability the Falcons have seen from him throughout training camp.
His performance is particularly important because Atlanta's running back room has become more competitive following Trey Sermon's placement on injured reserve.
Goodson has consistently shown the ability to create explosive plays, and Saturday was another reminder that he shouldn't be overlooked when Atlanta makes its final roster decisions.
The Falcons already know what they have in Bijan Robinson and Brian Robinson Jr. The question is who will earn the next spot.
Goodson is making a strong argument that it should be him.
Strand may have been the biggest winner of the afternoon.
The undrafted rookie quarterback put together another impressive performance, completing 12 of 17 passes for 212 yards and a touchdown while also rushing for a 16-yard score. He also delivered several impressive throws downfield, including a 36-yard completion.
Strand's performance continues to make the QB3 competition much more interesting.
Cooper Rush entered camp with the experience advantage, but Strand has repeatedly shown poise and playmaking ability. He now has legitimate momentum heading into the final preseason game.
Atlanta's quarterback room could look very different depending on what happens over the next two weeks.
And Strand is making sure the Falcons have a difficult decision to make.
Daniels continues to be one of the most intriguing young players on Atlanta's roster.
The rookie linebacker has been making plays throughout training camp and the joint practices, and Saturday gave him another opportunity to show that his development is translating to game action.
Daniels' emergence is especially important because Atlanta has been evaluating several players at linebacker while dealing with injuries elsewhere in the group.
He is giving the coaching staff a reason to consider getting him on the field sooner rather than later.
For a young player trying to earn a role, Daniels has done exactly what he needed to do during the preseason: make himself difficult to ignore.
Ojulari needed to stand out Saturday. Instead, he was relatively quiet.
That doesn't mean Ojulari played poorly, but in the current state of Atlanta's edge-rusher room, simply being solid isn't necessarily enough. The Falcons need someone to emerge after losing Jalon Walker for the season with a torn ACL and facing an eight-game suspension for James Pearce Jr.
Ojulari was expected to be one of the players capable of helping fill that void.
Saturday presented another opportunity to make that case, and he didn't consistently create the kind of impact that would separate him from the rest of the group.
That matters because players such as Keshawn Banks, Cameron Sample, Bralen Trice and others are trying to take advantage of the opportunities created by Atlanta's depleted edge room.
The Falcons recently added veteran Za'Darius Smith, further increasing the competition for snaps and roster spots.
Ojulari has the talent to be an important piece of this defense.
But with Walker out and Pearce unavailable for the first eight games, Atlanta needs its edge rushers to show they can create pressure.
The door is wide open. Someone needs to walk through it.
Tagovailoa didn't play Saturday, but that doesn't mean the questions surrounding him disappeared.
If anything, the quarterback situation became more interesting.
Tagovailoa struggled in Atlanta's preseason opener and then had an uneven start during the Falcons' first joint practice against Indianapolis. He improved during the second practice, but the overall evaluation remains incomplete.
Meanwhile, Michael Penix Jr. continues working his way back from his knee injury.
Penix has now been cleared to return to 11 on 11 work and that will now add to the competition.
That creates a potentially fascinating QB1 situation.
Tagovailoa currently has the advantage because he's healthy and has been able to participate. But if Penix returns and performs well, the Falcons could suddenly have a much more serious decision on their hands.
Tagovailoa needed to take control of the job.
His recent performances haven't completely accomplished that.
The next time he takes the field, the pressure will be even greater.
Harris wasn't necessarily a loser because of something he did Saturday.
He was a loser because of what happened around him.
The Falcons' projected starters weren't slated to play against Indianapolis, but Harris entered the game in the second quarter. That is notable because Harris has been working with the starting defense and is currently projected to be one of Atlanta's starting linebackers.
If Harris were firmly established as the unquestioned starter, there wouldn't be much reason to see him in a preseason game when most of the projected starters were being held out.
Instead, the Falcons gave him additional evaluation time.
And that's because the linebacker room is becoming much more competitive.
Daniels has continued to make plays throughout camp, while Harold Perkins Jr. has also shown flashes of the athleticism that made him such an intriguing addition to the Falcons' defense.
Harris still has the inside track to start.
But the gap may not be as wide as it appeared when training camp began.
The Falcons have young linebackers pushing for opportunities, and Harris now has to continue proving that he deserves to remain at the top of that competition.
The Falcons now have one more preseason game before the real roster decisions begin.
That game against Miami will be an important opportunity for the coaching staff to finish evaluating the roster and determine which players have done enough to earn a spot.
For players such as Goodson, Strand and Daniels, Saturday helped their cases.
For players such as Ojulari and the other edge rushers, there is still work to be done.
And then there are the bigger questions surrounding the quarterback room, where Penix's potential return could add another layer to the QB1 competition while Strand continues to push for QB3.
Next week represents one of the final opportunities for players to put something on tape before cut day is upon the Falcons.
At this point in the preseason, every snap matters.

title: Falcons Provide Major Update on QB Michael Penix Jr.
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons ’ quarterback battle is finally about to become a true competition.
Head coach Kevin Stefanski announced after the preseason game that Michael Penix Jr. has been cleared to participate in 11-on-11 work, removing the biggest obstacle that has prevented Atlanta from fairly evaluating Penix and Tua Tagovailoa for the starting quarterback job.
Penix has spent much of training camp working his way back from a knee injury that ended his 2025 season. He has participated in individual drills and 7-on-7 periods, but he had not been cleared for full-team work. That changes now.
For much of camp, the Falcons haven't been able to make a true comparison between their two quarterbacks.
Tagovailoa has been participating in full-team periods, playing in preseason action and gaining valuable experience in Kevin Stefanski and Tommy Rees' offense. Penix, meanwhile, has been limited while completing his rehabilitation.
Now Penix can finally operate in the same environment as Tagovailoa.
That means working against a live pass rush, navigating protections, making decisions under pressure and operating the offense in 11-on-11 situations.
Those are critical parts of evaluating a quarterback that simply can't be replicated in 7-on-7 work.
The Falcons can finally begin making a more complete comparison.
Tagovailoa still has an advantage because of the experience he has gained in Atlanta's offense and his ability to participate fully throughout camp.
However, he hasn't completely eliminated the questions surrounding the position.
Tagovailoa's preseason debut against Denver was underwhelming, and his first joint practice against Indianapolis wasn't particularly strong either. He did show improvement during the second joint practice, but the overall evaluation remains incomplete.
That makes Penix's return even more significant.
If Tagovailoa had consistently dominated throughout camp, Penix's return might have been less threatening to his position.
Instead, there remains an opportunity for Penix to make this a legitimate competition.
Penix doesn't need to immediately win every practice. His first priority will be showing the Falcons that he is physically ready to handle full-team work.
Once that is established, the evaluation becomes about performance.
Can Penix consistently move the offense? Can he handle pressure? Can he make the downfield throws that made him such an intriguing prospect coming out of Washington?
Those answers could determine whether he has a legitimate chance to reclaim the starting job. The Falcons still have time before the regular season, but not much.
Penix's clearance means the QB1 competition is no longer hypothetical. For the first time this offseason, Atlanta can truly evaluate both quarterbacks side by side.
And now, the pressure is on both Tagovailoa and Penix to prove they should be the ones leading the Falcons into Week 1.
