title: Cowboys Rookie Delivers Epic Postgame Speech Amid Historic Stint With Dallas
full_text:
It has been a historic year for Dallas Cowboys undrafted rookie and offensive tackle Shiyazh Pete.
Pete, who was signed by the Cowboys following the 2026 NFL Draft, is the first NFL player of Navajo heritage and played his second preseason game on Saturday night with in front of thousands of Navajo in attendance in Arizona.
The Kentucky product saw the field for six snaps in total and did not allow a pressure in what a was a strong showing for him.
Following the game, Pete delivered what can only be described as an epic speech in the locker room in front of his teammates.
"Well, that was an incredible win," Pete said. "I am very fortunate to be amongst you and to play on the same field, wear the same star, hold it on our chest, and I'm proud of us. Proud of how far we've come."
"This game, fate, brought us here as strangers, but this game, this star, this team will make us brothers," he concluded, which rightly drew a raucous reaction from his teammates.
this game, this star, this team will make us brothers 🗣️ pic.twitter.com/rEcvDTzSkd
If you don't have goosebumps after that last line, check yourself for a pulse.
Pete received a warm welcome from the Navajo in attendance and even received a standing ovation as he entered the game.
“The standing ovation was incredible,” Pete said, according to Nick Harris of the Fort Worth Star-Telegram . “I want to thank all of the fans that showed up to support me and wear my jersey. I lost count of how many Navajo Nation flags I saw. It was awesome.”
“I saw hope and courage,” Pete added. “It’s definitely etched in the history books. It was incredible. I’m just trying to find the words of how special and impactful that was."
“It was really cool to see him have that moment, but also our players to join in and helping to celebrate him,” head coach Brian Schottenheimer said. “That was really cool. I hadn’t seen that before. I’m really proud for him and for what he’s done for us.”
Given the fairly crowded situation the Cowboys have along the offensive line, Pete's chances of making the 53-man roster are slim.
However, there is always a chance he's kept on the practice squad, something the Cowboys should definitely consider if for no other reason than his postgame speech abilities.
Regardless of what his future holds, nobody can take away his special journey in the NFL. We will no doubt be rooting for him, regardless of where he ends up.

title: Top 4 Dallas Cowboys Trade Candidates Entering Preseason Week 3
full_text:
Every year, some tough decisions must be made as teams trim their rosters from 90 to 53 ahead of the regular season. That will be the case for the Dallas Cowboys this year, especially after they added plenty of depth during the offseason.
The new faces will make it hard for several of their returning contributors to make the roster in Week 1. Many of those players who are on the bubble have proven they can be contributors at the NFL level, meaning they will get a chance to shine elsewhere if Dallas moves on.
Some of the bubble players are also talented enough to warrant trade consideration. Here's a look at four such players, who the Cowboys could potentially find trade partners for ahead of roster cutdowns.
Markquese Bell was held out of the second preseason game, which is a strong indicator that he's going to make the 53-man roster. It could also mean that Dallas didn't want to expose him to a potential injury in case they wanted to use Bell in trade talks .
The former undrafted free agent has been a reliable player in an ever-changing secondary and even showed enough versatility to play linebacker under Dan Quinn. Ideally, he would make the roster, but if the Cowboys are facing some tough cuts (and they will be) he could be someone other teams would show interest in.
Jonathan Mingo has made things very interesting this summer. He's been turning in one solid performance after another, and recorded a 53-yard touchdown on Saturday to remind everyone why he was a second-round pick in 2023. He's still fighting for a spot on a crowded depth chart, and could be someone other teams are willing to bring in to shore up their receiving corps.
As soon as the Cowboys added Von Miller, Marist Liufau's spot on the roster became incredibly shaky. That's why Cowboys On SI's Josh Sanchez named Liufau the most obvious trade candidate following the Miller signing.
After playing a traditional linebacker role during his first two seasons, Liufau moved to the edge under Christian Parker. To his credit, he's shown progress every week, but the depth is too much for him to make the 53-man roster which is why he could be shopped to avoid losing him and getting nothing in return.
A second-round pick in 2023, Luke Schoonmaker has yet to live up to his draft status. Schoonmaker has fallen behind Brevyn Spann-Ford on the depth chart, but he's been able to perform well when given a chance. That included Saturday night when he made one catch for 19 yards before taking a seat.
The question now is whether he beats out Michael Trigg for the TE3 spot. If Trigg has the edge, the Cowboys would be wise to see if a team in need of help at the position would give up a Day 3 pick for Schoonmaker.

title: Cowboys' Top 5 PFF Grades Include Roster-Saving Performance From Jonathan Mingo
full_text:
In Week 2 of the NFL preseason, the Dallas Cowboys pulled off an impressive 34-13 victory over the Arizona Cardinals.
There was no shortage of standouts in this one, with multiple Cowboys doing themselves a favor as they fight for a roster spot. One player who may have saved his spot with his play on Saturday night was wide receiver Jonathan Mingo, who entered this year on the bubble .
Throughout the offseason, Mingo has been a star and that has been the case in the preseason as well. In Week 1, he had 20 yards on two receptions, which was a solid start. This weekend, he was even better with two receptions for 62 yards and a touchdown. That score was a 53-yard dime from Joe Milton III and was the first time Mingo scored in the NFL, regular or preseason.
Mingo's play wasn't just impressive in the stat sheet either. According to Pro Football Focus, he was one of the best players on the team, with Mingo earning a grade of 84.4. That placed him firmly in the middle of the top-five graded Cowboys in Week 2 of the preseason .
1. Jaishawn Barham: 89.9 2. Ajani Cornelius: 86.7 3. Jonathan Mingo: 84.4 4. Sam Williams: 84.3 5. Phil Mafah: 83.4
Dallas also has undrafted rookie Camden Brown proving himself worthy of a spot. Initially, the two were fighting for the WR5 position, but at this point, the Cowboys might decide to keep six. For Mingo, that would be huge as he's still out to prove Jerry Jones made the right call trading for him at the deadline in 2024.
As impressive as it was to see Mingo play well on offense, no one st ood out more than Jaishawn Barham . The rookie linebacker wore the green dot on Saturday and was all over the field. Barham recorded five tackles, one for a loss, and seeing him as the top-graded player is unsurprising, to say the least.
He was joined in the top five by Sam Williams, who is on the bubble, and recorded one sack. Williams might still be in danger, but this weekend helped his cause.
On offense, Mingo was joined by backup offensive tackle Ajani Cornelius, who could be in line for a spot as a backup tackle following his stellar preseason. Phil Mafah also did well, recording a late touchdown, although he's still behind Malik Davis and Jaydon Blue.

title: Joe Milton Flips Cowboys' QB2 Battle on its Head After Dominating in Preseason Week 2
full_text:
We have a new leader in the clubhouse for the QB2 job after Dallas Cowboys quarterback Joe Milton was outstanding against the Arizona Cardinals in preseason Week 2 on Saturday night.
Milton, who was trailing in the race going into the preseason but tightened the gap last week , completed 9-of-13 passes for 179 yards and two touchdowns to no picks, and he added a rushing score for good measure.
But Milton could have had more if not for tight end Zack Kuntz dropping a pass on the opening drive that prevented another scoring opportunity for the Tennessee product.
Compare Milton's night to fellow signal-caller Sam Howell, who went 7-for-10 for 65 yards with one interception.
Through two preseason games, Milton has easily been the better player. He outperformed Howell with the lesser unit in preseason Week 1, and he did the same with the twos on Saturday night.
Through two preseason games, Milton has completed 75% of his passes for 289 yards and four total touchdowns. Meanwhile, his counterpart, Howell, has a 68.2% completion rate for 159 yards and one touchdown to one pick.
It's more than just about the numbers for Milton, though. He has clearly shown improved pocket presence, decision-making and touch when throwing the rock.
Just look at these two throws, which were Milton's best of the night.
He showed both his big arm and touch on the 53-yard dime to wide receiver Jonathan Mingo. Later on, Milton threw on the run and across his body while escaping pressure from Cincinnati to set wide receiver Camden Brown up for a 70-yard gain.
Joe Milton III put his arm on full display tonight 🚀 9/13, 179 YDS, 3 Total TDs, 0 INT. What team needs to call up Dallas for Milton? pic.twitter.com/U1Nq7Drx8c
Safe to say, head coach Brian Schottenheimer was impressed with his backup quarterback.
"Joe has put together two really, really good halves," Schottenheimer said after the game.
"This game is about being able to control the RPMs of the football and throw it with different speeds and touches and he's done that at a really high level. But I thought the scramble to his left to Cam was a big play as well, and then he was able to get (into the end zone) with his legs as well," Schottenheimer added.
When the Cowboys added Howell earlier this offseason, that was no doubt a bad sign for Milton , who looked like he would succumb to the competition earlier in training camp.
Now, Milton looks like the superior quarterback over Howell and he would easily be the QB2 if 53-man roster cuts were today.

title: CeeDee Lamb Victim of $300K Robbery During Dallas Cowboys Training Camp
full_text:
The Dallas Cowboys took one step closer toward beginning the 2026 campaign following Saturday's 34-13 road win over the Arizona Cardinals in the second game of the preseason.
Dallas has officially left the Oxnard portion of training camp and will now head back to Frisco, TX in high spirits after a convincing preseason victory.
But right before kickoff at State Farm Stadium against Arizona, Cowboys wide receiver CeeDee Lamb was involved in some unfortunate headlines.
Lamb had his Fairview, TX home in the Dallas-Fort Worth area burglarized on July 30, per reports from Nick Harris of The Fort Worth-Star Telegram. The incident occurred during the team's fourth day of training camp in Oxnard and the second day of practice.
Over $300,000 worth of belongings were taken from Lamb's home, including four luxury bags, according to Harris.
There are no known suspects attached to the case nearly a month after its occurrence. Lamb and the rest of the team are getting a chance to return back to the Dallas area on Sunday, meaning he will finally be able to step foot in his home for the first time since the crime was committed.
Lamb is hardly the only notable NFL player who has had his home burglarized since 2024. The list includes some of the biggest names in the league.
Here are some members of the unfortunate list that Lamb is now a part of:
- Chiefs QB Patrick Mahomes and TE Travis Kelce (2024) - Bengals QB Joe Burrow (2025) - Eagles RB Saquon Barkley (2026) - Former Seahawks CB Richard Sherman (2025)
Many of the most notable robberies toward professional athletes over the past two years have been a result of what authorities say is the work of a crime ring.
At this point, it's unclear if the burglary at Lamb's residence has any connection to the string of incidents at the homes of other NFL players.
Though it's never comfortable knowing that someone else broke into your home, Lamb's current four-year, $136 million contract should certainly help ease any stress that comes with the financial loss.
He will look to close out training camp and preseason on a high note before the Cowboys visit the New York Giants in Week 1 on Sept. 13.

title: Dallas Cowboys Injury Report Following Preseason Week 2 Win Over Cardinals
full_text:
The Dallas Cowboys escaped their preseason Week 2 win over the Arizona Cardinals mostly unscathed when it comes to injuries.
We know of one player who left the game early and that was safety Julius Wood, who suffered a concussion. He'll now be entering the protocol this week.
"Julius Wood (concussion) is ruled out of this game by the Cowboys," Patrik Walker of DallasCowboys.com wrote.
Linebacker Curtis Robinson was another player who appeared to be shaken up during the game, but based on an observation from Nick Harris of the Fort Worth Star-Telegram , Robinson looked to be OK after the play.
"Cowboys LB Curtis Robinson was down but popped up and jogged off after being looked at by the training staff," Harris reported. "Looks to be OK."
Wood started at safety in preseason Week 2 and recorded four tackles and two run stops, according to Pro Football Focus .
He posted the sixth-best overall grade on defense (73.3) and was tops in tackling grade (86.5), second in run defense grade (76.7) and eighth in coverage grade (63.5). Wood has been having an outstanding offseason and will leave the Cowboys with a very difficult decision to make at safety.
Robinson recorded one tackle and shined in run defense with the fourth-best grade in that area (74.0). He has also been impressive during training camp and could find his way onto the 53-man roster or practice squad as a result.
The Cowboys have no doubt seen some injuries during training camp and the preseason, but they have avoided anything catastophic, which is great news.
Linebacker Jaishawn Barham and cornerbacks Devin Moore and Zion Childress all suited up after missing last week's game due to injury, according to Nick Harris.
Barham was an absolute menace in his preseason debut, with the third-round pick tallying five tackles, including one for loss, three run stops and one pressure.
The rookie has been hyped up when on the field at training camp and he showed exactly why that's the case on Saturday night.
Running backs Jaydon Blue, Phil Mafah and Israel Abanikanda were able to play, also, after dealing with injuries following last week's game.
Defensive lineman Jonathan Bullard remains sidelined and has now missed both preseason games and a ton of time in camp.
Along with Bullard, tight ends Michael Trigg and DJ Rogers were both inactive because of injuries. Trigg got hurt in preseason Week 1 and Rogers got hurt at practice last week.
Head coach Brian Schottenheimer noted during the week that there is no concern for Trigg's toe injury.

title: Every Cowboys Player Who Helped Their Roster Chances Against Cardinals
full_text:
It was a lopsided game in the desert as the Dallas Cowboys handed the Arizona Cardinals a 34-13 defeat in front of their home crowd.
The Cowboys were the more aggressive team throughout this one, showing more urgency on both sides of the ball. They're now 2-0 and have one final preseason game remaining, as they face the New Orleans Saints in Week 3.
Before turning our attention to that one, let's take a look at several players who stood out against Arizona and made a case for their spot on the Cowboys 53-man roster.
Entering the offseason, Jonathan Mingo seemed to have one foot out the door. Mingo has appeared in 14 regular-season games since being added in a trade during the 2024 season and has had just six receptions on 21 targets for 71 yards.
Mingo then put together a strong training camp and has been playing well in the preseason. On Saturday, he even recorded his first career touchdown, in the regular season or preseason, hauling in a beautiful deep ball from Joe Milton for a 53-yard score.
Joe Milton LAUNCHES it for a 53-yard TD pass to Jonathan Mingo 🚀 DALvsAZ on @nflnetwork Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/3LgWRZrsii
Mingo's primary competition for a roster spot in Dallas is undrafted free agent Camden Brown. The Georgia Southern product burst onto the scene with two touchdown receptions in Week 1 of the preseason. This weekend, he picked up where he left off, taking a pass over the middle of the field from Joe Milton and turning it into a 69-yard gain.
Joe Milton to Camden Brown for a 69-yard gain! DALvsAZ on @nflnetwork Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/spfULphQa4
Brown fumbled the ball when extending for the goal line, but was fortunate to see it go out of bounds. Even with the fumble, it was another great sign for Brown, who ran an excellent route and gave his team the ball at the one-yard line. Brown had a second catch, which was rather impressive as well, as he took a massive hit but held onto the ball.
Unfortunately, a concussion forced Julius Wood to end his night early, but he made an impact before leaving. Wood had seven tackles and was involved in multiple run stops. He's proven to be a fearless player who excels when attacking the ball. There are still multiple safeties ahead of him in Dallas, but Wood deserves to be on an NFL roster in 2026.
Sam Howell had the upper hand in the QB2 battle one week ago, but that's no longer the case. Milton got the start against Arizona and was calm and efficient throughout the first half.
Milton complete 9-of-13 passing attempts for 179 yards with two touchdown passes. He added another touchdown on the ground, and led the Cowboys into halftime with a 24-13 lead. Howell is still in the fight, but Milton took the lead back on Saturday night.

title: 6 Winners & 2 Losers From Cowboys Win vs. Cardinals in Preseason Week 2
full_text:
It's still the preseason, so we need to avoid overreacting, but the Dallas Cowboys look like a completely different team in 2026 than what we saw in 2025.
Dallas couldn't buy a stop last year, but under new defensive coordinator Christian Parker , they appear far more competent. Again, these are exhibition games, but it's still very encouraging to see everyone on the same page and playing hard.
Offensively, the Cowboys have to be just as happy. Even without playing their starters, the offense has made it look easy, especially on Saturday night against the Arizona Cardinals. The Cowboys were able to run away with one against the Arizona Cardinals, 34-13. There was no shortage of players to praise, so some will be left out, but here's a look at some of the winners and losers for Dallas in their Preseason Week 2 win.
A fourth-round pick out of Alabama, LT Overton might be one of the more undervalued rookies from the Cowboys' impressive draft class. Known for his work as a run-stuffer, Overton has flashed as a pass rusher during camp, and on Saturday, he recorded his first sack, which he followed with a Karate Kid celebration, which was a win in itself.
first career sack for @LebbeusO 🔥 📺: #DALvsAZ on CBS11 📲: Stream on NFL+ https://t.co/7pAfvQ9tid pic.twitter.com/7dRtDwdRfg
Overton's sack came on third and goal, forcing the Cardinals to end a promising drive with a field goal instead of a touchdown.
The depth behind Quinnen Williams and Kenny Clark has been questioned, but if Overton can play the way he did against Arizona, there's no reason to panic.
Malik Davis played late in the game last week, but was with the starters on Saturday and looked just as competent. He had 29 yards rushing on five attempts and scored the opening touchdown, catching a third-down pass from Joe Milton and taking it in for an eight-yard score. As Nick Harris said, he even proved his worth in blitz protection during the first quarter.
the offense turns the INT into a TD 💪 #DALvsAZ | @Campaign_Lik 📺: #DALvsAZ on CBS11 📲: Stream on NFL+ https://t.co/7pAfvQ9tid pic.twitter.com/3TOSx2hFAw
Davis fumbled at the end of a kick return, but as a runner, he was excellent. At this point, he has to be the favorite for the RB2 job.
Sam Howell had a good game in Week 1, but wasn't as sharp in Week 2. Coming into the game in the second half after Joe Milton started, Howell wasn't able to create explosive plays the way Milton did in the first half. He also had an ugly red zone interception in the fourth quarter. Howell threw off his back foot while facing pressure, tossing a 50-50 ball toward Anthony Smith, but Arizona defensive back Isaiah Oliver came down with the ball instead.
Malik Davis wasn't the only running back to stand out in this one. Jaydon Blue looked more comfortable in the offense than he has at any point in his career and led the team with 75 yards on 15 attempts. It was the exact type of game he needed to give himself confidence heading into year two.
Dallas had a promising opening drive that went 66 yards on 12 plays, but ended in frustration. The Cowboys went for it on fourth-and-one, and Joe Milton made a good play -fake and a decent throw to tight end Zack Kuntz, who was unable to bring it in . He also had another pass go through his hands late in the first quarter, but the Cowboys still got a first down there as the Cards were called for unnecessary roughness on the play.
Kuntz had a great opportunity to make an impact, with injuries limiting the Cowboys to just two active tight ends (Kuntz and Luke Schoonmaker), and he let that slip through his fingers.
Shavon Revel has been one of the hottest names throughout training camp for the Cowboys, and on Saturday, he had his best showing as a pro. Revel was flagged for illegal contact early on the opening drive, but made up for that by recording an interception off Gardner Minshew to set up the Dallas offense for their first touchdown of the game.
Revel was taken out of the game after that as rookie Devin Moore replaced him. The Cowboys saw enough and are likely ready to let Revel watch for the rest of the preseason.
Rookie third-round pick Jaishawn Barham made his debut on Saturday night and was given a huge responsibility. Barham was given the "green-dot" duties , meaning he would be calling defensive plays. He was not only able to handle that, but also showed why he's quickly become a fan favorite.
Barham made his presence felt with a tackle for loss on their second defensive snap of the game. Barham bullied his way into the backfield and stuffed Corey Kiner for a one-yard loss.
This is just silly from Jaishawn Barham pic.twitter.com/z5KARJ4qGS
Barham was all over the field, finishing with five tackles. Dallas entered training camp with questions about their linebacker depth and Barham may have answered all of those questions.
Joe Milton III was falling behind Sam Howell in the QB2 race, with Howell starting in Week 1 against the Seahawks. Milton came in off the bench and played well, earning the chance to start this Saturday, and he didn't disappoint. Milton led them on a long drive early, which should have extended had Zack Kuntz held onto his fourth-down pass.
Dallas scored touchdowns on the next three drives, the first two thanks to touchdown passes from Milton. First was an eight-yarder to Malik Davis on third down. Later in the first quarter, he dropped a dime into the hands of Jonathan Mingo, who brought it in for a 53-yard score.
A big development in QB2 & WR5. What a ball from Joe Milton III. pic.twitter.com/EhsesCXv9B
Milton continued to put points on the board, scoring on a one-yard touchdown run to cap off a four-play, 78-yard drive early in the second quarter, giving Dallas a 21-3 lead. In all, he was 9-of-13 passing for 179 yards with two touchdown passes, leading the Cowboys to a 24-6 lead going into the half.

title: Why I’m Buying Early Dallas Cowboys Hype Around Caleb Downs
full_text:
First-round picks are supposed to make a difference, so it’s no surprise that the Dallas Cowboys are expecting a ton out of their two 2026 selections in the opening round. And while the hopes are high for No. 23 pick Malachi Lawrence , the other defender taken 12 spots higher is destined to be “special.”
That’s the opinion on Ohio State All-American Caleb Downs by those who matter. The rookie safety out of Ohio State shined during the Oxnard portion of training camp and impressed in the preseason opener.
The Cowboys are counting on Downs to be a linchpin in the defensive revival for a squad with Super Bowl ambitions . That may be a lot to put on someone without any NFL experience, especially joining a defense that was historically awful last year, but there is something about Downs that matches the hype.
“ He’s constantly making the right decision ,” first-year defensive Christian Parker said. Those words were uttered back during rookie minicamp in May. Not much has changed.
Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer and Parker have consistently praised Downs for his ability to communicate on the field – rare for a 21-year-old rookie – as well as his high football IQ, versatility, preparation, playmaking and athleticism.
The defense will look drastically different this year. In addition to Parker transitioning the unit to an aggressive 3-4 scheme, the Cowboys made a splash by signing future Hall of Fame pass rusher Von Miller , locking up defensive tackle Quinnen Williams, and potentially rolling out as many as eight new starters .
Downs is officially a safety, but that position hardly defines his importance and impact on the field. He’ll be everywhere.
“He’s a corner sometimes, he is safety sometimes, he’s a backer sometimes,” Parker said . “He’s a defensive end when he’s blitzing. You want to have a guy who has natural instincts and ability to feel the game and play football.”
The proof is in the peers, at least in what they have to say. That’s no shortage of accolades when it comes to Downs.
“Man, he’s a dog, man,” edge Rashan Gary said recently on Good Morning Football . “It’s early, but he’s a pro’s pro, from how he, take notes to the man from how he asks questions to how he wants to be on top of the details. … So just from being a natural leader, he’s a great guy, and I just can’t wait for him to keep on growing and striving because we’re gonna need him.”
Going against All-Pro receiver CeeDee Lamb every day in practice could be demoralizing for a lesser player, if he wasn’t built for it. Downs is.
“Every play he gets a chance to line up against him, he feels like he’s going to win that rep, and that’s the type of mentality we want on this defense,” fellow safety Malik Hooker said . “Especially coming from a guy that we’re expecting to play a lot, and not only play a lot, but to be a difference maker in our defense.”
Downs echoes the Super Bowl chorus of owner Jerry Jones and his teammates. Those are the goals, and Downs tracks to be one of the focal points if and when the Cowboys end their championship drought.
A lot that has to go right for the Cowboys to get there. Don’t bet on Downs not being up for it.

title: One Concern That Hasn't Been Solved Yet (And How Broncos Can Fix It)
full_text:
With two of three preseason games in the books, the Denver Broncos appear to have a problem.
Denver's special teams have been concerningly rough this summer, and it hasn't shown any progress in the two preseason games. From bad long-snapping to botched field-goal attempts to poor punt and kick coverage, and even a kickoff out of bounds, the Broncos' third phase has left much to be desired in the preseason.
The Broncos allowed 28.8 yards per kick return to the Atlanta Falcons in preseason Game 1 and 39.7 per return to the Green Bay Packers in Game 2. Denver's punt coverage has been much better, but the kickoff coverage has been shockingly bad.
“Obviously that wasn’t good enough," head coach Sean Payton said after Friday night's loss to the Packers. "There weren’t a lot of things... I said this after the game—just pick a topic. Pick penalties, we lose there, kickoff, kickoff return, we lose that battle; rushing numbers, we lose that... You can’t not pay attention to these games, these scrimmages, these important steps towards the start of the regular season.”
It's worth noting that many of the players covering these kick and punt returns in the preseason won't be on the Broncos' roster come September. Still, third-phase mavens like Devon Key and JL Skinner have been involved in many of these returns, so it's a troubling trend regardless.
Special teams coordinator Darren Rizzi enters his second year with the club after spending the preceding six seasons with the New Orleans Saints. Before Rizzi arrived, the Broncos' special teams were in pretty good shape under Payton, beginning in 2023 with the hiring of Mike Westhoff as a third-phase expert and Ben Kotwica as the coordinator.
No special teams unit is going to be perfect. There were some gaffes under the Westhoff/Kotwica regime, the most noteworthy being Leo Chenal's blocked field-goal attempt in Kansas City during Bo Nix's rookie season, which saw the Broncos snatch defeat from the jaws of victory.
Shortly after that ignominious moment, Westhoff stepped down , citing his advancing age and health, while Kotwica marched ahead. The coaching tandem achieved some great things together, though, including Marvin Mims Jr. earning Pro Bowl and All-Pro honors in 2023 and 2024 as a returner.
Following the 2024 season, Payton fired Kotwica . It was a shocking move at the time, but it seemed to be preemptive so that the Broncos' head coach could make room on the staff for Rizzi, who was about to become a free agent, so to speak.
Payton hired Rizzi shortly after, and one of his first moves as coordinator was the scouting and drafting of punter Jeremy Crawshaw. The Broncos invested a sixth-round pick in the Australian-born punter, which was their way of ensuring they landed Crawshaw, rather than taking their chances competing with other teams for his services as a potential undrafted free agent.
Crawshaw started off a bit rocky as a rookie, but he eventually found his footing, and is poised to take a big leap forward in Year 2. Also notable in Rizzi's first year as special teams coordinator was Mims's failure to earn any returner accolades for the first time in his young career, despite averaging a healthy 15.6 yards per punt return, including a touchdown, and 26.3 yards per kick return.
However, it must be noted that kicker Wil Lutz really flourished after being reunited with Rizzi in Denver. Lutz was excellent in the clutch, kicking one game-winning field goal after another throughout the 2025 season. He was a big reason for Denver's 11-game winning streak last year.
Under Rizzi's purview, Mims may not have earned a Pro Bowl or an All-Pro selection for the first time in his career, but Key set a new franchise record for special teams tackles and was named first-team All-Pro as a third-phase ace. So, with Rizzi, there have been concerning special teams developments, but also plenty of success stories for Payton to hang his hat on.
Honestly, I don't expect the Broncos' coverage units to show much improvement during the preseason. And there's only one more game to go.
If the coverage units look this bad in Kansas City on Monday Night Football come September 14, then my concern will morph into true alarm.
For now, though, the Broncos will continue to play inexperienced guys like Miles Scott, Parker Robertson, Tycen Anderson, Brent Austin, Sean Fresch Jr., Dallen Bentley, Taurean York, and others in the preseason finale because the team has to evaluate its depth players to make the best decisions come roster cut-down day.
That day rapidly approaches, though. The Broncos' preseason finale vs. the Minnesota Vikings is on Friday, and two days later — August 30 — is the NFL's deadline to trim rosters down to the final 53 players .
I do hope the players I mentioned above, and many others, are able to capitalize on their opportunity against the Vikings, especially after the Broncos' depth looked so collectively lost in last week's 30-13 loss to the Packers.
As for Rizzi, I'm still waiting for that big aha moment that makes it clear why Payton dumped Kotwica for him. One thing I know for sure, though, is that Payton trusts Rizzi, and that goes a long way.

title: Projecting the Broncos' Week 1 Starting Lineup Right Now
full_text:
The Denver Broncos now have two preseason games in the books.
We've learned a lot about the state of the 2026 Broncos since training camp started in late July. With only one final preseason game left to go, the early returns on the Broncos are exciting.
Sean Payton doesn't like the term "picking up where they left off," but it sure looks like that's exactly what the Broncos are poised to do, after winning 14 games, the AFC West, and pushing all the way to the conference title game before a shockingly untimely injury torpedoed the team's Super Bowl ambitions.
The Broncos will host the Minnesota Vikings on Friday to close out the preseason. Two days later is the NFL deadline for trimming rosters down to the final 53 players.
Based on what we've seen this summer, here's how the Broncos' 2026 starting lineups are shaping up.
Running Back : J.K. Dobbins
Wide Receiver : Courtland Sutton, Jaylen Waddle, Pat Bryant
Tight End : 1a. Evan Engram, 1b. Adam Trautman
Left Tackle : Garett Bolles
Right Guard : Quinn Meinerz
Right Tackle : Mike McGlinchey
Prentice seems poised to make the 53-man roster out of camp. He's likely to get a few starts this season, depending on the opponent and game plan.
The only real developments on offense are the emergence of Bryant as the No. 3 receiver, and how the Broncos are using the tight ends. Bryant was the star of Broncos camp this summer, and while it hasn't translated to the field in the preseason, he's played a very limited number of snaps because the team wants to preserve him for the season.
Last year, the Broncos started Trautman at tight end more often than not because the offense tends to run the ball early on the first drive, and he's a better blocker than Engram. However, Engram has been asked to stay in to block a lot more this summer, which may have something to do with Davis Webb taking over as the offensive coordinator, and we're seeing the Broncos run a lot of two-tight-end sets.
Frankly, it wouldn't surprise me if the Broncos opened up in 12 personnel (one running back, two tight ends) as often as 13 (one running back, three receivers). In 12 personnel, Engram and Trautman will be on the field. Even if I'm wrong about the two-tight-end tendencies Webb has shown this summer, the Broncos seem determined to rely on Engram more as a blocker in order to keep him on the field more.
Going with heavy tight end sets will help the Broncos' run game, which then opens up the possibility for some deadly play-action passing. It'll be interesting to see how it all takes shape.
A quick note: Wattenberg has been hurt since Day 3 of training camp, but the Broncos have remained publicly confident he'll be good to go by the season-opener in mid-September.
Defensive End : Zach Allen
Defensive End : Eyioma Uwazurike
Outside Linebacker : Jonathon Cooper
Inside Linebacker : Alex Singleton
Inside Linebacker : Justin Strnad
Outside Linebacker : Nik Bonitto
Cornerback : Patrick Surtain II
Nickel Cornerback : Ja’Quan McMillian
Depending on the opponent, you can expect the Broncos to start many games in their nickel sub-package, which would take one linebacker off the field, to be replaced by McMillian. Consider him a starter.
This opening-day starting defense looks much the same as last year's, with one exception. Uwazurike will start at defensive end in place of John Franklin-Myers, who departed in free agency.
Like Engram and Trautman above, this defensive end spot could be a 1a. and 1b. situation split between Uwazurike and Malcolm Roach. However, in both preseason games, Uwazurike has gotten the start, with Roach rotating in regularly.
That could change come September, but I doubt it. About a week-and-a-half into training camp, Jones theorized publicly that Roach would win the Franklin-Myers job and " run with it ," but Uwazurike hasn't allowed that to happen.
In the final analysis, these two trenchmen will likely end up getting even snaps, but this article is about projecting the starting lineup, and Uwazurike seems to have the edge.
Long Snapper : Mitchell Fraboni
Punt Returner : Marvin Mims Jr.
Kick Returner : Marvin Mims Jr.
Kick Returner : Jonah Coleman
The Broncos gave it the ol' college try this summer by signing undrafted rookie long snapper Luke Basso to compete with Fraboni, but the proof is in the pudding. If the Broncos want reliability, Fraboni is the guy; Basso had a bad long snap in preseason Game 1, leading to a botched field-goal attempt.
Again, this unit looks the same as last year's with the exception of the second kick returner. In a perfect world, the Broncos would rather not use Coleman back there, but he did get some returner action during camp, including in the planned scrimmage about halfway through.
The Broncos have been utilizing undrafted rookie receivers Kolbe Katsis and Cameron Ross as the kick returners in the preseason. At punt returner, it's been Katsis and undrafted rookie cornerback Sean Fresch Jr., who has looked great on defense and explosive on special teams.
Mims has not played in the preseason yet due to a soft-tissue injury suffered about a week into camp, but even if he were healthy, I doubt the Broncos would have done anything differently because they know what he can do; they want to see what Katsis, Ross, and Fresch can bring to the table.
Alas, though, unless the Broncos intend to keep six receivers or six cornerbacks on the 53-man roster, the likely outcome for Katsis, Ross, or Fresch is the practice squad. The Broncos could still utilize them on game day by elevating them, but it would be curious to elevate one player strictly to return kicks alongside Mims for, say, two to five plays per game.
Then again, the Broncos have mainly used their practice squad elevations on linebackers, cornerbacks, safeties, and receivers who can contribute on special teams kick and coverage units, and each game usually offers only a handful of such plays.
Still, I'm doubtful that Katsis, Ross, or Fresch make the 53-man roster , and given that the Broncos have one of the NFL's elite returners in Mims, I'm rolling with Coleman as the second kick returner, despite how good this undrafted trio has looked this summer.
It could be a running back other than Coleman, like Jaleel McLaughlin, Tyler Badie, or Cody Schrader, but that's only if the Broncos opt to keep four running backs on the 53-man roster. That's what Denver has done over the past few years under Payton, but it feels like only three true running backs will be kept along with the fullback.

title: Broncos May Have Three Players Worth Trading Instead of Cutting
full_text:
As the Denver Broncos decide which players are most likely to make the 53-man roster, they have to be prepared to expose some players to the waiver wire. Any player who hasn't accrued at least four seasons is subject to waivers and, thus, could be claimed by other teams.
Waiver claims don't happen as often as fans think, but they are frequent enough to make people realize that the wire carries the risk of another team claiming a player who might otherwise be a good practice squad addition. Remember, practice squad players can be elevated on game day, and a team can always promote them to the 53-man roster at any point.
When waiver claims happen, though, they tend to be for players with a larger sample size of NFL snaps, whether from the regular seasons or past preseasons. When it comes to recently undrafted rookies, teams are more likely to focus on keeping their own for a practice squad, unless they have a desperate need for help at a particular position.
Because players with NFL experience to some degree could be coveted, teams with lower waiver priority might be willing to trade for them. The Broncos have a couple of players who have seen plenty of NFL snaps and might return something in a trade from a team that's lower in the waiver priority and wants to ensure they get that player.
Let's look at three such Broncos other teams might be willing to trade for the right price.
Franklin became a bigger part of the Broncos' offense last year, and while he was solid, he didn't make a big impact. He now finds himself buried on the depth chart with the arrival of Jaylen Waddle and the improvement shown by Pat Bryant this summer.
If the Broncos decide to keep just five wide receivers and opt to keep somebody other than Franklin as the fifth wideout, he would likely fetch considerable draft pick compensation because, while he's not an impact player, he could be good for a team that needs pass-catching help.
However, it remains to be seen whether the Broncos take a route that means exposing Franklin to waivers. They could cut Lil'Jordan Humphrey and sign him to the practice squad, and will likely be able to expose other players to waivers, then get them to the practice squad without worrying about another team claiming them.
To be clear, I'm not suggesting that Franklin is absolutely going to be cut; such a move would raise some eyebrows. However, his role has diminished and the Broncos may want to prioritize a more versatile skill set when it comes to the fifth receiver they keep on the roster, and Franklin can't block or play special teams.
The Broncos don't appear to be prepared to keep four running backs on the 53-man roster . That would mean McLaughlin would get exposed to waivers because he's only accrued three NFL seasons, and the top three running backs are set.
McLaughlin has done some good things but is buried behind J.K. Dobbins, RJ Harvey, and Jonah Coleman, all of whom have more to offer to the team for one reason or another. But McLaughlin could be a good fit with other NFL teams.
McLaughlin won't command significant trade compensation, but even if it were just a seventh-round pick, it would be better than nothing, and not a bad return on a former undrafted player.
Skinner has stuck around with the Broncos for the past three seasons because of his special teams play. However, the former sixth-round pick hasn't shown much on defense, particularly when it comes to the Broncos' need for the third safety on the depth chart.
The recent signing of Taylor Rapp indicates the Broncos aren't happy with their depth at safety. Add in the fact that the All-Pro Devon Key is the Broncos' best special teams player, and the roster math may not work out for Skinner to stick around.
In this case, it might be a long shot, but a team with a great need for special teams help might be willing to do a Day 3 draft pick swap to acquire Skinner.
Franklin has the most trade value of these players, but that doesn't mean the Broncos will move him. However, if a team made an offer too good to refuse, the Broncos would likely take it.
McLaughlin and Skinner are less likely to be traded because they aren't as valuable, but such trades can't be ruled out. One team that's low in waiver priority could be prepared to make a trade to ensure they get that player.
Other players I considered are unlikely to get traded for one reason or another. Case in point is linebacker Drew Sanders, who may have netted a draft pick if he had stayed healthy this summer, but his most recent injury means teams aren't going to be interested, especially given his history.

title: Broncos 53-Man Roster Projection 4.0: Game 2 Shakes Up the Roster Bubble
full_text:
Only one preseason game remains before the Denver Broncos have to cut their current 90-man roster down to the final 53 players. That deadline is on August 30.
By returning most of their 2025 roster, the Broncos have a good idea of who will make the cut this year. Honestly, analyzing this roster, there are maybe five spots open.
In the wake of the Broncos' 33-13 loss to the Green Bay Packers , it's time to project the 53-man roster and 16-man practice squad once again. Let's see how things may have been shaken up compared to our version 3.0 projection coming out of the Atlanta Falcons game last week.
There are no changes here, and fans shouldn’t expect any in the quarterback room. Stidham and Ehlinger aren’t in a true battle , and the Broncos seem unlikely to carry three quarterbacks on the roster.
Even with some injury concerns over Dobbins, the Broncos still only roll with three running backs. They could look for more on the practice squad, but it seems like Tyler Badie and Jaleel McLaughlin would land elsewhere, leaving Schrader as the practice squad back, and there are no qualms there, as he has outplayed Badie and McLaughlin in the preseason games.
There will be a fullback on the roster; Sean Payton has said as much, and new offensive coordinator Davis Webb clearly has something in mind for how to use him.
Due to roster math, Humphrey misses out on the 53-man roster, but he has a chance to make it, as Nix, Payton, and Webb seem to have a lot of trust in him as a weapon. The question is how the practice squad shakes up, and Ross has looked good on offense, with Katsis standing out as a returner.
Denver needs help in the tight end room, and until then, this will be the outlook for the room. Each day Lohner misses increases his chances of being one of the players put on injured reserve at the cutdown as someone who could potentially return.
With how bad Crum has been in the preseason, there is a chance the undrafted rookie could take his spot, as Miller has done quite well. However, Crum has been running with the second unit, while Miller has been with the fourth-unit offensive line, signaling a pecking order.
Throckmorton has been doing well in games and in practice, which should be making Forsyth feel some heat, as he wasn’t doing the best in practice before he got hurt. There's also positional versatility with Throckmorton, which you don’t have in Forsyth.
Outside of those two players, the interior offensive line is pretty much set.
Barring a trade, the Broncos' defensive line seems set, even for the practice squad. They like to keep seven on the roster, and those seven are clear.
With Miller, he saw the field in the second half against Green Bay, and the last defensive linemen didn’t take the field until the fourth quarter. Miller has done well and seems like a shoo-in for the practice squad.
The practice squad is up for a battle, and Denver could look outside the team to find another rush linebacker. Drew Sanders is hurt again, and Johnny Walker and McCullough haven’t been great. The Broncos' five outside linebackers are locks, barring a surprise cut or trade.
The top three seem pretty much settled, but the fourth spot is still up for grabs with Turner and Murdock competing for it. Both have had some bad moments, but also some bright spots.
Turner got the edge over Murdock here for special teams play, but it could honestly go either way. York is out of the running for the roster because of his lack of special teams ability, as he made multiple mistakes on special teams against the Packers.
There has been a debate about whether Denver would keep five or six corners, and Fresch is pushing for a roster spot with his play on defense and special teams, but the team could probably sneak him onto the practice squad.
The Broncos' top five corners are set, though, and that's great because it speaks to their depth.
Yes, Rapp makes it even as a new addition because he is a high-football-IQ veteran who should pick up the defense quickly, upgrading the third safety spot, which is much needed. This pushes Key back down into a key special teams player and the fourth safety.
Skinner sticks around for his third-phase play. Scott and Robertson have shown plenty of flashes to keep around and continue to develop.
No competition for Lutz or Crawshaw, and Fraboni is clearly ahead of Luke Basso. There doesn’t seem to be much of a long snapper competition after all.

title: Payton Provides Clarity on Broncos RB J.K. Dobbins for Finale
full_text:
Denver Broncos running back J.K. Dobbins was inactive for Friday's preseason game versus Green Bay , the second such missed contest this summer.
But head coach Sean Payton cracked the door, however slightly, for Dobbins to make his debut next Friday when the Broncos conclude exhibition play against the Minnesota Vikings.
“We’ll see. Yes," Payton said when asked if he expects Dobbins to suit up.
Dobbins suffered a soft-tissue injury during training camp practice earlier this month, the severity of which Payton confirmed was minor: "We’re just being smart with it."
With Dobbins down, the Broncos started second-year man RJ Harvey at running back in the 33-13 defeat to the Packers. Harvey handled only one carry, but finished with two receptions for 25 yards, including a 21-yard touchdown from quarterback Bo Nix.
“Well honestly, he was like that last year, so the growth I haven’t seen much because he started so far out in front as a pass catcher," Nix said of Harvey after the game. "I knew when he came in last year, seeing him for the first time at practice that that was going to be his strongest ability. The catch he made wasn’t necessarily easy. He’s just done that his career here so far, just over a year and some change. I’m excited to see him continue to develop. He’s a special football player.”
The Broncos also got contributions from several other RBs , including Jonah Coleman, Jaleel McLaughlin, Tyler Badie, and Cody Schrader. McLaughlin and Schrader tied for the team lead in attempts (4) and rushing yards (15), each posting a 3.8 YPC average.
It's understandable that Dobbins, if fully healthy, would want to go in the preseason finale. And it's understandable that Denver would want to get him out there, even for a few snaps, to prove he's ready.
But that's ultimately a game that doesn't count; the Broncos would be wiser to preserve him for the games that do -- starting Week 1 against the rival Kansas City Chiefs, a matchup in which his services will be required.
Given his checkered injury history, the Broncos indeed may mothball Dobbins until that moment, all the while continuing to evaluate the players behind him on the depth chart who struggled to perform up to snuff on Friday evening.
“Yes, it wasn’t good. It wasn’t good," Payton said of the rushing offense. "We’ll look at the tape, but we had too many minus plays, too many penalties offensively. I don’t know how many third-and-10 or more we had, but quite a bit, right?”

title: Sean Payton Offers Update on Riley Moss After Injury Scare vs. Packers
full_text:
Early in the Denver Broncos' 33-13 preseason loss to the Green Bay Packers , cornerback Riley Moss was in fine form.
Moss broke up Jordan Love's first pass attempt of the night, nearly picking it off and showcasing that sticky, feisty coverage that Broncos fans have come to expect from the fourth-year cornerback. A few plays later, Love completed a pass to Christian Watson with Patrick Surtain II in coverage, and as the Packers' receiver was going to the ground, the perennial Pro Bowler stripped the ball out.
Moss promptly scooped it up and was tackled by a gang of Packers, falling on the ball with a mountain of weight on top of him. He jumped up holding his ribs and wincing in pain, immediately exiting the field and entering the blue tent on the sideline. The receiver was ruled down, incidentally. No fumble.
Soon after, Moss was escorted by trainers to the locker room and did not return to the field. After the game, Broncos head coach Sean Payton was asked about Moss's injury.
“Good," Payton said. "We’ll see.”
Payton refuses to talk about player injuries and outside of the league's mandate to list player injuries on the practice report each week of the regular season, that's typically the most information Broncos fans ever get on a given player, outside of independent reporting. Unfortunately, there is no such NFL mandate for listing injuries during the preseason, so we're unlikely to get any additional insight from Payton or the Broncos on Moss.
Payton did say "good," though. We'll see how much Moss practices next week, but next Friday's preseason finale against the Minnesota Vikings will tell us more. If Moss plays, we'll know that he's indeed "good."
The Broncos' starters only played a couple of series on Friday night against the Packers. Payton plans to play the first-teamers again next week in the finale, though we don't know how much.
Moss has put together one heck of a training camp and preseason performance. Entering a contract year, the former third-round draft pick has signaled to the Broncos his motivation to get paid, although he has continued to defer when asked about his expiring contract.
"It’s about taking things day by day, being where your feet are, competing, and improving at one thing every day," Moss said on August 6. "The rest will take care of itself. I trust that God has a plan for me. Whether I have a bad practice or a bad game, there’s always something to learn from it. I trust Him, and that’s how I approach it."
Moss was one of the biggest winners of training camp , and he made plays in both preseason games thus far. Against the Atlanta Falcons last week, he had an interception , and despite only playing a few snaps against the Packers, he had a pass break-up and nearly a fumble recovery.
When it comes to an extension, what the Broncos are waiting on is unclear. Moss is continuing to show development, and proved late last season that he could provide reliable, sticky coverage without so often drawing a penalty for pass interference or defensive holding.
From the Broncos' Week 12 bye on, Moss was able to curtail the penalty problem, which had become a liability for the defense. When Surtain missed three games down the stretch with an injury, Moss rotated over to the No. 1 cornerback spot, and the Broncos' defense carried on apace, not skipping a beat. Denver won all three games.
The Broncos do have several other worthy players also entering a contract year, and that could be complicating matters with Moss. But of all the players on an expiring contract, he has stood out the most this summer, so it may be just a matter of time before the Broncos reward him.
The Broncos still have $37.3 million in salary-cap space, per Over The Cap , and while the team is bearing down for Bo Nix's contract extension next offseason, the bulk of the salary-cap impact won't be felt until 2029, at the soonest. That offers the Broncos the opportunity to strike while the iron is hot, and continue to invest into retaining as much of their core as possible.
Moss was drafted and developed by the Broncos. As a member of Payton's maiden draft class as Broncos head coach, Moss is very much a key part of the team's young core.
It doesn't sound like Moss's injury is serious. Rib injuries, if that's what it is, can be tricky and they can linger, but Payton doesn't sound too worried.
In the meantime, we'll continue to await news of the Broncos getting some extensions done. Over the past few years, GM George Paton has used the window between the start of training camp and the regular-season opener to sign key players to extensions — like wideout Courtland Sutton, defensive end Zach Allen, and rush linebacker Nik Bonitto last year — but he hasn't done so this summer.
Time will tell whether the Broncos view Moss as one of those key players deserving of a multi-year extension.

title: Broncos Player Grades From 33-13 Preseason Loss to Packers
full_text:
The Denver Broncos were unable to keep their preseason winning streak alive in front of their home crowd as the Green Bay Packers came to town on Friday night and pulled off a 33-13 victory.
There were many ugly individual performances by the Broncos in this game, something head coach Sean Payton was clearly unhappy about in his post-game press conference.
“Obviously that wasn’t good enough," Payton said post-game.
Not everything was ugly, though, and there were some good performances , though not as many as you'd hope to see. As we get into the player grades, I will highlight some of those good showings and point out some of the worst.
Since the preseason is about depth evaluation, starters and key players are not included in the player grades, with one exception. So, let’s get into this week's grades.
All eyes were on Nix in his first game back since his broken ankle in the playoffs, and he looked great out there , as did the first-team offense for the most part. It was great to see that he had no limitations from the injury.
Hopefully, Nix can stay healthy because the Broncos don’t have a capable backup, though Stidham is clearly the better option over Sam Ehlinger; it's like choosing between moldy pepperoni pizza and a moldy pizza with sardines and anchovies.
Ehlinger didn’t receive enough snaps to qualify for a grade, with only nine snaps (10 snaps are the minimum). However, if I overlook that requirement, he would have a grade of 5.3, which would be the lowest in nearly 10 years of my grading system.
There were many poor performances on defense, which made some of the better performers look bad. Reid was one of the standouts, as he worked beside Jordan Turner and Red Murdock (both of whom graded in the 30s), and most of the defensive linemen playing in front of Reid graded under 45.
Despite the issues around him, Reid flew around the field and kept multiple bad plays from becoming even worse.
There were a few good performances on offense, but Humphrey showed why Payton likes to keep him in his wide receiver unit. Humphrey did have a drop, which is an issue, but he ran good routes, caught two of his three targets for 32 yards, and really stood out as a blocker.
Denver has something special in Robinson. With how quickly he fires off the snap, he's difficult for offensive linemen to handle, and he is showing surprising strength and power to avoid being a liability against the run.
Multiple teams could start Robinson, as their third pass rusher, at the very least.
There has been some under-the-radar hype about the undrafted rookie coming out of training camp, and he showed why. Unlike most of the other depth safeties, Robertson was rarely out of place and was quick to fly downhill and mix it up as a run defender.
On one of the Packers' touchdown drives, Onyedim blew up five or six plays behind the line of scrimmage, though he couldn't finish consistently until a big stop near the goal line. He stood out as a run defender against a mostly second-unit offense and generated a QB pressure.
After an unremarkable game against the Atlanta Falcons, Key had a good outing against the Packers. He fought off some tight coverage to make himself a target and showed effort as a blocker. The effort wasn’t enough, as his technique let him down, but he at least showed there is something to work with as a blocker.
There were a few good performances from the offense, but Ross consistently stood out, though he wasn’t always great. He gave good effort as a blocker with moderate success, ran good routes, and got himself open for more than the two targets he actually received, but pressure on the quarterback killed his chances to make a play.
Schrader once again put together a good game, and some of his plays came against the same Packers defensive unit that Tyler Badie and Jaleel McLaughlin struggled against. While Schrader is still clearly the lowest running back on the depth chart, it would be nice to see the Broncos reward him by moving him up, but we all know Payton likes his guys, and Badie and McLaughlin seem to be exactly that.
Due to injury, this was McCullough's first game action, and at one point, he was getting hype as an undrafted rookie with a shot at making the roster. With this being McCullough's first in-game exposure, one is left wondering whether the practice squad is even an option. Denver could look elsewhere for a practice squad player.
Crum has been a disaster in both preseason games, and it was on another level of woe against the Packers. He was consistently getting run around, even by third- and fourth-string pass rushers, including one player whom the Packers added earlier this week. Sure, he has effort, but that effort means little when it's made to overcome a bad mistake made earlier in the rep.
Both Williams and Miller sit at the very bottom of the defensive line depth chart and are competing for a practice squad spot. Both were consistent liabilities and got bullied in the run game. Denver can and should look outside the organization at this point for its practice squad defensive linemen.
The Krull experiment should be over. His blocking was a liability, both on offense and on special teams, and he doesn’t make up for it as a receiver. Krull isn’t able to get separation, even against linebackers and safeties, and his routes are easy to read.
After a good first outing in Atlanta, Manjack struggled with route running to create separation, which is one reason he went undrafted. Without special teams ability, his chances of making the roster were already low, but if he doesn’t bounce back, this performance may even eliminate him from practice squad consideration.

title: Broncos' Biggest Winners and Losers in 33-13 Loss to Packers
full_text:
Two-thirds of the Denver Broncos' preseason is in the books.
In Game 2, Bo Nix's return to the field headlined the night , but the Broncos turned in an overall lackluster performance, falling to the Green Bay Packers 33-13.
We've shared 10 bite-sized takeaways and the good, bad, and ugly , but now it's time to highlight the Broncos' biggest winners and losers from preseason Game 2.
Nix played 15 snaps over two possessions, and both of his drives quarterbacking the Broncos' first-team offense ended in points. He went 6-of-9 for 76 yards and a touchdown, putting 10 of Denver's 13 total points on the board.
Nix may have felt a bit rusty, but he certainly didn't look it. Coming off of ankle surgery this offseason, his mobility didn't appear to be restricted in any way. The Broncos have the face of the franchise back.
Stidham was unable to follow up his impressive performance in Game 1 with another strong showing. He was given most of the game, but could only produce three additional points.
The interception Stidham threw was concerning, as he stared down a receiver. Although he led all quarterbacks with 15 attempts, he finished with just 82 yards passing — not that it matters; it would seem that Denver has already made up its mind on the QB2 issue. It's 'Stiddy' again.
Waddle only played a handful of snaps, but his 35-yard catch-and-run down the right seam was one of the biggest plays of the night. Nix found Waddle on third-and-long, and after hauling in the catch, the sixth-year receiver turned on the jets, crossing midfield and setting the Broncos' offense up to score shortly thereafter.
The speed element is real, and how Waddle changes the math for opposing defenses will redound to Denver's great benefit this season. He's going to eat, make no mistake, but so will Courtland Sutton and others.
After an impressive preseason debut last week, Barron took a step back against the Packers. He was on the field a lot, which shows that Denver values him, but he allowed a touchdown in coverage, and his typical reliability as a tackler was absent, although he did finish with three tackles (two solo), including one for a loss.
Barron's place on the team is secure. But those looking for strong signs that he's turned a corner in Year 2 are left feeling a little uneasy about the Broncos' 2025 first-round pick.
Robinson looked unstoppable against the Packers. His pass-rush pressure was consistent, and while he was flagged for roughing the passer, his hit on Tyrod Taylor was clean.
Robinson finished with the Broncos' only sack of the night, two quarterback hits, and two tackles, both of which were solo. Denver has to be feeling particularly excited about its 2025 fourth-round pick.
I hate to say it but Ortega was bad against the Packers. He had a fumbled snap and allowed a sack, which led to a big hit on the quarterback.
Now, in fairness, the undrafted rookie has exceeded expectations this summer, in that, he was expected to play some guard with the third-team offense, but the Broncos' rash of injuries at the center position forced him into action. In that respect, Ortega deserves credit for stepping up, but his performance against Green Bay was one that he'll hope to make up for in the preseason finale next week.
The rookie third-rounder had one heck of a game playing on a defensive line that got bullied most of the night by the Packers. Onyedim finished with four tackles (one solo), and was hustling around the field, chasing ball-carriers to the edge and to the second level.
Onyedim seems to have the upper hand on Sai'vion Jones in the Broncos' defensive line pecking order, and if that was uncertain going into preseason Game 2, the coaching staff should have no further questions on the matter.
Once again, with the eyes of the NFL on him, Butler had his chances to show what he could do, but he came up small. I'm starting to worry that the 6-foot-5 behemoth of a wideout is a 'looks like Tarzan, plays like Jane' type of player.
Against the Packers, Stidham gave Butler an opportunity to do what he does best, and use his big body and catch radius to win a contested-catch situation, but he failed to haul it in. It would have been a touchdown. Stidham looked Butler's way on the very next play, targeting his back shoulder, but the pass was inaccurate.
Reid seems to have one of the two open inside linebacker roster spots on lockdown. He looked great in Atlanta last week, and followed that up with another impressive showing against the Packers.
Reid's instincts and football IQ were on full display, as he flew around the field making plays. He finished with three tackles (one solo), and made it clear that he's currently the Broncos' best linebacker after Alex Singleton and Justin Strnad.
I'm not sure what the Broncos' fascination with Badie has been, but he was quite forgettable in his touches against the Packers. He carried the ball four times but gained just two yards, and caught one pass for three yards.
So, with five touches, Badie netted the Broncos five yards from scrimmage. Meanwhile, Jaleel McLaughlin showcased his burst and had a couple of decent gains called back by penalties, and Cody Schrader again ran hard, displaying his physicality and vision.
If the Broncos keep four running backs and a fullback, it still feels like it's McLaughlin's job to lose, but Badie's play on the field this summer should have him far removed from consideration. Schrader has been much better and maybe even the best running back overall after Jonah Coleman.

title: Broncos Fall to Packers at Mile High: The Good, Bad, and the Ugly
full_text:
The Denver Broncos were vanquished by the Green Bay Packers 33-13 in Bo Nix’s long-awaited return to the field.
Both the Broncos’ first-team offense and defense came to play; however, their effectiveness declined sharply when the backups took the field.
As we continue sifting through the aftermath of preseason Game 2 , let’s talk about the good, the bad, and the downright ugly of the Broncos' blowout loss, starting with the return of the face of the franchise.
You’d never guess that Nix was coming off two ankle surgeries, as he showed off his mobility in the pocket and carved up the Packers’ secondary. Nix fired a pass over the middle to Jaylen Waddle for a 35-yard gain, who also saw his first action of 2026 on Friday night, giving Broncos Country a taste of how dynamic this duo can be.
That speed after the catch is scary. Jaylen Waddle, it's gonna be a GREAT year! pic.twitter.com/T1btl9VaVJ
Nix capped off his first drive with a beautiful 21-yard touchdown pass on a wheel route to RJ Harvey. The Broncos’ second drive stalled, but Nix managed to pull them into field-goal range after hitting Lil’Jordan Humphrey for 14 yards.
There were no signs of Nix’s ankle bothering him throughout his two drives, eluding pressure and delivering the ball on the run. He may be stronger and hungrier than he’s ever been heading into a season, and that bodes well for the Broncos’ Super Bowl aspirations.
While the Broncos easily handled Tua Tagovailoa and the Atlanta Falcons last week, the same can’t be said for stopping Jordan Love and the Packers. Love drove down the field on the Packers’ opening possession, using play-action, which the Broncos’ defense bit on several times, leading to first down after first down for the Cheese Heads.
Love hit backup running back MarShawn Lloyd for an easy pitch-and-catch touchdown with Dondrea Tillman in coverage after a defensive miscommunication. Denver’s backup defenders didn’t fare any better, letting running back Pierre Strong Jr. chip away at them on the ground while Jahdae Barron gave up a two-yard touchdown pass.
There’s no reason to panic about the Broncos' defense; preseason is the time to iron out any kinks they may have, but their performance against the Packers was one to forget.
The Broncos’ special teams unit was abysmal once again, giving up several huge gains on punt and kick coverage. Strong had a 68-yard return on a kickoff, and Skyy Moore had a 16-yard return on a punt that should’ve been snuffed out as quickly as it hit his hands.
While Wil Lutz drilled field goals from 53 and 38 yards, he botched a kickoff out of bounds, giving the Packers the ball on Denver’s 40. It's extremely aggravating how undisciplined the Broncos have been on special teams, especially when you consider that Ben Kotwica was axed so Sean Payton could hire his buddy Darren Rizzi, and ever since, this unit hasn’t been the same.
The Broncos have only one preseason game left against the Minnesota Vikings to finalize their roster and work out any remaining issues. With the return of Nix, this team is primed to make another strong push to the AFC championship game, but it must figure out why its special teams aren’t so special anymore.

title: 10 Bite-Sized Takeaways From Broncos' 33-13 Loss to Packers
full_text:
The Denver Broncos took on the Green Bay Packers at Mile High in their second preseason game of the summer.
The Broncos got a lot more of their first unit out there on the field on Friday night, with Bo Nix and Jaylen Waddle seeing the field and connecting on a big play. The Broncos ultimately lost the game 33-13, so what did we learn?
Here are 10 bite-sized takeaways from the Broncos' second preseason game.
Sai’vion Jones ended up being the sixth player to take the field in the unit, but it was on a third down. More noteworthy is how early Jordan Jackson saw the field, getting reps with the first-team unit.
There is a clear sign that Jackson is the fifth guy on the D-line depth chart, with Jones and Tyler Onyedim competing as the sixth and seventh guys in the pecking order.
Due to an injury to Levelle Bailey , Red Murdock was the fourth linebacker against the Atlanta Falcons last week, but Jordan Turner is back, and he was the fourth linebacker against the Packers after missing the first game.
A battle between the two will be decided in the preseason finale, but Murdock once again led the team with seven tackles while Turner had one.
This isn’t a surprise, and it was only a small sample size, but the change Waddle brings to the passing game was easy to see. The Packers had to adjust their coverages to account for Waddle's speed.
It led to some big openings in the passing game, one of which Waddle himself exploited on a 35-yard reception on third down.
That speed after the catch is scary. Jaylen Waddle, it's gonna be a GREAT year! pic.twitter.com/T1btl9VaVJ
There has been a lot of talk about Denver cutting Adam Prentice and bringing him back on the practice squad, which could still happen, but it seems unlikely.
Webb has shown he has a clear plan for using Prentice in multiple ways, so why risk him going elsewhere?
Look, if there were a legitimate backup quarterback battle , Sam Ehlinger would have been the second quarterback and not Jarrett Stidham. The Broncos stuck with Stidham behind Bo Nix, and while he played poorly, they gave him a lot of run against the Packers.
Limiting Ehlinger's opportunity makes it clear there isn’t a battle here. Stidham is the QB2.
Que Robinson and Dondrea Tillman are the fourth and fifth rush linebackers, and they both made some big plays for the Broncos' defense. Robinson had a sack, and Tillman did extremely well against the run, even while those around him struggled.
Both players could be legitimate third-down rusher options with other teams.
Cameron Ross, Sean Fresch Jr., and Kolbe Katsis are getting looks as potential depth returners who can be on the practice squad or even the roster if the roster math works out.
What's more is what they showed on their respective sides of the ball. Katsis was the best as a returner, but Ross and Fresch did better on offense and defense, respectively.
Not only did Barron get beaten for a touchdown, but he also got beaten off the snap in this one. And he looks bad as a run defender. Known as a reliable tackler, he missed at least one against the Packers.
Kris Abrams-Draine looked okay, but Barron was a mess. The former first-rounder is trending in the wrong direction for the Broncos, to the point where his future may not be at cornerback.
Some of the Broncos' backup offensive linemen looked solid, like Calvin Throckmorton at center, but that's about it. At tackle, Frank Crum was getting beaten consistently; undrafted rookie center Gavin Ortega had a botched snap and gave up a sack; rookie right guard Kage Casey was up and down; the veteran Matt Peart was beaten fairly often, and that's only the beginning.
This game should lead to a lot more questions about the Broncos' offensive line depth.
After the top three backs, the Broncos went with Tyler Badie, then Jaleel McLaughlin, and ended with Cody Schrader. That clearly indicates the pecking order, but nothing about these running backs' play illustrates why, beyond familiarity.
Badie’s best play was a single pass-protection rep; McLaughlin remains inconsistent, and how he carries the ball raises some concerns; and Schrader consistently runs hard, looks good, and makes good plays.

title: The Good, Bad and Ugly of Lions Preseason Victory Over Commanders
full_text:
On Saturday, Detroit had their only home game of the preseason and took down the Washington Commanders 17-13. With the game came plenty of tape that will help shape the roster as Detroit finishes their last of the preseason next Saturday.
It also gives fans a preview as to what worked with the backups at the wheel, along with what worked for the Lions. Here are the good, the bad, and the ugly of a preseason win over the Commanders.
Yet again, the Drew Petzing offense is clicking on all cylinders when it comes to running to football. The Lions had a dominant game on the ground despite their top two backs, Jahmyr Gibbs and Isiah Pacheco, not playing a snap on Saturday.
The backs by committee even lost a player midgame with Jabari Small heading to concussion protocol. It did not matter, as the Lions saw Jacob Saylors, Trayveon Williams, and Raheem Blackshear all show flashes.
Additional credit goes to the offensive line and pass catchers for their efforts in the run blocks. Blake Miller had a play where he slipped on the turf and recovered to push a defender out of the hole on an eight-yard gain. Tyler Conklin and Tay Martin combined for two massive blocks on a 50-yard touchdown run by Joshua Dobbs.
Even on fourth-and-two, the Lions handed the ball off to Blackshear to seal the victory. All around, it was a great day for runners and run blockers.
Quarterback Pressure and Dominant Defense
In a repeat of last week, the Lions were able to harass the Commanders quarterbacks . D.J. Wonnum and Derrick Moore each made their preseason debuts and had a sack in their limited reps. Skyler Gill-Howard could have been charged rent in the Washington backfield by the end of the game. Undrafted EDGE Eric O’Neill impressed again with solid flashes and dismantling a go-ahead drive attempt by the Commanders.
Levi Onwuzurike provided a solid push. Devin White nearly sacked Jayden Daniels on the opening pass attempt of the game. Keith Abney II nearly got home twice in one drive on nickel blitzes. Malcolm Rodriguez recorded a quarterback hit. Kelvin Sheppard’s defense only allowed nine first downs all game.
In a friendly environment, procedural penalties such as false starts are inexcusable. The Lions saw their fair share of mental mistakes, including back-to-back false starts by Seth McLaughlin and Miles Frazier. Melvin Priestly added his own false start with the Lions on the verge of the red zone in a go-ahead situation in the second half. Larry Borom lined up improperly on a strip sack that was recovered in the end zone.
Mistakes like these will come back to haunt players trying to earn a spot on the 53-man roster or practice squad in the next few weeks. Additionally, rookie defensive back Keith Abney II had a holding penalty on what would have been a sack, alongside getting a whistle for pass interference later in the game.
For the second time, the starting quarterback for the Lions opened the game by giving the ball away on the first possession. Joshua Dobbs got the start and fumbled the ball on his first pass attempt. He followed that up with a poorly advised throw across his body into double coverage while under pressure in his second drive, giving him a multi-turnover game.
Luke Altmyer had flashes, but did not have the same sharpness he seemed to possess against the Bengals in week one of preseason. It was not a day where either player vying for the backup job “won” it. Joshua Dobbs’s best play came with his legs, while Altmyer avoided turnovers, but also had a series where he took three sacks.
Last week saw the Lions escape Cincinnati without any major losses, but that is likely not the case this week. Wide receiver Cedrick Wilson Jr. suffered an injury where the prognosis was worrying, per Dan Campbell. Offensive lineman Michael Niese was carted off the field and seen exiting the locker room in crutches.
Those two losses could be on the long term end of the scale. Additionally, running back Jabari Small exited the game and is in concussion protocol. Miles Frazier left the game for injury at one point, but later returned. Jacob Saylors, Christian Mahogany, and Chuck Clark all suffered minor bumps and bruises.
When combined with Sam LaPorta’s Week One status in doubt, there is some concern for the season already.
While the offensive line deserved flowers and a ton of credit for an organized run game, the pass game was not the same story. When there were not procedural penalties that should be avoided, the pass blocking suffered.
The opening play of the game saw Borom get beat badly, preventing Dobbs from stepping into a throw and susceptible to a blitz by former Lion Amik Robertson. Seth McLaughlin allowed a sack by assuming a defensive tackle would give up on a play. Borom allowed a pressure on the Dobbs interception.
Tyler Conklin got blown by on a block that resulted in a sack. Colby Sorsdal got benched in the second quarter, and that might be it for his chances of making the roster.
At the end of the day, the Lions won, but the top priority appears to be keeping the starting offensive line healthy after Washington’s defense and backups dominated the reserves whenever a pass was attempted.
