title: Six Winners and One Key Loser From Packers’ Victory Over Broncos
full_text:
Preseason performance does not matter. A team could win or lose by 70 points and it would not affect it in any capacity once the regular season begins.
That being said, the last time the Green Bay Packers were in Denver for a preseason game, it was one of the worst performances they’ve had under coach Matt LaFleur. The Packers were bludgeoned 27-2 by the Broncos in August 2024.
Friday night’s performance was a little different. The Packers scored more than two points, as Jordan Love’s only series of the night yielded a touchdown on an impressive 12-play drive that came against one of the league’s best defenses.
The Packers would score 26 more points, with another big night from one of their biggest stars in the preseason.
With just one game left on the exhibition slate, here are our winners and losers from Green Bay’s 33-13 win.
When the Packers drafted Trey Smack, Brian Gutekunst was asked how to scout a kicker. Gutekunst raised his arms in the air as if to make the “good” sign.
Gutekunst was joking, but he’s right.
So far, that’s the only signal that Smack knows in games as an NFL kicker.
They don’t hand out MVP awards in the preseason but, if they did, it would be hard to argue against anyone other than Green Bay’s rookie kicker winning the award.
Smack was impressive in his debut in Pittsburgh, but the more good performances he can put together, the more confident he can become before the opener against Minnesota.
Smack was a perfect 7-for-7 against Denver with four field goals and three extra points. The highlight came on a 59-yard bomb that had plenty of room to spare. It’s early, and he has yet to kick in a game of consequence, but the Packers have to be thrilled with the progress of their rookie kicker in the summer.
Apart from Trey Smack, there may not be a player who needed a good training camp more than third-year running back MarShawn Lloyd.
Lloyd has always had the talent, but has needed to prove he could stay healthy.
Lloyd has made it through two games and showcased the talent that the Packers have been excited about through his injury-riddled career. The highlight of Lloyd’s night came as the capper of Green Bay’s opening drive on offense. Jordan Love found Lloyd on a Texas route in the middle of the field for an easy touchdown. It was his first touchdown in more than 1,000 days .
THINGS YOU LOVE TO SEE! 📺: Packers TV Network pic.twitter.com/9mk7y1ry1o
“Honestly, trust my training,” he told reporters after the game. “It’s a choice route, so you could either break in or break out. Because of his leverage, I was able to break in. He gave everything off the inside, and once I got through the inside, I was able to get to the end zone from there.”
That is the type of impact that Lloyd can make in the passing game, and if the Packers can get him through one more preseason game healthy, he’ll be able to showcase it in a regular-season game for the first time since Week 2 of the 2024 season.
With roster cuts looming, the Packers needed someone to separate themselves from the bottom of the safety depth chart. Late in the first half, safety Mark Perry threw his hat into the ring, jumping a route as Denver’s backup quarterback, Jarrett Stidham, was trying to lead a 2-minute drive.
Perry jumped in front of Lucas Krull to grab his first interception of the preseason. His big play gave the Packers the ball back with a chance to put more points on the board, and it led to one of Trey Smack’s biggest plays of the night.
Mark Perry came out of nowhere 😳 GBvsDEN on @nflnetwork Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/I7Jsn4Fi9u
With Evan Williams, Xavier McKinney and Javon Bullard all set in stone on the roster, the Packers are trying to find some depth at that position. There’s room to make a run at a roster spot here, and Perry gave himself something to build on going into the final week of the preseason.
“It was a big confidence booster for me,” Perry said . “Every day in practice, trying to make the plays that come to you and not chase plays. … I think that was big for me and, obviously, it juiced the team right before the half (and) was able to score some points."
Who would play in the slot if Javon Bullard is injured? That’s a question the Packers hope they never have to answer when the regular season comes around, but they have to for the time being as Bullard is sidelined with a foot injury.
One of the candidates is Kamal Hadden, who returned to the field for the first time since suffering a horrific ankle injury in last year’s blowout loss to the Ravens.
Hadden is proving to be quite the versatile piece in the defense. He was drafted by the Chiefs in 2024 as a boundary corner. For the Packers at training camp this week, he started working in the slot, and he played well at his new position on Friday by making five tackles, including two for losses.
The more you can do, the easier it is for the general manager to decide to keep you on cutdown day. Right now, Hadden is trying to prove he can do just about anything on the field.
Remember when Aaron Rodgers smiled for the NBC broadcast following their season-opening 10-3 win over the Bears in 2019 and said, “We’ve got a defense.”
Perhaps the Packers are feeling that way after Friday’s game about their special teams, in general, and return game, in particular.
Through two games, Trey Smack has yet to miss a kick. On Friday, Pierre Strong had a 68-yard kickoff return and Skyy Moore had a 30-yard kickoff return and 16-yard punt return.
Strong’s return was set up by good vision and excellent blocking from those in front of him, including Kristian Welch and Collin Oliver. This likely goes without saying, but it would have been the longest for the Packers last season.
Pierre Strong Jr. with a 68-yard kick return 🔥 GBvsDEN on @nflnetwork Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/QpchpKwmr0
Achord has been a breath of fresh air with the youthful energy and exuberance he has brought to a special teams that has been largely dormant during Matt LaFleur’s tenure as the head coach.
The job is not finished, as Achord has yet to coach in a real game for the Packers, but the early returns are encouraging.
Who is the young player who is going to make a run at the back end of the roster? Perhaps that could be Anthony Campbell.
Campbell has been swatting away passes during training camp like he’s Dikembe Mutumbo, but gave a glimpse that perhaps he could do a little more in Friday’s game. Campbell had one of the team’s two sacks and joined Chris McClellan on a tackle for loss. PFF credited him with a team-high four pressures.
Green Bay’s defensive line has been a surprising strength during the summer. Devonte Wyatt, Javon Hargrave, Karl Brooks, Warren Brinson and Chris McClellan are all very likely to make the team. Jonathan Ford has had a strong summer, and Nazir Stackhouse is someone the Packers liked enough to keep around all year a season ago.
Campbell is trying to state his case to force the Packers to make him their sixth defensive lineman, or perhaps roll with an extra guy in the early portion of the season.
If nothing else, Campbell has continued to make plays that should have him on the radar, whether in Green Bay or elsewhere.
On a night when there were not a ton of negatives for the Packers, one big one reared its ugly head early that could be a cause for concern when the regular season begins.
Green Bay’s pass rush has more than a few question marks surrounding it as Micah Parsons will not be ready for the start of the season. The quartet of Brenton Cox, Lukas Van Ness, Barryn Sorrell and Dani Dennis-Sutton have all had nice moments during training camp.
The three who played were silent during the cameo Green Bay’s starting defense made Friday night. Of the combined 21 pass-rushing opportunities for Van Ness, Sorrel and Cox, they contributed only one pressure (Cox). Including Collin Oliver’s five chances, they went 1-for-26.
Sure, the Broncos have one of the best offensive lines in football, but they’re going to…

title: Five Packers Who Helped Themselves vs. Broncos, Including Three on Bubble
full_text:
Life comes at you fast. In the NFL, it comes at a young player in the equivalent of a 4.4-second time in the 40.
So, a player like Green Bay Packers quarterback Kyle McCord can’t afford to look too far down the road. He’s got goals, though, and his performance at the Denver Broncos in Friday’s preseason game will help make them possible.
He’s one of five young players who really helped themselves in the 33-13 victory.
Kyle McCord is not going to make the 53-man roster. He could have thrown for 300 yards and five touchdowns against the Broncos and it probably wouldn’t have changed that reality.
Nonetheless, his second consecutive solid performance has all but ensured he will be the team’s No. 3 quarterback this season. That means a spot on the practice squad.
However, this year’s No. 2 quarterback, Tyrod Taylor, is 37 years old and on a one-year contract. It’s quite possible that being the No. 3 quarterback this season will jump McCord to the front of the line to be the No. 2 quarterback next season.
“Yeah, I would say that’s definitely the long-term goal,” McCord said this week. “But, at the same time, I feel like it’s so easy to get caught up in those long-term, down-the-line type of goals. I think the most important thing is being where your feet are and making the most out of every preseason game, every practice, every rep you get.”
This pass was perfectly placed 🤌 (Via @NFL ) pic.twitter.com/ceKVjyprb7
McCord did that against the Broncos. He was 12-of-19 passing for 118 yards. Two of the seven incompletions were drops. Another came when it appeared the intended receiver missed the hot read as the Broncos sent an all-out blitz.
McCord played the final 32 minutes. The name of the game as a quarterback is to lead the offense to points. In five possessions, he led the Packers to three field goals and one touchdown.
Will Sheppard spent his final collegiate season at Colorado, making this game a homecoming of sorts.
He was the king of the receivers, catching all six targets for 47 yards and one touchdown. The touchdown was elite-level stuff as he got both feet down before being pushed out of bounds.
The catch. The toe tap. INSANE TD by Will Sheppard 🙌 GBvsDEN on @nflnetwork Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/a4Qprlj3uN
“At the catch point, it was kind of like slow motion almost,” he said. “I felt myself drag the toe, but I didn’t know exactly where I was on the field until the replay.”
The Packers’ top six receivers seem pretty well established. Could the Packers keep seven? Sheppard isn’t as flashy as Isaiah Neyor or J. Michael Sturdivant, but he’s been more consistently productive during camp.
Against Denver, Neyor was guilty of two penalties and one drop and Sturdivant didn’t return after a helmet-to-helmet tackle.
Pierre Strong has played well enough on the practice field to merit a spot on the roster, but the depth chart has made that an uphill climb . Josh Jacobs is the established starter, MarShawn Lloyd is healthy and ready to be the backup and Chris Brooks handles the intangibles such as pass protection and special teams.
Strong, however, had a 68-yard kickoff return and added eight carries for 37 yards.
YOOOOOOOOO 📺: Packers TV Network pic.twitter.com/ytx4vBIY8m
“Not everybody can do special teams,” Strong said. “Some coaches say, ‘You have to be special players to be special teams.’ Just doing whatever coach asks me to do and get on special teams because not everybody’s good at special teams.”
Strong was a fourth-round pick by the Patriots in 2022. He boasted a 5.0-yard average during his first three seasons but was released by the Browns at the end of training camp last year. He spent all of last season on Green Bay’s practice squad without getting in a game.
With excellent vision and speed, Strong has produced several explosive cutback runs at practice. Now, with a strong game, he’s built some momentum headed into the final week of camp.
“I’m just doing my job, just bringing my best, being the best that I can be every single day,” he said. “So, you call it momentum, but I just call it consistency.”
The battle for the fifth spot at safety has been a spirited one between a pair of undrafted players, Mark Perry and Murvin Kenion.
To win the job, someone had to make a play .
Late in the first half, Perry read veteran quarterback Jarrett Stidham, made an explosive break on the ball and grabbed an interception.
OUR BALL 📺: Packers TV Network pic.twitter.com/zYe9WKxDIW
“Yeah, it was a coverage we repped in practice,” Perry explained. “I had my eyes on the quarterback, and seeing the release of the tight end, I knew he was running that seam [route] because the release he had. Once I saw the quarterback let it go, it was just a matter of contorting my body to get inside, trying to get the ball. I knew it was coming and was able to come up with that play.”
Perry went undrafted in 2024. The Packers are his sixth team; he’s never been on a 53-man roster or played in a game. Before training camp, he said this opportunity “feels a little different” than the past couple seasons.
It was his first interception since the 2021 season, when he was a redshirt sophomore at Colorado.
For rookie kicker Trey Smack, it’s all about consistency.
After kicking inconsistently in OTAs, minicamp and the start of training camp, Smack made all four field-goal attempts at Pittsburgh. Critically, he did it again against Denver .
Officially, Smack is 7-of-7 on field goals during the preseason. Unofficially, he is 8-of-8 with four makes beyond 50 yards.
“I don’t know if there’s certainly a message that I can give to them,” he said of the Packers. “I’m just kind of trying to do my job, trying to live up to the expectation that they want me to. I’m very grateful that I’m here. I’m very grateful that I’m a Green Bay Packer. That never wants to change for me. I always want to be a Green Bay Packer, so whatever I can do – I’m not sure what that is – just make my kicks and honor that.”
That the Packers beat the Broncos is irrelevant. These are the three things that did matter. ⬇️ https://t.co/ugNFs94gvg

title: Here Are the Three Things That Mattered From Packers’ Victory Over Broncos
full_text:
The Green Bay Packers trounced the Denver Broncos in a preseason game on Friday night. Nothing could be more irrelevant than the final score of 33-13.
However, two of the most important developments imaginable for the success of the upcoming season took place in Denver. They highlight our three postgame takeaways.
Other than the return of Tucker Kraft, arguably nothing could be more important to the development of Green Bay’s offense than the emergence of MarShawn Lloyd.
A third-round pick in 2024, you know his story too well. He spent most of his first two seasons on injured reserve due to one injury or setback after another. Lloyd played in one game as a rookie and zero games last season.
Lloyd has had the football equivalent of perfect attendance this year. He didn’t miss a practice during the offseason and he hasn’t missed a practice during training camp. The more he’s practiced, questions about his availability have begun to take a back seat to questions about his ability.
Really, did anyone have the foggiest idea if Lloyd was any good? Talented, obviously. But good at football?
Lloyd was good at Denver. The rushing numbers might not show it, with six carries for 17 yards, but the third-and-2 conversion in which he fought past cornerback Pat Surtain II is the type of play a running back has to make. That play set him up for his 11-yard touchdown catch from Jordan Love, with Lloyd posterizing Dondrea Tillman, who was as effective in coverage as either one of us.
Lloyd was the No. 1 read on the play, Love said.
“Man, that was great,” Love told reporters. “I think really the whole drive, he had some really good runs. Being able to cap it off with that touchdown catch was great. MarShawn’s journey, dealing with different injuries throughout preseason games and things like that, for him to be out there and be putting up plays and just be able to see him is great.
“I think he’s done a lot of good things all throughout camp. Just keep building on it.”
It was a big moment for Lloyd, as evidenced by his celebration. And for good reason. It was his first touchdown since USC’s loss at Oregon on Nov. 11, 2023. That was 1,014 days ago. It was his first touchdown catch since Sept. 29, 2022, while at South Carolina – a span of 1,422 days.
“It was special, it was fun. It was definitely fun,” he said. “It had been three years since I even touched the end zone. I’ve been in the end zone in practice but, in the game, it’s different. It was fun. They had their starters out there, so it was fun to get those good reps, just good reps. I enjoyed it.”
Without Lloyd, the Packers the past two seasons paired Josh Jacobs and Emanuel Wilson. Essentially, they were the same running back. Now, the Packers will go into the season with Jacobs and Lloyd – just like they envisioned when they signed Jacobs and drafted Lloyd in 2024. Their different styles should open some new possibilities for an offense that needs to be much more productive than it was last year.
There’s an elephant in the room that’s about as big as Lambeau Field.
Until Micah Parsons not only returns but returns to dominating form, who’s going to rush the passer ?
The answer on Friday night, at least when the starters were in the game, is nobody.
Given plenty of time by his polished offensive line, Bo Nix was 6-of-9 passing for 76 yards. Facing Green Bay’s starting defense for two series, he led the Broncos to 10 points. On the opening series, which resulted in a touchdown, Nix converted a third-and-5 and a third-and-6 with downfield throws.
At one point, Lukas Van Ness had a one-on-one against a tight end and made no headway.
Van Ness has had some really good days at training camp. So has Brenton Cox. But the consistency hasn’t been there. To be sure, it will help when Devonte Wyatt and Javon Hargrave – neither of whom played against Denver are on the field. Plus, defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon will dig into his bag of tricks.
But an elite edge pass rusher is one of the most important players in the sport. It’s why the Packers gave up so much draft capital, talent and money to acquire Parsons. At some point, Van Ness and Cox and Barryn Sorrell are going to have to make a play. When that moment comes, are they capable of making it?
After he missed so many kicks during the offseason practices and the start of training camp, it’s no wonder why general manager Brian Gutekunst and coach Matt LaFleur were cautiously optimistic about rookie kicker Trey Smack following the Pittsburgh game.
“Good performance from one day, right?” Gutekunst said this week.
Now, it’s good performances from two days.
Smack made all four field-goal attempts against the Broncos. That includes kicks of 51 and 59 yards. Counting the one that was nullified by a penalty last week, Smack is 8-of-8 during the preseason and 4-of-4 from 50-plus yards.
“Feel great but … he’s got to do it again,” LaFleur said after the game. “That’s life in the National Football League. You’re only as good as your last performance and he’s put two pretty darn good performances back-to-back. The talent’s there. He’s just got to continue to be consistent.”
When Smack was struggling on the practice field, special teams coordinator Cam Achord said he was more concerned about how the rookie performed in stadiums. Well, he went 6-of-7 at Lambeau Field on Family Night and is officially 7-of-7 in the preseason. That’s 13-of-14 – or 16-of-17 if you count extra-point attempts.
“I feel good,” he told reporters after the game. “I don’t want to get too high on it because I know I’ve got to stay locked in in this business and you can’t get complacent with yourself. So, just trying to improve every week.”

title: Smackdown: Packers Blow Out Broncos for Preseason Victory
full_text:
The Green Bay Packers’ preseason victory over the Denver Broncos on Friday night was as meaningful as their loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers last week was meaningless.
Still, a 33-13 victory over a team that might have reached the Super Bowl had starting quarterback Bo Nix been healthy was impressive. It kicked off a pivotal stretch for the Packers, who have a couple starting positions up for grabs and quite a bit of uncertainty at the bottom of the roster.
Coming up, the Packers will host the Arizona Cardinals for a joint practice on Wednesday and the final preseason game next Friday. Two days later, on Aug. 30, general manager Brian Gutekunst must cut his roster from 91 players to 53.
The Packers “competed in really every phase,” coach Matt LaFleur said after the game.
“That’s a really good football team and we knew that that’s a physical bunch, so we knew we had to match that,” he continued.
Highlighted by four field goals by Trey Smack, who probably clinched the kicking job after a rocky offseason and start to training camp, the Packers led 23-10 at halftime. Sure, it’s the preseason, but it was a quality performance given how poorly they played in last week’s 28-9 loss at the Steelers.
The Packers won the opening coin toss and drove straight down the field for a touchdown. Jordan Love on fourth-and-1 hit Matthew Golden for 20 yards, with Golden continuing his excellent August by making a one-handed catch on a ball thrown just below his hip.
Then, MarShawn Lloyd did his thing. First, on third-and-2, he put his shoulder into All-Pro cornerback Pat Surtain II and fought for the first down. Finally, on third-and-3 from the 11, he destroyed a Broncos defender on his route, caught the ball at the 8 and sprinted into the end zone. Lloyd celebrated like a player who hadn’t scored a touchdown since he was at USC in 2023.
Love was 5-of-7 for 56 yards and the touchdown, good for a passer rating of 134.5.
“The whole operation,” impressed coach Matt LaFleur, he said during his halftime interview. “I thought he was poised, making the right decisions. It was a collective effort.”
The Broncos answered with a touchdown; Xavier McKinney gave up a 35-yard catch on third-and-5 and Edgerrin Cooper gave up the touchdown.
Denver took a 10-7 lead early in the second quarter before the game swung Green Bay’s way. Pierre Strong returned the ensuing kickoff 68 yards to the 32. The drive didn’t go anywhere but Smack bombed a 51-yard field goal.
A pair of defensive penalties helped the Packers take a 17-10 lead with 3:07 left in the half. On third-and-goal from the 2, Tyrod Taylor threw a fade to Will Sheppard, with the former Colorado player making a superb toe-dragging touchdown catch.
The Packers weren’t done. And neither was Smack. First, Jaylin Simpson had the coverage on a fourth-and-5 incompletion, which gave the offense great field position. Smack smacked a 59-yard field goal – his fourth of longer than 50 yards this preseason. Smack was fired up long before the ball split the uprights with plenty of distance to spare.
Moments later, safety Mark Perry – who’s in the thick of the chase for a roster spot – made a sensational read and picked off veteran quarterback Jarrett Stidham. Smack kicked a 43-yard field goal to give the Packers a 23-10 lead at halftime.
Green Bay’s offense was one-and-done with its touchdown. It required some good fortune. On the second play, Christian Watson caught a slant and picked up a first down before he was stripped by All-Pro cornerback Patrick Surtain. The Broncos recovered but Watson was ruled down on a bang-bang play.
The defense played two series. Broncos quarterback Bo Nix was 6-of-9 passing for 76 yards and one touchdown. The pass rush was mostly nonexistent.
At cornerback, Brandon Cisse and Keisean Nixon started and played the opening series. Benjamin St-Juste and Nixon played the second series; Cisse appeared to be shaken up on special teams, so it’s not certain if he played one series by design or by necessity.
Green Bay’s special teams under new coordinator Cam Achord might be on the upswing.
Strong’s 68-yard kickoff return picked up a number of key blocks, including by veteran special-teams standout Kristian Welch. Skyy Moore had a 16-yard punt return. And Smack made all three field-goal attempts, making him officially 6-of-6 through six quarters of the preseason.
It was huge for Smack, who added one more field goal in the fourth quarter, to turn one good preseason game into two.
“Good performance from one day, right?” general manager Brian Gutekunst said this week in light of the Pittsburgh game. “You know, that’s what that is, and he’s had a bunch of them during the camp but that, obviously, was the most important one. That’s the one that actually counts for points in a game. Those are what you want.”
Welch and Arron Mosby had two tackles apiece in the first half.
The Broncos pulled within 23-13 late in the third quarter. Chris McClellan had a tackle for loss and cornerback MJ Devonshire and Jaylin Simpson prevented completions to former fourth-round pick Hakeem Butler.
Green Bay answered, though, on Jaden Nixon’s 3-yard touchdown run. Kyle McCord might have clinched the No. 3 job – meaning a spot on the practice squad – on this drive. First, he hit Isaiah Neyor for 27 on the final play of the third quarter and Neyor for 11 more at the start of the fourth quarter.
Nixon then burst up the middle for 16 to the 3 behind blocks by center Dylan Barrett, right guard Travis Glover and right tackle Brant Banks. One play later, Barrett led the line’s surge that got Nixon into the end zone for a 30-13 lead.
On the ensuing possession, Jonathan Ford’s quick pressure up the middle set up Nyjalik Kelly for a sack/strip that the Broncos quarterback Sam Ehlinger recovered. On the next play, Anthony Cambell continued his incredible August by destroying Gavin Ortega for a punishing sack to force a punt.
On the next drive, just before the 2-minute warning, McCord went over 100 passing yards by hitting Sheppard between two defenders for 20 yards. Smack belted a 38-yard field goal to cap the scoring.
Sheppard caught six passes for 47 yards and the touchdown and Strong had a team-high 37 rushing yards. The Packers finished with 299 yards. Rookie defensive tackle Chris McClellan was tremendous with a team-high six tackles. Hadden had five tackles, including two for losses.

title: Studs, Duds for Packers During First Half at Broncos
full_text:
The Green Bay Packers lead the Denver Broncos 23-10 at halftime on Friday night. Here are the studs and duds.
The Packers struck first against the Broncos with a 12-play, 63-yard scoring drive. On third-and-2, MarShawn Lloyd roasted outside linebacker Dondrea Tillman for an 11-yard touchdown. It was a mismatch, and Lloyd took full advantage. He caught the ball at the 8, strolled into the end zone and celebrated as if he were a third-year player who hadn’t scored a touchdown in his career.
More impressive, though, was a third-and-2 earlier in the drive. Drake Dabney had a good block at star outside linebacker Nik Bonitto, which left Lloyd with a one-on-one against elite cornerback Pat Surtain II to get the first down. Lloyd put his shoulder into Surtain and fought for every inch. He needed every inch; Lloyd got the first down after a virtual replay review.
On the second drive, with the backups in, Lloyd ran through an arm tackle by Bonitto for a 7-yard gain and a first down.
“All you guys that have been around know, when players miss time, that’s tough,” general manager Brian Gutekunst said this week. “That’s tough on these guys. They’re young guys, and they want to be out there so badly. You saw Tuck [Tucker Kraft] get out there for the first time the other day; no different than MarShawn.
“When they get out there and they’re playing football, they’re usually at their happiest. And so, whenever you see guys go through things and then get back out there, you can kind of see the joy in them. And I’m happy for him.”
On the opening drive, Matthew Golden had a one-handed catch of a slightly off-target pass on fourth-and-1. The 20-yard gain set up the opening touchdown.
You can’t fumble. Christian Watson fumbled once each of the last two seasons. On the opening series, he was bailed out on a bang-bang play, with review showing Watson’s knee hit the turf the smallest fraction of a second before Watson had the ball ripped out by Patrick Surtain.
New starting left tackle Jordan Morgan had tough duty with a measuring-stick matchup against All-Pro outside linebacker Nik Bonitto.
Morgan did an excellent job, including on the back-to-back passes to Christian Watson to start the drive. On the touchdown pass to MarShawn Lloyd, Morgan didn’t have to protect for long but was a brick wall against Malcolm Roach.
“I think we’re very comfortable with him there,” Gutekunst said. “He’s going to have to go out and do it over a full season and year in and year out. But he’s done a really nice job through the spring, really nice job so far.
“I’m looking forward to getting some more reps here in the preseason and then get ready for the regular season. We think he’s got a super-bright future to be a really good player in this league. I’m sure he’ll go through his ups and downs like they all do at that position because that’s one of those positions where you’re going to have some of that. But I’m excited for him.”
This play was indicative of Green Bay’s pass rush against Denver’s offensive line: On the second possession, after Denver picked up a first down, Bo Nix threw downfield but missed Pat Bryant despite having all day.
Lukas Van Ness lined up on the left edge. The matchup was against tight end Evan Engram, which should be a mismatch in Green Bay’s favor but was a mismatch in Denver’s favor in reality.
A rookie is going to lose at times. On third-and-1 at the start of the second possession, a handoff to the fullback gained the first down because veteran right tackle Mike McGlinchey torqued rookie Chris McClellan out of the hole.
Later in the drive, though, McClellan stormed up the middle to force Bo Nix to dump it off to the running back. Then, on third-and-18, McClellan beat veteran left guard Ben Powers’ one-on-one block and limited a draw play to just a few yards.
Early in the second quarter, McClellan drew a holding penalty to ruin a drive.
On the first drive, starting right guard Jacob Monk was flagged for holding. On the second drive, backup right guard Donovan Jennings was beaten badly by Malcolm Roach on a failed third-and-6. On the third drive, left guard Jager Burton had a good block but was flagged for holding at the end.
Pierre Strong had a 68-yard kickoff return to Denver’s 32. Kristian Welch, Collin Oliver and Thomas Yassmin were among the players with key blocks. That set up rookie kicker Trey Smack’s 51-yard field goal.
“That's just kind of my job,” Smack said this week. “I’ve got to make kicks, so I’ve got to treat it like that's my job, and I’ve got to keep going with that. Build on the confidence part. That's what I'm supposed to do. That's why I'm here. So, that's kind of the way I view it.”
The Broncos had an explosive return on the ensuing kickoff – Smack had the tackle – but the defense held firm and Skyy Moore returned the punt for 16 yards.
Finally, late in the first half, Smack belted a 59-yard field goal. He started to celebrate a nanosecond after the ball left his foot. He’s 4-of-4 from 50-plus yards in the preseason. Then, on the final play, he split the uprights from 43 yards.
Welch had two tackles on special teams, as well.
Will Sheppard, who played collegiately at Colorado, had a big-time, toe-tapping touchdown catch on third-and-goal late in the second quarter. The catch came against last year’s first-round pick, Jahdae Barron.
Isaiah Neyor was flagged for an egregious illegal block in the back before making a tremendous catch on a pass thrown too far in front of him. After that superb catch, Neyor had a bad drop on the next possession.
Kamal Hadden, playing in his first game since last year’s devastating ankle injury, made a pair of open-field tackles. The first was a tackle for loss on a pass and the second was on third-and-10.
In the battle to be the fifth safety, somebody needed to make a play between Mark Perry and Murvin Kenion III. Late in the first half, with the Broncos trying to eat into Green Bay’s lead, Perry jumped Jarrett Stidham’s pass to tight end Lucas Krull and delivered a sensational interception to set up the Packers for one more field goal.
Here are 13 players to watch for the Packers at Denver tonight. The Broncos will play (most) of their starters, so there are some intriguing measuring-stick matchups. ⬇️ https://t.co/HhrwqQLrB9
- These players were the equivalent of regular-season inactives: edges Micah Parsons and Dani Dennis-Sutton, safety Javon Bullard, running back Josh Jacobs, receiver Jayden Reed, cornerback Carrington Valentine, long snapper Matt Orzech, right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele, left guard Aaron Banks, offensive lineman Darian Kinnard, tight ends Tucker Kraft and Luke Musgrave, and defensive tackles Devonte Wyatt, Jordon Riley and Javon Hargrave.

- Isaiah McDuffie, Zaire Franklin and Hadden had tackles for losses in the first half.
- Jaylin Simpson, who was victimized in slot coverage at Pittsburgh, had coverage to prevent a fourth-and-4 completion late in the first half.

title: 13 Most Important Packers to Watch at Broncos, Including Starters vs. Stars
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers will play most of their starters against the Denver Broncos in Friday night’s preseason game. So will the Broncos.
Thus, this should be a good litmus test between two Super Bowl contenders. The Packers are 6.5-point underdogs – the line was 5.5 at the start of the day – at FanDuel Sportsbook . Both starting quarterbacks will play.
Here is a look at a baker’s dozen of the most important players.
The Broncos have an elite pass rush and a premier cornerback with Pat Surtain II. There could hardly be a better test for Jordan Love, who really struggled when pressured last season.
“Like I talked about last week, it’s another away game, so another chance for us to have that communication in the huddle, make sure everything’s on point and we’re hearing everything right,” Love said after Tuesday’s practice.
“It’s a lot different than being at practice with just the music blasting, so just being in that environment if we’ve got to go work on our operation with silent (count). But just make sure the operation’s smooth, everything’s crisp. We’ll be seeing new looks, so make sure everybody’s on the same page. Really just getting those game jitters out, so when Week 1 hits, everybody’s ready to fly around.”
Love’s over/under , for what it’s worth, is 20 passing yards.
Could the Packers keep seven receivers?
General manager Brian Gutekunst wouldn’t rule it out.
“I think if you’re going to do that, there’s going to be a couple of those guys are going to have to be pretty valuable teams guys. And I think we have some of those,” Gutekunst said.
If the Packers keep a seventh, it will be one of these players. They’ve all had their moments at training camp but haven’t strung together consistently productive days. Isaiah Neyor led the team with four catches at Pittsburgh; J. Michael Sturdivant had two productive practices this week.
Jordan Morgan is the team’s new starting left tackle. For however long he’s in the game, he will face a premier matchup against Broncos outside linebacker Nik Bonitto.
Bonitto is Denver’s right outside linebacker so will see plenty of Morgan. The two-time Pro Bowler had 13.5 sacks in 2024 and 14 sacks in 2025 with a total of 30 tackles for losses and four forced fumbles.
“I think he’s done some great things,” Love said of Morgan. “I think he’s definitely improved tremendously. And I think it’s one of those things where I just want to get to the games and see how we just keep building and how he looks out there. But definitely got a lot of confidence in him, a lot of trust. That’s one of those things where my back’s going to be to him all game. So, got to have that confidence that he’s going to hold it down and he’s been doing great things.
Starting left guard Aaron Banks finally took part in team reps this week. Regardless of whether it’s Banks or rookie Jager Burton manning the position at Denver, he will face an enormous challenge against Zach Allen.
Allen, who lines up mostly on the right side of the defense, is one of the most underrated defensive linemen in the NFL. He led all interior rushers in pressures each of the last two seasons, when he was second-team All-Pro in 2024 with 8.5 sacks and 15 tackles for losses and first-team All-Pro in 2025 with seven sacks and four TFLs.
“I think there’s plenty to work on,” Burton said on the heels of starting last week at Pittsburgh. “Always for me, it’s the consistency. When I do it right it looks good, just like anybody else, but finding a way for that to be every time – my best every time – is really what this game is all about.
“It’s kind of chasing ghosts getting there because it’s probably never going to happen, but you want to get as close to that as possible. That’s why this game is so awesome.”
Jonathan Ford has taken the lead in the race for the starting job at nose tackle. Nazir Stackhouse isn’t going to go quietly into the night, though, in a battle in which only one might make the roster.
Broncos coach Sean Payton played his No. 1 line a lot last week, with at least 25 snaps for all three interior starters – a group that includes elite right guard Quinn Meinerz.
“Just consistency,” Ford said of what he needs to show over the final two games. “I think that’s the biggest thing in this league is being consistent and being able to show coaches you can do it snap after snap. If you have a bad snap, you can correct it – take the corrections, bring it back on the field and do it the right way that coaches coached you to do it.
“I think the biggest thing for me is being consistent and showing that I’m a player down in and down out and I can do my job and do it at a high level.”
The coaches seem reluctant to replace Keisean Nixon in the starting lineup. After a horrendous missed tackle at Pittsburgh in the game last Thursday night, Nixon took all the No. 1 reps at the next practice.
If Nixon shows up and plays fast and physically against the Bo Nix-led Broncos offense, he might wrap up his spot in the starting lineup for Week 1 at Minnesota.
“Kei has always answered the bell,” coach Matt LaFleur said this week. “Every time we’ve given him any opportunity, he’s performed. He’s a very competitive dude.”
The Packers have lined up without nickel Javon Bullard for more than a week. What would the Packers do if Bullard were to miss a game that matters?
Coming off last year’s season-ending ankle injury, Kamal Hadden has been fully integrated into practice. A perimeter cornerback by trade, he took a lot of first-team reps in the slot this week. If Hadden plays well against the Broncos – their backup quarterback is veteran Jarrett Stidham – he might win the job.
If the Packers keep five safeties, one of these players will win the job. Perry went undrafted in 2024 and hasn’t played in a regular-season game in his career. Kenion went undrafted this year and might be the team’s best bet to extend its streak to 22 consecutive years with an undrafted rookie on the Week 1 roster.
Both players displayed the desired physicality last week. Now, can either make a big play to push the battle in his favor?

title: How Wade Woodaz's Latest Injury Changes Texans' LB Room
full_text:
The Houston Texans' linebacker room has been hit with another injury: fourth-round rookie Wade Woodaz .
According to KPRC2 's Aaron Wilson , Woodaz is expected to undergo surgery following the broken thumb injury he sustained in the Texans' preseason game against the Las Vegas Raiders.
His timeline for return reportedly remains undetermined, but placing Woodaz on injured reserve before the season remains a possibility.
It's one of multiple injuries the Texans have seen in their linebacker unit before Week 1 of the regular season.
Woodaz joins both E.J. Speed (quad) and Jake Hansen (ankle) as candidates who could end up missing the start of the year, and thus makes the position group even thinner from what they were working with.
Let's break down what the injury to Woodaz means for the Texans' linebacker room moving forward:
After the Texans' training camp work and two games of preseason, it felt like Woodaz was the primary candidate in the lead to claim Houston's LB3 role before the season .
It's been a spot that's been open on Houston's defense since E.J. Speed first suffered his quad injury earlier this summer, but felt increasingly settled in Woodaz's hands, especially after his 80-yard pick-six on Fernando Mendoza against the Raiders that really made a statement on top of what he had already done through training camp.
But now, the Texans could have that LB3 job back up for grabs, at least to begin the 2026 season while Woodaz is off to the side. Perhaps that comes via someone already on the roster, or maybe Houston goes out to acquire someone via trade to really fill the position.
The two names who stick out with the most likely odds to get work in Houston's linebacker room are veteran Marte Mapu and seventh-round rookie Aiden Fisher .
Both have performed well throughout the past few weeks that the Texans have been back in the building, and will now have even more opportunity on their hands––especially if Woodaz is going to be placed on injured reserve to start the year.
Two other names to keep an eye on: fourth-year linebacker Jamal Hill and offseason free agent signing Jake Hummel. Each might be more geared towards being primarily a special teamer, but as the room continues to get slimmer, they'll have a better chance to lock themselves into a 53-man roster spot, but also into a bigger role defensively.
The Texans have already acted by adding extra depth within their linebacker room since Woodaz's injury, reportedly signing veteran Caleb Johnson. who's entering his sixth season in the NFL.
#Texans set to sign veteran linebacker Caleb Johnson after successful workout, per a league source. Johnson, the first @HouChristianU #NFL player in school history, Has 40 career tackles, one forced fumble, one fumble recovery, previously #Bears #Jaguars #Falcons #Dolphins … https://t.co/aqb3QREnEi pic.twitter.com/2OcqJXTAQv
The undrafted product out of Houston Christian has been mostly a special teamer throughout his five years in the pros, having played for the Chicago Bears, Jacksonville Jaguars, and Miami Dolphins. He has 40 career tackles and one forced fumble throughout his career.
Johnson has over 1,100 snaps on special teams throughout his time in the league. With the Dolphins last season, he played just two games and just 22 snaps, suffered a shoulder injury, and saw his 2025 campaign shortened because of it.
He may not have an inside track for the Texans roster with a week to go until cutdown day, but he will be someone to watch getting snaps in preseason later this week, as Houston travels to face the Carolina Panthers for their final preliminary showing on Friday, August 28th.

title: Derek Barnett's New Deal Proves Texans Got a Steal on Jadeveon Clowney
full_text:
A former piece of the Houston Texans' defense found a new home over the weekend.
According to a report from NFL insider Jeremy Fowler of ESPN , the Cleveland Browns have agreed to sign free agent defensive end Derek Barnett to a one-year, $5.5 million deal.
Defensive end Derek Barnett is signing with the Cleveland Browns on a one-year deal up to $5.5M, per source. The former first-round pick is back for Year 10, spent previous three years in Houston. pic.twitter.com/zyJT0hKM8q
The move for the Browns comes after their starting defensive end, Alex Wright, would be ruled out for the 2026 season with a ruptured Achilles, thus requiring Cleveland to go out to plug up their depth on the defensive line.
Barnett, still on the free agent market less than a month away from the regular season kicking off, made sense to fill that hole, as he now makes Cleveland his next stop after spending the past three years with the Texans.
Before Barnett had found his new home in Cleveland, there had been chatter leading up to training camp linking him to a potential reunion with the Texans this season.
Houston was in need of edge depth. Barnett had been familiar with their defense for three seasons, and he was a veteran on the market still looking to find somewhere to play for 2026.
Barnett had played 39 games with the Texans through the past three seasons, had over 60 tackles and 12 sacks, finishing his 2025 campaign with five sacks and 20 games.
Texans general manager Nick Caserio even made mention during training camp that the front office had conversations with Barnett on a new deal earlier this offseason. So Houston still clearly had its eyes on Barnett as a potential signing deep into the summer.
But the Texans went in another direction for that depth on their defensive line. They went out to sign former No. 1 overall pick Jadeveon Clowney, who, by most accounts, is an upgrade over what Barnett brings to the table.
Last season with the Dallas Cowboys, Clowney was more productive as a pass rusher and in defending the run than Barnett while playing fewer games. He had over 40 tackles and eight sacks through 13 games.
And now entering the 2026 season, the Texans brought in Clowney at virtually the same price as Barnett just went for in Cleveland. And they did so two weeks after Barnett signed.
While Barnett will be netting $5.5 million on his contract for the 2026 season, Clowney will be due a maximum of $8 million with incentives , a $5.5 million base value, and $4.5 million guaranteed.
So the Texans upgraded their defensive line by adding a presence like Clowney , but did so at essentially the same price that Barnett just went for.
It's a credit to not only the great business the Texans did with their acquisition of Clowney, but also to Clowney himself for being willing to take a pay cut in order to join a situation like Houston's.
Clowney noted at his opening press conference with the Texans that he could've gotten more money to join another team and likely get more snaps in the process. But his priority was to win games.
And in Houston, with the talent they have on their defense, he's got ample opportunities to do just that––albeit on a bit of a pay cut.
As a result, the Texans' defensive line will be looking deeper, stronger, and even more potent from how they finished their 2025 campaign, where this pass-rush may have already had the best one-two punch at the position with Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter.

title: DeMeco Ryans Explains Texans’ Zay Jones, Sterling Shepard Signings
full_text:
Earlier this week, the Houston Texans went out to add a couple of new veteran wide receivers to their 90-man roster: Sterling Shepard and Zay Jones .
It's no secret as to why the move was done. The Texans, after they saw second-year wide receiver Jayden Higgins go down with a season-ending ACL tear earlier in the week, felt the need to go out and add more depth at the position.
Shepard and Jones were brought in for a workout. Houston liked what they saw. And now, both guys will be competing for a spot on the 53-man roster.
But after the Texans' latest training camp practice, head coach DeMeco Ryans was able to open up on his thoughts about his two newest wide receivers in the building.
In Ryans' mind, he sees a ton of veteran experience within the two guys they signed on in Sterling and Jones. And after the loss of Higgins, their presence could end up being pretty valuable.
"We signed two veteran guys, and we’ll see what they can provide," Ryans said after the Shepard and Jones signings. "When it comes to adding depth in our receiver room, it’s no secret that we lost a very significant piece in our receiver room in Jayden Higgins.”
"We’re still trying to find a way to help out in our receiver room, and that’s what those two guys provide: veteran experience, guys who have done it before, done it at a high level, played in a lot of different systems, and we will see what they can bring to us.”
When it comes to receivers who were on the free agent market, not many are left up for grabs who offer that necessary edge of experience, while still potentially being a productive piece on the field.
Sterling and Jones, though, who each are over 30 years old with over eight years of NFL experience, seem to have enough upside to bank on to bring into the building and essentially try out for their 53-man roster.
Sterling is fresh off another 300-yard campaign with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. He's played 10 years in the NFL with 4,800 career receiving yards and 25 touchdowns.
He'll be entering his age-33 season here in Houston, but he's remained a consistent depth piece in the receiver room both in Tampa Bay and the New York Giants, that makes him a worthwhile dart throw to bring onto the roster.
As for Jones, he's only a few years removed from his 800-yard campaign with the Jacksonville Jaguars in 2022, but also has a ton of experience in multiple receiver rooms that could end up being beneficial for this Texans group.
In nine years pro, he's played for the Jaguars, Arizona Cardinals, Las Vegas Raiders, and the Buffalo Bills, and has collected over 300 receptions, 3,200 receiving yards and 18 touchdowns.
Will either Shepard or Jones showcase enough to warrant the Texans bringing them onto the 53-man roster? That depends on how they show up in practice and in their final preseason game of the year vs. the Carolina Panthers before cutdown day hits next weekend.
But based on the current state of the Texans' wide receiver room after Higgins' injury , nothing can be ruled out for how the front office opts to approach the position ahead of Week 1. So keep a close eye on both Sterling and Jones and their chances to make the roster in the days ahead.

title: Texans' QB3 Spot Looks Less Certain After Raiders Preseason Game
full_text:
The Houston Texans' QB3 spot was shaken up significantly earlier last week when second-year signal-caller Graham Mertz went down with a torn ACL , effectively ending his 2026 campaign.
In the days following, the Texans went on to sign veteran quarterback Brett Rypien , an experienced name at the position who became an easy favorite to fill into that QB3 spot for the season and play the next couple of preseason games to prove that he's worth it.
But with week two of the preseason down against the Las Vegas Raiders , there's a chance that the Texans' QB3 outlook now looks a little more complicated than expectations were shaping up after the Rypien signing.
In Rypien's Texans debut, his performance wasn't exactly exemplary. He played the entire second half of the game and entered as Houston was up 20-3, and proceeded not to score another point.
In all, Rypien completed six of his 10 passes for 44 yards, was sacked twice, threw an interception on the last drive of the game, and lost one of his two total fumbles on the night. Houston would be outscored 19-0 in the second half and drop their second preseason game in a row.
For a performance in which the quarterback is battling for staying power and a roster spot for Week 1, it's not exactly the most ideal outing. C.J. Stroud had a strong performance, Mills played well in his first quarter reps, but Rypien fell short of expectations.
Of course, it's one preseason outing, and Rypien probably isn't going to get many snaps for Houston this season anyways. There are certainly other pressing matters to address around the roster.
But for the Texans, at the very least, Rypien's lackluster day might just open up the question of whether or not they should add another name to the position for their third and final preseason game to add some more competition under center.
The Texans have three routes they could take for their QB3 position: they roll with Rypien, they bring in another name off the free agent market or via trade, or they simply carry two quarterbacks into Week 1 with C.J. Stroud and Davis Mills.
All three have a real possibility of being the end result. The outcome that can't be ruled out is the Texans bringing in just two quarterbacks for Week 1 if they can't find a strong enough QB3 in the time between now and cutdown day.
However, it's certainly a bit more complicated of a situation compared to what Houston entered their second preseason game with.
When it comes to the Texans' first and second quarterbacks on the depth chart, there are no doubts about who will be the two filling things out. But that third spot––whether it ends up being Rypien, someone else, or nobody else––will remain one of the bigger question marks in the days ahead of cutdown day at the end of August.

title: Predicting Texans' WR Depth Chart After Shepard, Jones Signings
full_text:
The Houston Texans' wide receiver room has taken a bit of a different shape from where things stood this time last week.
Jayden Higgins is out for the season with a torn ACL. Guys like Tank Dell and Jaylin Noel are still slowly recovering from their respective injuries . And just recently, the Texans added two new veteran wide receivers onto their 90-man roster: Sterling Shepard and Zay Jones.
The #Texans are signing veteran WRs Sterling Shepard and Zay Jones, sources tell me and @RapSheet . Both impressed in a workout today and join the mix in Houston after the loss of Jayden Higgins to a torn ACL. pic.twitter.com/oYlmSVJ4BT
So now feels like about as good a time as any to break down how the Texans' wide receiver room is expected to shake out, how the depth chart could be ordered, and who might be in (or out) of the 53-man roster picture once cuts arrive at the end of the month.
Let's sort through everyone on the Texans' roster at wide receiver and see where they stand less than 10 days out from cutdown day:
With or without Jayden Higgins on the field, Nico Collins was always going to be bound for the most snaps as the Texans' X wide receiver, and the most targets in the offense as a whole. But without Higgins there to complement him as his No. 2, there's a chance that Collins could be en route to the best season of his career.
Last season, Collins had over 1,100 yards and 71 receptions with six touchdowns in 15 games. There's a good chance he surpasses all three of those marks in 2026, so long as he's able to remain healthy.
This is right where you'd expect to see Higgins in the Texans' depth chart. Now, the offense has to pivot, and the wideout with the best chance to fill the void that he leaves is fourth-year veteran Xavier Hutchinson.
Hutchinson is coming off a career season in 2025 with over 400 receiving yards, has been with C.J. Stroud in Houston every year since he arrived in 2023, and has the ideal skillset to complement Collins on the opposite side of him in the offense––even if not as athletically gifted or as explosive as Higgins is.
Jaylin Noel is slowly returning to the Texans' lineup after suffering a hamstring and a finger injury at the start of training camp . And as long as he's good to go for Week 1 of the regular season, he's the clear favorite within this wide receiver room to take the most reps in the slot.
The second-year wideout could have a case to be one of the Texans' biggest breakout candidates since Higgins' injury. He's a young pass-catcher who's due for a huge jump in snaps offensively, had a similarly productive offseason to Higgins, and Houston invested a good bit into him last year as a third-round pick. He'll be someone to keep an eye on in the weeks ahead.
Once cutdown day hits, the Texans' wide receiver room could come down to six to seven names. Four of those––Collins, Hutchinson, Noel, and Dell––are virtual locks. So the final two to three are widely up for grabs.
I think of the two newest signings, Sterling Shepard has a better chance to make it to Week 1 . He's been more productive than Zay Jones in recent seasons, even if Jones fits a better physical profile to what the Texans need. Lewis Bond has been a camp star worthy of a 53-man spot, and a veteran like Justin Watson might now be more valuable to have with Higgins out.
Zay Jones could still make it to the 53-man roster, but he needs to prove that he can still remain on the field consistently at 31 years old, while also being a productive pass-catcher at this point in his career. Since 2023, he's played in 208 games and averaged less than two catches and 25 yards per game.
Jared Wayne is also someone to keep a close eye on . He's been someone making noise throughout camp and in preseason, and as a 6-foot-3, 210-pound wideout, maybe the Texans could value him as a bigger target to have in the room, who's also been around the building since 2024.
These five wide receivers are still listed on the Texans' 90-man roster, but don't exactly have an inside track to make it past cutdown day at the end of the month.
Perhaps a practice squad nod is in store for one or multiple of them. Daniel Sobkowicz has been someone many have liked when he was picked up as a UDFA in April , so maybe he finds his way in there. But when compared to the nine players clearly sitting ahead of them in the pecking order, it doesn't feel like anything more is within reach for anyone in this tier.

title: Texans Announce Release Date for New Rivalries Uniforms
full_text:
The Houston Texans have announced the release date for their newest Rivalries uniforms for the 2026 NFL season .
And it looks like the release of those new uniforms for Houston sits right around the corner.
The Texans put out a promotional video for their upcoming uniform release, where players around the roster reacted to the new threads for the first time.
And in that video, the Texans revealed that those uniforms will be officially unveiled to the public on Tuesday, August 25th .
No peekingggg 👀 pic.twitter.com/oC1xmJDmy6
The reviews from some of the players were clearly positive, which could be a sign of things to come for next week’s reveal.
"That s---- gas," said Tank Dell.
"Oh, that's tough," was what Reed Blankenship said.
"I can get jiggy with that," came from Kamari Lassiter.
And along with the release date and the reaction video from the players, the Texans also released a new teaser for the new uniforms on the horizon––where the uniform was described as a set that'll seek innovation, being different, and "the most Houston thing that you've ever seen on the gridiron."
Houston, this one’s for you 🤘 pic.twitter.com/LmCAaELDCv
With the Texans set to receive their Rivalries uniforms for next season, it'll be one of five uniforms that Houston will be able to wear throughout the year: their typical home and away jerseys, their all-red alternates, and their dark-blue "Space City" themed uniforms, and now, another set of alternates.
On most weeks, the Texans will be wearing their typical home and away uniforms as they typically do. But for three weeks throughout the season, Houston will bring out those alternates.
For their Rivalries set, that'll come during their Week 11 matchup against the Indianapolis Colts , a game that'll take place on Thursday Night Football at Houston in Reliant Stadium for one of the Texans' more exciting games throughout the regular season altogether.
The NFL first kicked off Rivalries uniforms across the league for the 2025 season, where the league and Nike released eight new uniforms for the AFC East and the NFC West to wear one time throughout the year for three seasons in a highlighted divisional matchup.
And the theme of those uniforms was designed to put together a more unique, modern look for each team that wore them. Nike describes the Rivalries uniforms from last season as ones that "celebrate storied local traditions and unite fan communities with designs unique to select cities and teams."
After the first two divisions got their uniforms last year, the AFC South and the NFC North would be next up on the list to receive their Rivalries uniforms in 2026. In 2027, the AFC West and NFC East will get their own.
But following a long and anticipated wait , the release of those uniforms for the 2026 slate is right around the corner for the Texans and every other team in this wave of announcements.
Expect the reveal for the Texans' Rivalries uniforms to come at 9 a.m. CT on Tuesday morning, along with the other seven teams in the mix who are in for their own.

title: Nick Chubb Retires From NFL After One Season With Texans
full_text:
Nick Chubb, the former Houston Texans running back, has officially called it a career in the NFL.
According to an emotional social media post from Chubb, the 30-year-old runner will be retiring from the NFL after eight seasons of playing.
Chubb was one of the top stars at his position throughout the first few years of his time with the Cleveland Browns. He had four straight seasons logging over 1,000 yards on the ground, and had over 8,000 yards from scrimmage throughout his career since 2018.
The best season of Chubb's career came with the Browns in 2022, where he found his way to over 1,500 yards on the ground and 13 total touchdowns.
And it was at the tail-end of that career of Chubb's where he played one season with the Texans––a campaign that came off an injury-riddled 2023 and 2024 season with the Browns, and signed late in the 2025 offseason after Houston first learned about a foot injury suffered by Joe Mixon.
Chubb, in his retirement post, said that he wanted to end his career on a healthy season and on a winning team. And with the Texans back in 2025, he was able to do just that.
Chubb played 15 games with the Texans throughout the 2025 season, ultimately totaling 122 carries for 506 yards and three touchdowns.
He was a top-two runner in Houston's offense throughout the season next to rookie Woody Marks, which came as a result of the season-ending injury that Mixon suffered earlier in the offseason .
All things considered, with a tenure that came on short notice and after an injury-riddled season the year before, Chubb's 2025 campaign wasn't too bad of a turnout.
He was healthy throughout most of the season, a productive player in his role as a bruising, powerful complement to a smaller, explosive back in Marks, and a steady veteran Houston could rely on in a room that lacked depth and overall firepower.
Eventually, Houston would call it a wrap on their partnership with Chubb this offseason . His one-year deal came to an end, and the Texans didn't have interest in running it back for 2026 as they would turn in another direction at running back for the season ahead.
At the same time, it's not to say that Chubb's time in Houston could be considered a failure. From Chubb's perspective, that brief period with the Texans is a bit of a perfct statement to end to his career on.
The presence Chubb brought to Houston for the 2025 season won't stack up to his Cleveland days, where he emerged as one of the most powerful and explosive backs in the NFL that powered an otherwise lackluster Browns offense for multiple years.
But his one-year period with the Texans does mark an important time in his turbulent career: a quiet, yet graceful end to one of the league's more unlucky stars health-wise in recent memory, but an ending he's also able to make happen on his own terms.

title: Texans Sign Pair of Free Agent WRs After Jayden Higgins Injury
full_text:
The Houston Texans have added not one, but two wide receivers from free agency after learning that second-year wideout Jayden Higgins would be missing the 2026 season with a torn ACL .
According to a report from NFL Network 's Mike Garafolo, the Texans are signing veteran wide receivers Sterling Shepard and Zay Jones.
The two wide receivers were in Houston for a workout on Friday, and reportedly performed well in each of their showings.
The #Texans are signing veteran WRs Sterling Shepard and Zay Jones, sources tell me and @RapSheet . Both impressed in a workout today and join the mix in Houston after the loss of Jayden Higgins to a torn ACL. pic.twitter.com/oYlmSVJ4BT
Therefore, the Texans bring in both to their 90-man roster, and have a pair of veteran wide receivers who can compete for a spot past cutdown day, which now sits a little under two weeks away.
The Texans were due to add more depth at wide receiver after the Higgins injury . And with these two signings, Houston wanted to go with the approach of adding a couple of older, experienced guys to the position. Both Shepard and Jones are 31 years old or older and have at least nine years of NFL experience.
Shepard comes off of two years with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers after spending eight seasons of his career with the New York Giants, where he found his place as a depth option at receiver.
In 2025, Shepard played in 13 games to collect 39 receptions for 371 yards and a touchdowns, which turned out to be a more productive and more efficient season than his 2024 campaign in Tampa Bay.
As for Jones, he's played for four franchises across his nine years in the league, most recently with the Arizona Cardinals from 2024 to 2025.
His past two seasons in Arizona have been a little more limited compared to what he's seen in earlier seasons of his career, but he is not too far removed from his 2022 campaign with the Jacksonville Jaguars, where he saw 121 targets, 83 receptions, and over 800 receiving yards.
Both might be in the back-nine of their careers with some of the better years of production behind them, but clearly, the Texans liked what they saw from both Shepard and Jones in their recent workouts, and they each could have a case to be worthy of a 53-man roster spot in Houston if they continue to perform well.
Even after the Texans decided to add a couple of veterans here in Shepard and Jones, that certainly doesn't put them out of the race to trade for another pass-catcher in the days ahead, especially as roster cuts loom closer and closer.
Earlier on Friday, the Texans were linked to potential trades for New England Patriots wide receiver Kayshon Boutte , as well as Baltimore Ravens wide receiver Rashod Bateman–– according to KPRC2 's Aaron Wilson –– each of which would rank ahead of Shepard and Jones in the event they came to Houston.
But until the Texans decide to make another move to the position, Shepard and Jones can add a couple of wide receivers who are proven serviceable guys in the league who can compete for a roster spot in camp, and get snaps in preseason next week against the Carolina Panthers.
Are either in a favorable spot to make the 53-man roster come time for next weekend's cuts? It depends on what their next week of production looks like in practice and in-game. However, based on the track record they've shown through their career and the shallowness of the Texans' wide receiver room, the chances of either of them making the cut are far from zero.

title: Texans 53-Man Roster Projection 3.0: How Jayden Higgins' Injury Changes Things
full_text:
The Houston Texans have two of their three preseason games in the books.
And after a couple of preseason games , a joint practice with the Las Vegas Raiders, and a whole lot of training camp practices since the end of July, there's been a few noteworthy changes around what to expect for the Texans' 53-man roster cutdown.
One of those, of course, is the newest injury suffered by second-year wide receiver Jayden Higgins, effectively ending his 2026 season. That absence for Higgins can certainly create a bit of a ripple effect as to how this 53-man roster changes because of it.
At this point, cutdown day is less than two weeks away––sitting at the end of the month on August 30th. The clock is ticking before the Texans are tasked with making some tough decisions around the roster, and determining who are the 53 players best suited to be on the roster come Week 1 against the Buffalo Bills .
Let's break down a brand-new 53-man roster projection based on what we've seen since the start of camp:
(2): C.J. Stroud, Davis Mills
The Texans could decide to roll into the year with Brett Rypien as their QB, but as of his latest showing against the Raiders, he hasn't presented any compelling evidence as to why he should be in line to have a 53-man roster spot.
Perhaps the Texans could sign somebody else to compete for that spot on the depth chart, or give Rypien an extended run in preseason game three. As of now, though, I don't think he's locked into a spot by any means.
(3): David Montgomery, Woody Marks, Jawhar Jordan
The Texans did feel likely to give British Brooks a roster spot here. But he broke his foot earlier in training camp , and doesn't have a clear timetable for his return. So right now, Houston could be primed to keep three backs onboard for Week 1.
Noah Whittington could have a chance to make it past the cut, but there might be a better possibility he hits the practice squad instead of a call-up to the 53-man roster. Jawhar Jordan is also injured at the moment, but feels more likely to be ready to go for the regular season as opposed to Brooks.
(6): Nico Collins, Jaylin Noel, Xavier Hutchinson, Tank Dell, Lewis Bond, Justin Watson
Here's where the Texans' roster sees the biggest change since last week: now Jayden Higgins means Houston’s wide receiver room could turn out a little bit slimmer , and of course, not quite as strong as it looked to start training camp.
Jaylin Noel and Xavier Hutchinson are due for even bigger roles than they were before. Lewis Bond feels way more settled into a 53-man roster spot, and Justin Watson could be the last name to squeeze in. Jared Wayne, while a preseason standout, could be geared towards the practice squad, unless Houston wants seven wideouts..
(4): Dalton Schultz, Marlin Klein, Foster Moreau, Cade Stover
Brevin Jordan seems to have been dealing with an injury through the past couple of weeks, so there are no guarantees he'll be ready for Week 1. But even if he were, these four guys have seemingly set themselves apart as the top four names in the Texans tight end room.
The biggest surprise of anyone here? Second-round rookie Marlin Klein, who had the Texans' biggest play of the day offensively in Week 1 of the preseason, then proceeded to lead Houston in catches against the Raiders. There's a better and better chance he begins the year as TE2 on the depth chart .
(4): Aireontae Ersery, Braden Smith, Trent Brown, Blake Fisher
As to who starts at right tackle might still be a bit of a mystery. But based on Blake Fisher's recent performance in joint practice against the Raiders, there's a world where the 2024 second round pick might be getting looks for a 53-man roster spot to provide extra depth at a position that already has some question marks.
Especially with the health concerns that both Braden Smith and Trent Brown have dealt with throughout their careers, Fisher provides a little extra insurance at the position in the event either of them misses time.
(6): Keylan Rutledge, Evan Brown, Ed Ingram, Wyatt Teller, Jarrett Patterson, Febechi Nwaiwu
The combination of Keylan Rutledge and Evan Brown starting on the inside of Houston's offensive line has gained some traction since their second preseason game against the Raiders. Even if Brown doesn't start over Wyatt Teller, though, it feels pretty likely that both of them will make the 53-man roster.
Then, Houston will likely have to decide between Jarrett Patterson and Jake Andrews for that final spot. Considering the Texans just guaranteed more money on Patterson's contract for next season, that might be a sign there are plans in store for him this season.
(5): Will Anderson, Danielle Hunter, Jadeveon Clowney, Logan Hall, Dominique Robinson
Houston could bring another edge rusher in here for extra depth behind their top three guys, but no one else within the Texans' current roster has stood out besides Dominique Robinson . He's one of three players on the roster to record a sack in two preseason games.
Thought that Dominique Robinson played well on Thursday and was definitely the best of the DEs. He played well against the run, which is the main thing to watch for that DE4 spot where he is competing with Dylan Horton & Solomon Byrd. pic.twitter.com/P60cF4jgDa
Regardless, the Texans will be set to play Will Anderson, Danielle Hunter, and Jadeveon Clowney a large share of the snaps off the edge. So adding another backup next to Robinson as a DE5, as Logan Hall could take more snaps on the interior, might not be the biggest need for Houston's Week 1 roster.
(5): Sheldon Rankins, Tommy Togiai, Kayden McDonald, Mario Edwards, Naquan Jones
The majority of the reps in the Texans' defensive tackle room should be going to the top three names on the depth chart. Kayden McDonald might be third in the pecking order to start, though it certainly wouldn't be a surprise to see him rise to the top by the end of his rookie season.
But considering Houston went out of their way to re-sign veteran Mario Edwards to the roster in training camp, along with Naquan Jones' positive production in camp in the preseason, rostering both of them to expand into a five-man defensive tackle room isn't totally unreasonable.
(5): Azeez Al-Shaair, Henry To'oTo'o, Wade Woodaz, Marte Mapu, Jake Hummel
When it comes to the Texans' LB3 battle, the leader in that race has clearly emerged to be fourth-round rookie Wade Woodaz . That was emphasized in Houston's preseason game against the Raiders when Woodaz ran back an interception on Fernando Mendoza for an 80-yard touchdown for their best defensive play of the game.
OPEN UP A CAN OF WOODAZZZZZZ 🤯 📺: @nflonespn pic.twitter.com/Ke0lrYupPs
Marte Mapu and Jake Hummel are both tenured veterans and proven special teams contributors that feel likely to get the call on the 53-man roster as well. The toughest cut in the room? Rookie linebacker Aiden Fisher, who might be better slated for a practice squad spot early in the season.
(5): Derek Stingley Jr., Kamari Lassiter, Jaylin Smith, Tremon Smith, Alijah Huzzie
The Texans' cornerback room, if constructed like this, can host a great combination of star power and depth that can compete with some of the better units around the league at the position––especially when an All-Pro like Derek Stingley sits atop the depth chart.
The one name here who's seen some of the most praise in training camp is Alijah Huzzie, who feels due to be the Texans' backup nickel corner and a special teamer. UDFA Collin Wright remains a name to watch as well, though his recent injury could cloud his status moving into the season.
(5): Reed Blankenship, Calen Bullock, Jalen Pitre, Kamari Ramsey, Jaylen Reed
The top three of these safeties are locks and due for a big role. The other two guys in the room, Kamari Ramsey and Jaylen Reed, are both extremely appealing young pieces for the future, and can work into the defense in rotational roles and contribute on special teams throughout the 2026 campaign.

title: Texans Could Make Notable O-Line Change After Raiders Preseason Game
full_text:
The Houston Texans spent a ton of time reworking their offensive line this offseason.
After trading Tytus Howard to the Cleveland Browns , signing multiple veterans in free agency, and even drafting multiple interior offensive linemen, this unit looks a whole lot different than it did this time last year.
And after the dust had settled this offseason, one primary offensive line configuration had emerged as the most likely starting group that Houston entered Week 1 with: Aireontar Ersery and Trent Brown at right tackle, Wyatt Teller and Ed Ingram at guard, and rookie Keylan Rutledge at center.
However, after just two preseason games, it seems like the Texans could have a chance to make a shift on their offensive line that would be a little different than those initial projections––and it doesn’t involve their right tackle spot.
According to KPRC2's Aaron Wilson, the Texans are giving "serious consideration" to the idea of starting Keylan Rutledge at left guard, while Evan Brown starts at center.
#Texans are giving serious consideration to this offensive line configuration of Evan Brown at center, Keylan Rutledge at left guard, but no final decisions made. As Cole Popovich has said, they have time to land on their top five guys https://t.co/DuAPW7N6wH
The Texans have previously stated that while there isn't an exact timetable to determine a starting offensive line, they'll certainly have it ready to go once they're preparing for their first game against the Buffalo Bills.
But this bit of intel tells us that the Texans' interior offensive line could be set to switch things up compared to expectations entering training camp.
Houston opted to start the duo of Rutledge and Brown in their second preseason game against the Las Vegas Raiders on Thursday, where they played next to Ersery Ingram and Trent Brown on the first drive of the day.
Since the Texans signed former Pro Bowler Wyatt Teller on a two-year deal this offseason, most have slotted him in as the most likely candidate to claim that left guard spot.
Teller has played right guard throughout his time with the Cleveland Browns, but with Ed Ingram already settled on the right side in Houston, Teller was expected to flip over to the other end.
He was paid $16 million over his two-year deal, and has over 100 career starts with two Pro Bowl selections to his name, setting him up to be an easy-startable, plug-and-play guy even in the back-nine of his career.
Then, Rutledge could be the one to slide over to center , so long as he could make the transition from his college position of left guard.
If not, last year's starter, Jake Andrews, is still on the roster, so he could be someone who retains his spot until the rookie can slide over to center, or is ready to get called up to the first unit.
Houston might have other plans in mind for their starting offensive front, though. Their other veteran interior lineman signed from this offseason, former Arizona Cardinals starter Evan Brown , has been making noise throughout camp and preseason that's put him on the map to start.
He's someone that, while on a one-year deal, has positional versatility to play either guard or center, and has started nearly 70 games at three positions throughout his seven-year career.
The Texans clearly like what he brings to the table, and might just be giving him a real chance to start at center against Buffalo.
That decision to start Brown would also allow the Texans to hand the starting job to their rookie, Keylan Rutledge, on the left side of him at guard, and play a position geared more towards his natural skillset as a right guard at Georgia Tech.
A ton of time still remains before the Texans determine their official starters for that Week 1 game.
Another preseason game and a joint practice against the Carolina Panthers, along with the entire events of roster cutdown day, are still on the horizon. A ton of things could change on the Texans' offensive line from where they stand now.
However, at the very least, based on where the Texans' competition upfront stands now, there are three starting jobs at left guard, center and right tackle that still seem widely undetermined as to who will be starting there to begin the regular season.
But as for Keylan Rutledge, he feels pretty destined to get a call-up. And for Evan Brown, his chances of getting a starting nod his way seem to keep on growing.
