title: Saints Bring In Two Receivers for Workouts After Tyson Injury
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints held tryouts for veteran free-agent wide receivers Chase Claypool and Josh Reynolds , according to NFL insider Mike Garafolo .
The workouts came after rookie wide receiver Jordyn Tyson suffered a right hamstring injury that could sideline him for up to two months. The injury occurred on Thursday during the Saints’ joint practice with the Jacksonville Jaguars at the Ochsner Sports Performance Center in Metairie.
The Saints have not provided an official timeline, but a two-month absence could put Tyson’s return around Oct. 18, when New Orleans plays the New York Giants.
“Jordyn’s had a great camp. He’s played really good football. Inevitably, this is the unfortunate part of what preseason and training camp football is,” head coach Kellen Moore said. “We’ve already had a few of these guys, that you just have something that comes up and ... we’ll just work through it.”
Claypool, 28, was a second-round draft pick by the Pittsburgh Steelers in 2020. Most of his 175 career catches, 2,261 yards and 13 touchdowns came during his first three seasons in Pittsburgh, a span of 39 games.
Following his tenure with the Steelers, Claypool’s career trajectory included stops with the Chicago Bears and Miami Dolphins , marked by periods of inactivity. He hasn't recorded a catch since 2023, as a 2024 season-ending injury with the Buffalo Bills forced him off the field for all of 2025. A spring 2026 tryout with the Green Bay Packers failed to secure him a roster spot.
Reynolds, 31, was drafted by the Los Angeles Rams in 2017 after setting Texas A&M’s single-season record with 13 touchdown catches. He has 244 receptions for 3,228 yards and 20 touchdowns over 121 career games.
Reynolds briefly played for the Tennessee Titans before playing for the Detroit Lions for three seasons. He later played for the Denver Broncos and Jacksonville Jaguars in 2024 and most recently spent time with the New York Jets in 2025, when his season was cut short by a hip injury.
The Saints are in Oxnard, California, where they are holding training camp ahead of their preseason game against the Rams. New Orleans held a joint practice with the Dallas Cowboys on Tuesday and also will practice with the Rams.

title: Tyler Shough Stays Hot, Saints-Cowboys Joint Practice Erupts into Chaos
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints held a joint practice with the Dallas Cowboys in Oxnard, California, ahead of their upcoming preseason matchup on Tuesday.
The practice gave both teams a chance to evaluate their rosters in a competitive setting, especially with most starters expected to see limited action during the preseason.
New Orleans traveled to the Los Angeles area for training camp ahead of its preseason game against the Los Angeles Rams . Before turning its attention to the Rams, the Saints met with the Cowboys at River Ridge Playing Fields , where Dallas is holding training camp.
The Saints are scheduled to hold a joint practice with the Rams on Thursday before the teams meet in a preseason game Saturday.
New Orleans and Dallas will face each other again in Week 3 of the preseason at 7 p.m. Friday, Aug. 28.
Here are some takeaways from the joint practice.
Tyler Shough was on fire again, throwing multiple touchdown passes to wide receiver Chris Olave and tight end Noah Fant , with just one interception off of Cowboys safety Jalen Thompson .
NewOrleans.Football's Nick Underhill said Shough completed 81.8% of his passes, including two throws that traveled more than 20 yards downfield. Olave was difficult to cover throughout.
Back-to-back touchdowns for Tyler Shough and the #Saints offense. Noah Fant in the back corner for six. https://t.co/CfnZZ23jUN pic.twitter.com/1kox54Rkd1
Shough also threw multiple touchdown passes last week in the Saints’ joint practice with the Jacksonville Jaguars . It seems like he is finding a groove at the right time.
Dak Prescott was not at his best, throwing to the wrong colored jersey today.
Dak picked off pic.twitter.com/9DFOItoQia
While the Cowboys and Saints have more storied rivalries, they remain competitors, and both fan bases want to see their teams get the better of each other. Maybe not literally, though some fans might enjoy that, too.
They got their wish, as multiple fights broke out and quickly spread across social media.
Appeared to be a punch thrown at Javonte Williams… leading to a little scuffling pic.twitter.com/f3Pst36l05
Things are getting way out of hand at Cowboys-Saints pic.twitter.com/6dz65OnRG9
It was perfectly summed up by a tweet from Nick Underhill of NewOrleans.Football :
"Another fight. This is absolutely out of control.”
However, the one that has made the rounds was when Saints wide receiver Brock Rechsteiner performed a German Suplex on Cowboys safety Jalen Thompson.
BAH GAWD THAT'S BROCK RECHSTEINER'S MUSIC! #Saints and #Cowboys in another huge fight. Wait for the slam at 0:17: pic.twitter.com/hDt71jfnbC
It should come naturally for Rechsteiner as he is the son of pro wrestling legend Scott Steiner.
Several players left practice early, most notably running back Alvin Kamara and cornerback Quincy Riley . Moore later said Kamara was dealing with a knee issue and Riley had a groin issue. The severity of the injuries is unknown.
Wide receiver Ronnie Bell was carted off the practice field because of a heat-related issue.
Olave was checked by trainers after taking a hit while making a catch, but he stayed on the sideline for the remainder of practice. He returned late in the session for the final team-drill sequence, which took place in the red zone.

title: Giants Defense Grades: Deonte Banks Shows New Physicality in Dolphins Win
full_text:
The New York Giants defense wasn’t on the field very much against the Miami Dolphins–just 36 times. So the sample size for grading isn’t very large, though some stood out and others didn’t.
Having earned the start this week, Murphy rewarded the coaches’ confidence in him by delivering a team-leading four tackles.
Though we haven’t been thrilled with Murphy’s pass rush game to date, his playing instincts and nose for the football are hard to ignore.
He also has the physicality the coaches are looking for in their outside linebacker room.
We suspect if the Giants keep four at this position, it will come down to Murphy or Khalid Kareem. If it were up to us, we’d go with Murphy, whose mobility and low power are more intriguing qualities.
The other starting outside linebacker this week, Kareem has provided good, consistently physical edge play in both preseason games and has a chance to augment the lean athleticism with his big body and physicality.
We think Caleb Murphy is a little bit better at finding the ball, but Kareem’s physicality can certainly play a role.
This active but undersized outside linebacker continues to flash, attacking gaps and edges with consistent aggressiveness that is hard not to like.
Though he only got credit for one tackle, we thought Ford’s penetration on the edges, even his pass coverage against tight ends, were flash plays.
We will always appreciate his defensive temperament and his attack mentality, even if he lacks the length to be a consistent contributor.
Getting a starting assignment but only playing two series, the ball never found the first-round rookie as he played mostly pass coverage.  He still was able to assist on the game’s opening tackle.
McFadden recorded the defense’s lone turnover when he jumped on a first-half fumble.
McFadden only played a couple of series and left with this only dent on the stat sheet.
Kelly received 20 snaps at inside linebacker and had a mostly positive showing. His lone glitch came when he badly overran his gap on one cutback run that went for 15 yards, a play that was fortunately called back by a holding penalty.
Kelly filled several gaps with his long reach and recorded his lone tackle in space.   That aforementioned bad read was simply a rookie mistake, and hopefully one he’ll learn from.
One of the defense’s biggest plays of the game was Barnes reading a screen near the Miami end zone, making the solo tackle in space, and never nearly recording a safety.
It was Barnes’ lone tackle of the day, but with that said, we have little doubt that Barnes is making this team not just for his contributions on defense but more so for his special teams ability.
Though his name came up empty on the defensive stat sheet, we swear we saw Muasau get in on several late-game tackles. That said, Muasau’s ticket to a roster spot is on special teams, where he had a mostly quiet, yet solid showing.
This long-shot summer signing barely got on the field, playing just three snaps, and did not flash.
Back from his hamstring strain, Adebo started the game and responded with two tight press coverages and one tight tackle as a result of tight zone coverage.  Adebo only played two series before leaving the game for good, but they were a positive showing.
Also back from injury—Newsome had been sidelined with a knee sprain—Newsome came out fast with an instinctive run tackle, a coverage knockaway, then another edge leverage run stop for little gain, as you draw it up on the blackboard.
We loved Newsome’s fiery aggressiveness, something this room could use a whole lot more of. Newsome did little to hurt his chances of locking down one of the starting cornerback jobs on this team.
Banks knocked away two balls with tight trail coverages, then jumped into the fray with two run game tackles. Banks has been playing like a much different player this year, one who is not only full of confidence but also more physical than ever.
Banks has always had the physical goods to back up a physical style of play, but has lacked the want-to. So far this summer, he’s showing both, and we’ll take that every day.
Banks finished with the two tackles and the two knockaways before leaving after several impressive series on the field.
Another cornerback who returned from injury (knee), Phillips looked bad early on when he couldn’t find the ball while covering a go route, and then he grabbed the receiver to draw a flag. To make things worse, the receiver caught the ball for a 30-yard gain.
Coverage being a struggle at times, Phillips then showed greater effectiveness in attacking the line of scrimmage.
He blew up a slip screen out of the slot all by himself, making the tackle for no gain.  Then he run-blitzed off an edge, knifed in, and attacked the ball carrier, who seemed surprised by the ferocity of Phillips’ hit and lost the ball, which turned into the Giants’ lone defensive turnover.
We’re not sure what can be done about Phillips’ problems in coverage, but when it comes to everything else on the field, he is all-football and as physical pound-for-pound as anyone on this team.
He sees things fast, and he attacks them hard, but only if it happens around the line of scrimmage.  Trap him in space, and he becomes almost a different player. Phillips finished with three tackles in six snaps.
Getting 10 snaps at corner with the two’s and three’s, Green held up to the physical demands as always, but he wasn’t challenged in coverage at all.
Similar in style to Dru Phillips, Jones’s instinctive reactions to plays at or around the line of scrimmage are something to like about his game.
Jones isn’t as vicious a hitter as Phillips, but he is better in coverage.  He drew a hold on a wide run and made another short-gain tackle out of the slot.
Jones finished with two total tackles in limited snaps.
We’re not sure Jones has a place on this defense, but we really respect how well he sees the play and the angles he takes to limit those plays.
Getting just 13 snaps this week on defense, Black made more of an impact on special teams.
Getting three boundary snaps late in the game, we remain impressed by Woods’ size but are unsure of his ability to keep up with NFL receivers.
He’s a safety by nature, so this move to corner is in its infancy.
Continuing to be the most active of the safeties fighting for a starting job, Pinnock made one play in deep coverage.
But it was his discipline, shown in his contain against the run during the scrimmage, that was really impressive. Pinnock had one tackle on the day, but he was around the ball more often than not.
Pinnock’s competition for that starting safety job that’s up for grabs, Nubin flashed early on a deep middle throw and knocked it away.  He also had a good close against a tight end’s catch that went for little gain.
However, we did not like how slow Nubin looked attempting to close on that deep 30-yard completion that most starting safeties would have been able to knock away or intercept.
Nubin was so deliberate on his turn-and-go that it’s obvious why he’s been a target in the league for two years now, and we can see why there might be some question as to whether he’s starting material in this league.
Washington made one early run blitz from the edge and closed down the play from pursuit for the tackle.
If there’s one way to help out a floundering run defense, it’s to provide occasional edge blitzes to help out.  It’s not something to do regularly, or you could get burned, but early on it can be an effective deterrent.
Washington’s too small to plug in as a starting safety, but he’s got that Swiss Army knife element to his game that, combined with his aggressiveness, gets him near the action an awful lot of the time.
This veteran safety was once again spotted playing some press corner on the boundary. Though the ball never came his way, he looked competent enough.
Owning cornerback size, Campbell plays with a safety’s demeanor, which makes for an intriguing combination.
He’s also a good special teamer.  We…

title: Malik Nabers Could Shed No-Contact Jersey This Week, Harbaugh Says
full_text:
It’s been a long road back for New York Giants wide receiver Malik Nabers from his ACL injury suffered last season in Week 4. Still, the third-year receiver could be on the verge of taking yet another significant step forward toward a Week 1 return.
Head coach John Harbaugh told reporters that there was a “possibility” that Nabers, who over the last week-plus has been practicing wearing the red “no contact” jersey, could shed that garment from his locker this week.
"That's a possibility," Harbaugh said. "We'll just have to see where that's at. I don't think it's a necessity this week. We're still three weeks out from the game, the first game and then after that. We'll see where he's at this week. We'll see how he feels tomorrow."
Nabers, who is not expected to play in the preseason finale Friday night against the Jets, has been shielded from having contact in team drills.
Harbaugh has declined to mention a firm date for Nabers to take the next step, but he did say that he didn’t think the receiver would spend the rest of the summer in the red jersey.
“He'll be out of a red jersey before he plays in a game,” Harbaugh said last week. “He's going to have to get bumped around. You just have to feel that and know how to deal with it to protect yourself.”
“There are certain formulas that we use that kind of tell us what the risk factors are in practice,” he added.
“That's part of it with him. It's also to your eye. It's also how he feels, and then ultimately with the doctors. So, I think you do it slowly, and you just keep building to the point where it's not like all of a sudden he's doing something, and now he's doing everything. You work your way towards that.”
Harbaugh said that offensive lineman Joshua Ezeudu was kicked in the back of the leg in the team’s 26-3 preseason win over Miami, an injury that forced him out of the game preamturely.
The good news is that the injury is not beleived to be serious and that the young offensive lineman, who has been snake-bit throughout his entire NFL career, would be day-to-day.
Harbaugh also said he anticipated having offensive lineman Francis Mauigoa, who suffered a stinger in the joint practice with the Dolphins, and cornerback Colton Hood, who was sidelined most of last week with an undisclosed ailment, back at practice this week.
Otherwise overall the Giants came out of Saturday's preseason game clean injury-wise.

title: Giants Preseason Snap Counts: Who Played the Most and What Did We Learn?
full_text:
The New York Giants are celebrating after a 26-3 win against the Miami Dolphins inside Hard Rock Stadium in the second week of the preseason.
The Giants mostly played their second string on both sides of the ball, but they were still able to dominate the Dolphins, who have one of the worst rosters in the league going into the 2026 season.
Regardless, the Giants get a massive boost with the win, as the confidence should trickle down the depth chart following a win like this.
Here's a look at the snap counts for each side of the ball, according to the NFL gamebook, and what to take away from the coaching staff's decisions about who to play:
The Giants didn't invest a lot of playing time with many starters, but they started sixth-round rookie J.C. Davis in the game, and he went the distance.
The offense was dominant throughout the game, playing 81 snaps compared to 36 for the Dolphins. Davis played extremely well, and his high level of visibility against the Dolphins likely secures his spot on the 53-man roster.
From the quarterbacks, Jameis Winston was the player most active with 38 offensive snaps. He drew the start for the Dolphins and immediately set the tone for the contest, which gave the Giants the green light to impose their will on Miami.
“Absolutely. You expect Jameis to play just like that. Jameis was in control. He ran the show. He's poised in the pocket,” Giants head coach John Harbaugh said.
“He was very accurate with his passing. He played at a high level just like you'd expect him to. That's a great thing to have a quarterback like that as your number two. Jameis has been a starting quarterback in this league for a long time. He's started a lot of games. I thought he played exactly the way we’d expect him to.”
The Giants opted to keep most of their defensive starters on the sidelines for the game. The Giants only had 36 total defensive snaps, and nobody on defense played more than 24.
The starters who saw the field and are worth noting are outside linebacker Caleb Murphy, who led the way for the Giants, defensive tackle Darius Alexander, who appeared 21 times, cornerback Paulson Adebo , who was there for 20 snaps and safety Tyler Nubin, who logged 17.
Players on the defensive roster bubble made their moments count against the Giants, and it's clear that there is a lot of competition to try and make the final 53-man roster. The urgency shown against the Dolphins shows exactly where the team is, which should please Harbaugh and the coaching staff.
"Well, I mean, our guys, our younger guys, we played our backups so to speak. But there's a lot of guys fighting for jobs on this team. And I thought they came out and they made a point to try to make their case. And they did a good job of it," Harbaugh said.
Preseason snap counts don't mean a ton in the grand scheme of everything because there still has to be production during practices and training camp. The Giants treated the joint practice and the preseason as two separate practices, which is why many of the starters didn't participate in the game.
In a dominant win, the Giants had the snap counts. That may give clues as to who has an edge in the final couple of roster spots, but there is still a lot of work that needs to be done between now and the 30-roster-cut deadline this next week. That should be the true determining factor in who makes the roster and who's heading to the practice squad.

title: Giants O-Line, D-Line Preseason Week 2 Grades: Depth on Display Against Dolphins
full_text:
If, at the start of the preseason, we had told you that the New York Giants ' offensive line depth was as deep as it has been in years, would you have believed us?
Neither would we, and yet that was the case for the Giants' offensive line backups, which were no match for the Dolphins' backups. Overall, the offensive linemen gave up just four of the team’s five quarterback pressures and got good movement against Miami’s backups.
“I thought they did well,” head coach John Harbaugh said after the game. “The protection was good. We ran the ball well. All that was good.”
The defensive line? Mixed results, including some carryover from last week that is becoming more of a concern. With that said, let’s get into the grades.
Getting the start at right tackle, Mbow played the entire first half and really shined with his pass-blocking.
There were a handful of running game misses that he’d like to have back, but it’s obvious Mbow is a lock for the swing tackle spot.
Though he didn’t get the start at right guard—the role went to Aaron Stinnie—Ezeudu eventually stepped right in at the position on the game’s second possession and, to be frank, he looked most comfortable there.
There were some easy power run-blocking snaps inside out of Ezeudu, who moved very well as a guard.
He also got some snaps at right tackle in the second half and looked solid enough, though there was another mental mix-up in the protection Ezeudu was involved in that led to a sack.
Also, late in the game, Ezeudu had to leave with a lower-body injury, which seems like a weekly occurrence with this snake-bit athlete.
Based on talent and skill alone, Ezeudu should make the final 53, but there has to be a trust issue with this player when it comes to his availability.
Getting the start at left tackle and going the distance, Davis played it very well throughout.
We didn’t spot a single pass-blocking loss in Davis’ game.  His run blocking had enough plus plays to earn him a passing grade there, too.
Davis has a good feel for angles and dealing with the unexpected.  It’s called football instinct, and we think Davis has plenty of it.
He’s also got the size, arm length, and balance you would want at the position, as well as the mental game—not a single flinch or tug in two games so far.
For years, this organization has struggled to find quality offensive tackles. Still, suddenly, the Giants have five legit offensive tackles on their roster, plus a longshot UDFA (Ryan Schernecke) who should end up on the practice squad as a developmental guy.
Davis, a sixth-round draft pick with legit starting potential, has obviously made this team.
Of course, there’s the matter of stepping up in class somewhere down the road that must be addressed, but against second- and third-teamers, he has been dominant.
If there’s a choice to be made at the cutdown date between Davis and Ezeudu, the choice is clear in our eyes: it’s got to be Davis.
Schernecke got some third-quarter snaps and all the fourth-quarter snaps at right tackle.  Suffice it to say that he is far from ready, but that’s to be expected given he comes from the small school program at Kutztown.
We still like how quick Schernecke is off the ball, his feistiness, his size, and his mental game, but we haven’t yet seen the mobility, balance, or athleticism required to compete at this level.
Some of his movement snaps have been hard to watch.  This kid lacks experience and strength, and there is a lot to work on here. That said, technique has gotten many a blue-collar blocker a place in this league.
Through two games, Schernecke has not allowed a sack or committed a penalty, though there have been times when he’s been living on the edge.  The practice squad beckons.
One of two starting offensive linemen to get a start this week—John Michael Schmitz was the other—Runyan, in one series, lost his first run-blocking assignment but bounced back with a bunch of smooth pass-blocking snaps, the strength of his game as always.
Where Runyan continues to struggle is in run blocking, with his 52.3 PFF grade this week the worst among the offensive linemen. Runyan has always been more of a finesse technician who excels in zone blocking rather than a mauler with heavy hands to win at the point of attack.
The Giants can get by with him at left guard if they need to, but the more we see him play, the more we are convinced that he doesn’t fit the offensive line profile that John Harbaugh has favored in the past.
Getting the start today at right guard thanks to Francis Mauigoa nursing a stinger suffered in the joint practice, Stinnie was solid in every aspect of the position.
He resembles a bowling ball out there, banging into walls and crashing into pins without ever giving an inch.
He also received some snaps at left guard in the second half and acquitted himself there well, too. If he doesn’t make this team, we’d be stunned.
Getting all of his 43 snaps at left guard, we spotted three Kubas pass-blocking losses that led to hurries and hits on his quarterback; this against Miami’s third stringers, mind you.
Though he had plenty of snaps where he mixed things up pretty well, especially on running downs, the pass-blocking misses in space were hard to ignore.
Kubas can give the team snaps at guard and center, but he still needs some additional development, which is why he might be better suited for another run on the practice squad.
Getting all of his second-half snaps today at right guard, Neal did nothing to solidify his spot on the roster.
His size and power and high first-round draft pedigree will always persuade some team to give him a shot.
Still, the lack of movement skills and the fact that he may just be too tall to play inside—his struggles with keeping his pad level low are a big problem—don’t bode well for his long-term future with this team.
Returning from a concussion he suffered early in the penultimate practice in West Virginia, the team’s de facto starter at center started and only played the first two series, leaving the game late in the first quarter.
Schmitz’ game was reliable and economical; he always seems to get his man while rarely hitting him.  The grades are there, but the physicality we suspect the coaches want is not.
Also returning from an injury-related absence that caused him to miss the preseason opener, Patrick got all the second-team snaps at center, and it was obvious to see what this veteran brings to the table.
His experience showed in his play, with zero hesitation; his reliable mental game is his greatest asset at this point in his career.  This 33-year-old, nine-year vet knows how to play the position and run an offense.
He’s not the niftiest player out there, but he’s got enough size to hold up to power and the smarts to know where to be on every snap.
A knee issue needed to be managed early in camp, making Patrick’s chances at landing the backup center role shaky. But if the trainers have that under control so it won’t be an issue moving forward, that bodes well for Patrick’s chances of a roster spot.
Shunted back to the third team with the return of Schmitz and Patrick to the field, Hudson played the majority of the second half over the ball.
We were disappointed that Hudson did not get any snaps at guard for versatility’s sake, but the young interior offensive lineman did well again in his opportunities.
He once again played his simple, clean type of game snap-to-snap with a preference for mixing things up in the pit, with just enough mobility to make the occasional block in space.  Hudson still looks like starting material to these eyes.
This veteran signed for depth purposes when Schmitz and Patrick went down, got today’s final possession and did not embarrass himself.  He ran the offense smoothly and kept everything in front of him.
Getting a start to salvage his sinking chances of making the team, Fotu worked his way into two tackles with some positive movement plays.
However, he wasn’t much of a factor in the pit, as his instinct…

title: Giants Offensive Skill Position Player Grades: Winston Shines, Beckham's Drop Stings in Dolphins Win
full_text:
You’re going to see this said a lot in our review of the New York Giants individual player performances in their 26-3 Week 2 preseason win over the Miami Dolphins.
The Giants have serious depth, which will make for tough decisions ahead for head coach John Harbaugh and general manager Joe Schoen on cut day.
“I thought we did a lot of things really well,” Harbaugh said after the game. “I like the way we handled having the lead in terms of continuing to play in such a way as to extend the lead. That's really important to learn how to do that as a team. We did that.
“I do believe we're a better team than we were Wednesday when we came down here (for the joint practice). That was the goal. And now we move forward.”
Here is our look at the offensive skill position players. Overall, there was a lot to like as the competition heats up.
With the Giants sitting their starters, Winston got the starting nod and was just as good as he was last week.
On his first possession, he led a 7-play drive for a touchdown, capping off this efficient drive with a 13-yard run on a 3rd-and-6.  Winston did well to break the pocket, find space, and exploit it all the way to the pylon for the score.
All told, Winston quarterbacked six first-half possessions and left the game with a 20-3 lead.
To top off his positive effort, he ran a solid 2-minute drill for the field goal that finished that half.  His final numbers were 15-of-21, for 150 yards, and one 11-yard run for a touchdown. His longest throw was a 29-yard in-cut to Darius Slayton.
The offense attempted just one downfield throw of 20+ air yards which wasn’t completed, though there did seem to be opportunities for more. Instead, there were a handful of intermediate throws, as it sure seems this offense is gearing up for chunk plays by first perfecting the ball-control offense that should match up with the power running game the coaches desire.
One of Winston’s many strengths is how tall he stands in the pocket; he doesn’t get very many balls disrupted at the line of scrimmage.  Once again, he ran the offense smartly, never once put the ball in harm’s way, and played the position at a high level.
Allen took over at the start of the third quarter and quarterbacked three possessions, leaving the field halfway through the fourth quarter.
His second possession was a 9-play drive that resulted in a field goal.  His final possession was a mammoth 17-play drive that also resulted in a field goal.  Allen finished 13-of-18 for 101 yards, absorbing one 9-yard sack and taking good care of the ball.
His attempts consisted of a bunch of checkdowns and short throws; his only completion of consequence was a 17-yard middle throw to Isaiah Hodgins.
Allen also smartly connected with Dalen Cambre on a 3rd-and-7 and a 3rd-and-8 for first downs.
Overall, the Giants got a better performance out of this veteran quarterback this week, but there was little to write home about.
Getting the game’s final possession, this 4-year veteran who was recently picked up after Allen’s terrible performance last week ran a 9-play drive of his own before it finished up with a punt.
Haener finished 3-of-3 for 15 yards in the passing department, his best throw being to Cambre on a 9-yarder that converted a 3rd-and-8. All three of Haener’s attempts were of the very short variety.
It’s tough to judge this performance, as Haener has only recently arrived. Still, he did seem more naturally attuned to the playing of his position, especially when handling the pocket and throwing from the pocket, than Allen did.
Getting the start with Cam Skattebo given the week off and Tyrone Tracy still licking his wounds from last week’s big screw-up, Singletary delivered some solid ball.
His biggest play was a bounce-out wide from 13 yards out, outrunning the Miami pursuit to the front corner of the end zone for a score.
The coaches obviously trust this veteran’s game to handle all the little things besides scoring touchdowns.  Interestingly, included in his very good 40 yards on eight carries (5.0 average) was a third down where he lined up as a lead-blocking fullback and took the inside handoff into the teeth of the defense to get the first down.
He also caught a ball out of the backfield for 4 yards.  Singletary is the type of player who will never lose you a game, but he might help you win a few with his reliability alone. There’s nothing flashy about Singletary’s game, but one thing that can be said is he’s as reliable as the day is long.
After reeling off successive runs of 11 and 12 yards, Tracy fumbled without being touched at the Miami 10-yard line.  The wet conditions were partly to blame for the red zone turnover, but the egregious misplay is still on Tracy’s shoulders.
Tracy followed that up with a couple of too-careful touches, and an inside blitz pickup that fell well short of the mark.  On this block, Tracy squared up the linebacker, but he ducked his head and stopped moving his feet, allowing the backer to swim around him for the pressure that hurried an incompletion.
On the day, Tracy finished with 26 yards on six carries and 22 yards on three catches. We wouldn’t say he’s played his way off the team, but with the addition of Najee Harris this week, Tracy is squarely in the fourth-string territory at running back, which does not guarantee a final roster spot on this or any team.
Getting most of the second-half running back duties, Gray ran for 26 yards on six carries and logged a productive 37 yards on six receptions.
One of this week’s offensive highlights was the low sideline throw that Gray out-fought a Miami backer for, in the process converting another 3rd-and-long for the offense.
Showing very quick feet but a lack of size and physicality, Bankston needs to bulk up a bit even to be considered NFL material.  He didn’t get any help out there while gaining only 5 yards on 7 carries, and 2 yards on 2 catches.
Getting this week’s start, Slayton got going fast with the game’s first two catches, the second one going for 29 yards for the Giants’ longest play of the day.  This came off of a neat in-cut catch that Slayton took for another ten yards upfield.
Slayton caught two more balls and finished with a solid 58 yards on four receptions.
The value that Slayton brings is the respect defenses have for his speed—you can see it when defensive backs play a larger cushion against him, which opens up space.
Slayton remains the king of the uncontested body catch, however. Put him up against the other guys’ third and fourth teamers, and he can be something of a weapon. Unfortunately, that won’t be the case very often, if at all, once the regular season begins.
Austin started things off with an 11-yard punt return, making the first man miss.  His next touch was a jet sweep that he took for 21 yards, showing the acceleration in tight quarters to gash a defense.
His next touch was a 17-yard punt return, once again making the first man miss.  Austin was next called for a phantom offensive pass interference foul.  He then converted a 3rd-and-14 by catching a short pass and using his vision and feet to avoid traffic and get 20 yards.
Austin has the game to be this team’s starting slot receiver.  He’s got very good running instincts and can stop on a dime.  He’s very dangerous after the catch, and seems like a big play waiting to happen.
Getting plenty of snaps on the boundary to impress, Beckham caught two short balls and drew a defensive holding call, but dropped his big chance to come up big.
At the Miami 14-yard line, Beckham did well to get open in the back of the end zone and went up for the high throw.
He came down with two feet in play but without the ball.  It was a huge drop, the ball being right where it belonged, so only Beckham could catch it.
Beckham’s movements looked sharp and smooth out there, but at his age—he’ll turn 34 during the season—it’s going to be hard to spend a roster spot on this oft-injured veteran.
Hodgins came up with a good middle catch, holding on…

title: Why the Giants are 'a Better Team' Following 26-3 Preseason Win vs. Dolphins
full_text:
There is only so much one can take away from a Jaxson Dart-less New York Giants team that is facing a rebuilding Miami Dolphins squad in a preseason matchup. But Saturday's game was about building good habits more than the outcome itself.
Big Blue succeeded on both fronts, earning a 26-3 victory at Hard Rock Stadium . The Giants accumulated 390 total yards of offense in 79 plays, while holding the Dolphins to a measly 102. They won the turnover battle 2-1 and dominated the time of possession, 41:00 to 19:00. It was a well-rounded effort.
And most importantly, it was a step in the right direction.
"Appreciate the effort by the guys," head coach John Harbaugh said. "I thought we did a lot of things really well. I like the way we handled the lead, continuing to play in a way that extended it.
"That's really important to learn how to do that as a team. We did that. I do believe we're a better team than we were Wednesday when we came down here. That was the goal. And now we move forward."
The Giants just need to focus on perfecting “Harbaugh ball,” ramping up their physicality and playing smart. If they can complete those basic objectives, then overcoming obstacles in the regular season should be much more manageable.
This was a fine warm-up showing, even if several core members of the team did not participate.
Backup quarterback Jameis Winston completed 15-of-21 passes for 150 yards and struck the first blow with an 11-yard rushing touchdown on New York's opening drive. Veteran running back Devin Singletary logged eight carries for 41 yards and a TD of his own.
The perpetually scrutinized Darius Slayton did a nice job of finding space, recording four receptions for 58 yards to lead all wide receivers. The offensive line was the primary catalyst, enabling offensive coordinator Matt Nagy to call a fairly clean game.
If the Giants' versatile weapons have time to operate, they should be able to produce meaningful plays more times than not. The team as a whole carried itself with pride and urgency, indicating the growth the squad is experiencing under Harbaugh.
"I think it’s the leadership, the leadership all around," Winston said.
"We understand the responsibility that we have, and I think that’s the most beautiful thing about training camp and preseason football is everyone knows that time is almost up, so being present and being willing to do whatever is required to be your best is going to be your best chance to make the team."
Many players rose to the occasion. JC Davis was an iron man at left tackle, holding his own and seemingly improving his stock; fellow rookie sixth-round draft pick Bobby Jamison-Travis recorded a sack, and the secondary played with ferocity under defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson.
Unfortunately, not everyone stepped up. Tyrone Tracy Jr. continued his preseason descent, following up last week's missed block with an untouched fumble versus the Dolphins. With Najee Harris joining Big Blue's running backs room, Tracy is not promised a sizable workload. He must snap out of this funk pronto.
Overall, the Giants emitted positive vibes from Miami Gardens, as they inch closer to their Sept. 13 season-opening clash with the Dallas Cowboys. There is plenty to like, but when a franchise is attempting to end a terrible losing streak and reinvent itself , the process tends to be gradual.
Luckily, New York still has some time to address its flaws and spruce up its game plan.
"We kind of look at it like we have a lot of work to do between now and then," John Harbaugh said. "That's three weeks away. We will start looking at our first few games in terms of our preparation, because those are the games that count.
"But there are still roster battles. So we're going to try to take it one day at a time, try to be a better team. We'll be back Monday and try to be a better team after practice Monday than we were when we started."
The Giants conclude preseason play next Friday against the New York Jets.

title: Giants' Abdul Carter Explains Why He Chose Jersey No. 3
full_text:
Plenty of analysts and fans slapped a "generational talent" label on Abdul Carter leading into last year's NFL Draft, and the outside linebacker only fed into the hype machine by asking to wear the retired numbers of New York Giants legends Lawrence Taylor and Phil Simms.
The Hall of Fame linebacker declined Carter's request to use his No. 56, and the Super Bowl XXI MVP quarterback's family did not feel comfortable with anyone wearing No. 11 (Carter's number at Penn State).
After being rebuffed by Taylor and Simms, the young Giants player chose No. 51. Now, he is switching to No. 3.
Why, you ask? His motives aren’t tied to franchise history. The number says more about his own journey.
"It was honestly the best number available after I had 51," Carter said. "It is some crazy numerology. I was born on October 3, 2003, and I was the third pick."
The 22-year-old is hoping that No. 3 continues to hold special meaning in his life. If everything goes according to his plan, then future rookies will be asking him for permission to wear his number.
Carter obviously has a ways to go before reaching such status, but this upcoming season figures to be a huge step in his development. Following an inconsistent 2025 campaign that saw him struggle to get home against quarterbacks until late in the year, he is looking to perform like a true game-wrecker in 2026 .
Questions about his production, punctuality, or anything else should not enter the equation. The focus must be on his on-field contributions, and the team and fan base expect them to be bountiful.
Carter totaled 66 total pressures , per Pro Football Focus , 13 more than All-Pro teammate and NFC sacks leader Brian Burns. If the 2024 Big Ten Defensive Player of the Year and Unanimous All-American continues to push around offensive linemen at that rate, he will record far more than four sacks in a single season.
The right men are in the building to foster his growth. John Harbaugh is a Super Bowl-winning head coach who demands accountability and commands respect. Dennard Wilson is an aggressive defensive coordinator who knows how to maximize his star players' best traits.
Burns is a seasoned pro coming off a career campaign. Fellow veterans DJ Reader and Shelby Harris can impart some wisdom as well. Left tackle Andrew Thomas offers invaluable competition at practice. Abdul Carter is equipped to excel on the Giants. Now he has to do it.
If he succeeds, then No. 3 jerseys will fill MetLife Stadium for some time.

title: 9 Winners and 3 Losers From the Giants' 26-3 Preseason Rout of the Dolphins
full_text:
The New York Giants dominated the Miami Dolphins 26-3 in Preseason Week 2. Head coach John Harbaugh rested many of his starters, including quarterback Jaxson Dart, but the backups stepped up in a big way.
With the roster cut deadline rapidly approaching, multiple Giants players needed strong performances to secure their spots. Some met the challenge in a big way, potentially vaulting themselves up the depth chart. Others fell short, risking their places on the final roster.
With just one more preseason game to go, here are a few winners and losers from the Giants' win over the Dolphins.
Slayton has had a quiet summer since being cleared physically to return from an offseason hernia procedure. It also hasn’t helped that he’s had rookie Malachi Fields nipping at his heels for the No. 2 receiver spot.
So after a quiet 2026 preseason debut in which he didn’t have any pass targets thrown his way, Slayton did all he could to prove his worth against the Dolphins, catching four of six pass targets for a team-leading 58 yards.
The veteran wideout was especially productive on New York's first drive of the game, picking up 34 yards on two catches, which helped put the Giants in position for Winston's touchdown scramble.
Phillips had a clear lowlight in the first quarter, when he committed a pass interference penalty while allowing a long completion to Dolphins wideout Kevin Coleman Jr.
The slot defender, in his first preseason action of the summer,  quickly turned things around, though.
Phillips forced fumbles on back-to-back plays on Miami's second drive. The first was hardly noticed, as the receiver immediately recovered the ball. The second was definitely noticed when linebacker Micah McFadden recovered it for an early turnover.
Phillips finished second on the Giants’ defense with three tackles this week.
Austin had an all-around productive game on both offense and special teams.
Offensively, he made defenders miss when he had the ball in his hands, as he caught both of his pass targets for 24 yards and a long of 20. Austin even converted on a long third down on New York's final drive of the first half.
The Giants made it a priority to get the ball into Austin's hands. He took an early jet sweep for a 21-yard gain, caught a screen pass, and was the primary punt returner in the first half, where he had two returns for 29 yards, his longest being 18 yards.
In an offense that prioritizes quick passes, Austin's ability to pick up yards after the catch—he had 10 this week, which was sixth on the team—will be valuable.
The Giants’ rookie sixth-round draft pick went the distance at left tackle and only allowed one pressure, this after allowing no pressures in his preseason debut last week. Davis was part of a backup offensive line that was stellar this week, but more specifically, Davis might very well have locked up a roster spot with his play this week.
The projected starting cornerback duo on the perimeter was back from missing last week due to injuries, Newsome with a knee and Adebo with a hamstring strain.
Between the two of them, they allowed just one reception on four pass targets (the one allowed by Adebo for just 12 yards) and combined for two forced incompletions and one pass breakup.
That might not sound like a lot, but considering the Dolphins only attempted 16 passes all game long (completing eight), Newsome and Adebo’s combined effort certainly stands out.
The young rookie defensive lineman, who now wears No. 97, feasted on the Dolphins this week. He recorded one tackle, one sack, one tackle for loss, and one quarterback hit, all of which were apparently enough to feed his football appetite, with Jamison-Travis finishing as the Giants’ fifth-best run defender this week.
New celly alert 🍽️ pic.twitter.com/yPQAsVlkQd
Nubin rose to the challenge this week by finishing as the Giants’ highest-graded defender in coverage. He allowed just one completion for three yards, forced one incompletion, had one pass breakup, and recorded a stop against the run in what was one of his better showings of the summer.
Winston, who started off the summer looking out of sorts, was as close to perfect as could be this week.
Getting a full half’s worth of work, he finished 15-of-21 for 150 yards and had an 11-yard touchdown run in what was as solid a showing as one might see this week from a backup quarterback.
For the second consecutive week, Tracy had one of the most impactful negative plays of the day for the Giants.
After a couple of nice runs late in the first quarter, he fumbled the ball after taking a handoff from Winston. The Dolphins quickly recovered, forcing New York's only turnover of the game.
After being listed as a co-starter next to Cam Skattebo in the team's initial unofficial depth chart, Tracy may be falling behind.
Beckham, the fan favorite, dropped a sure touchdown pass late in the second quarter—a ball that was right in his hands.
While he continues to fight to get open and get the ball, miscues like these aren’t going to help his quest for a roster spot, no matter how open he gets or how popular he might still be among the fan base.
For the second week in a row, second-year man Darius Alexander was virtually invisible against the run. In nine run defense snaps, he did not record a single tackle or stop, finishing 31st among 32 Giants defenders against the run, per Pro Football Focus.
With Chauncey Golston, who was the eighth-best Giants-graded run defender this week, having himself a strong summer, it might be worth watching if he starts to take snaps from Alexander, especially as Golston continues to get more reps at defensive tackle.

title: Takeaways from Giants’ 26-3 Victory Over Miami Dolphins
full_text:
The New York Giants might finally have one of those “good problems” that any head coach would trade his soul for.
That problem is a dearth of depth across the board—solid depth in most cases, at that—which was on display in Saturday's 26-3 win over the Miami Dolphins at Hard Rock Stadium.
The Giants, coming off a dominating showing against the Dolphins in their joint practice on Thursday, continued their dominance sans most of their starters and key reserves.
It didn’t matter. The Giants took a commanding 20-3 lead by halftime and never took their foot off the gas pedal, capping their second-half scoring with a pair of field goals by Ben Sauls, who handled the kicking duties in the second half in relief of Dominic Zvada.
So what else did we learn from the Giants’ first preseason win of 2026—and their first win under head coach John Harbaugh?
When the Giants signed Najee Harris, many people wondered if that meant the end for Devin Singletary, the third running back on the team’s unofficial depth chart before the signing.
It turns out that maybe it’s Tyrone Tracy Jr. who might need to be worried. Tracy had a bad week in the preseason opener when he whiffed on a blitz pickup against Vikings safety Jay Ward that led to a crushing hit on quarterback Jaxson Dart.
This week, while Tracy was better in his blitz pickups, he also had an ugly fumble deep in the red zone, which Miami recovered.
Tracy has five career fumbles in regular-season play and last year looked to clean up that problem once and for all. But it reared its ugly head again this week, and while there is no good time for a fumble, it’s especially not good to have it happen deep in the opponent’s red zone.
Singletary finished as this week’s Giants rushing leader with 40 yards on eight carries and a touchdown, his best run being 13 yards.
Singletary continues to be a solid pass protection blocker, having yet to give up a quarterback pressure in two preseason games. Is it possible that he will move ahead of Tracy in the pecking order if he delivers another strong performance in next week’s preseason finale against the Jets?
Supporters of Odell Beckham Jr. will point to how he keeps getting open but doesn’t get the ball thrown his way, and that’s fine. But when the ball does get thrown his way, he has to catch it.
Beckham, who caught two of four pass targets for a rather harmless 17 yards, had a big-time whiff in the closing seconds of the second quarter when a 14-yard pass, a somewhat serious attempt from quarterback Jameis Winston, went straight through Beckham’s hands and fell to the ground.
While one play shouldn’t necessarily dictate a player’s fate, Beckham's shortcoming cannot happen given his still-unstable hold on a roster spot.
This doesn’t mean he’s going to be cut tomorrow, but his summer production —four out of eight pass targets caught for just 23 yards, two yards after the catch, and one drop—doesn’t exactly scream roster-worthy.
Between his injuries and having a defensive coordinator who didn’t have a clue how best to utilize his talents, defensive lineman Chauncey Golston seemed like he was a wasted roster spot.
Not so much this summer. Golston has been the best and most consistent of the defensive linemen, and it’s not even close. Although he didn’t have any pressures this week, he did have a pass breakup to go along with one assisted tackle.
It’s still too soon to say if Golston is going to get a starting role, but it’s probably fair to say he’s going to play a lot for this defense if he stays healthy.
If the Giants go with five inside linebackers, as is believed to be the way they are leaning, the fifth spot behind starters Tremaine Edmunds and Arvell Reese and projected backups Micah McFadden and Jack Kelly will come down to either Darius Muasau or Zaire Barnes.
This week, Barnes might have gained the edge in that competition with his spectacular goal-line tackle-for-loss.
Dominic Zvada has been lights out all spring and summer. Still, the feeling was that before anyone officially anointed him the winner of the kicking competition, it was important to see how he did in games, both on scoring attempts and on kickoffs.
Zvada answered both questions with aplomb. He hit two field goals of 43 and 32 yards, the latter having been pushed back thanks to a false start called on Evan Neal. Zvada also hit his lone extra point attempt following Devin Singletary’s 13-yard run in the second quarter.
The Giants ended up winning the starting field-position battle as well, with New York’s average starting line of scrimmage at their own 32 (on two returns) and Miami’s at their own 29 (on six kickoff returns).
Zvada and Sauls put all of their kickoffs inside the 10-yard line. However, on his four kickoffs, Zvada put three inside the 5-yard line (two of those at the 2-yard line) while Sauls, on his two kickoffs, put his first one on the 2-yard line and his second on the 7-yard line.
As anticipated, more than a dozen Giants starters and key reserves were scratched, most of them healthy scratches. The list is as follows:
The absence of defensive lineman Josh Tupou is something of a headscratcher. Last week after a rocky start, Tupou ended up with two stops and an overall defensive grade of 89.5 from PFF.
Perhaps this week, the coaches wanted to see the rest of their defensive line depth in action, including Zacch Pickens, Marlon Davidson, and Anquin Barnes Jr.
While on the subject of lineups, it was not a surprise to see the Giants’ players who were returning from injury—cornerbacks Paulson Adebo, Dru Phillips, and Greg Newsome II, and center John Michael Schmitz—get snaps in this week’s game.
What was interesting is that the Giants decided to play starting left guard Jon Runyan this week.
Runyan and Schmitz made up two-fifths of the starting offensive line, but as noted, Schmitz’s playing time this week wasn’t a surprise considering he missed last week’s game while recovering from a concussion.
While Runyan getting playing time was initially a surprise, in retrospect it shouldn’t have been.
Per PFF, Runyan graded out as the worst of the Giants’ 14 offensive linemen in last week’s preseason opener and the second-worst in the run-blocking department. He did, however, grade out as the fifth-best pass-blocking offensive lineman of the lot. So perhaps this was a chance for Runyan to redeem himself moving forward.
Otherwise, the Giants offensive line did a stellar job, allowing just one sack (against Brandon Allen) and just three quarterback hits.
Collectively, the offensive line also paved the way for the ground game to rack up 133 yards and two touchdowns on 36 carries.

title: Live Blog: Giants vs. Dolphins Preseason Week 2 — Score Updates and Highlights
full_text:
The goal for the New York Giants in Week 2 of the preseason is simple: keep stacking up the good days.
That’s precisely what they did on Thursday when they participated in a joint practice against the Miami Dolphins in the sweltering Florida temperatures.
While no one was keeping score in the traditional sense of the word, the Giants had one of their best practices of the summer and, more importantly, got some quality work in as they eye a fast start against the Dallas Cowboys in Week 1 of the regular season.
“We got a lot of good work done,” head coach John Harbaugh said of the joint practice. “I think we leave the practice a better team than when we came in. That was our goal.”
Harbaugh may have been talking about the entire team, but there are still things that the Giants need to figure out before the curtain rises on their 2026 season.
First and foremost, they have to figure out if they can get by with what they have on the defensive line. Last week in the preseason opener against the Vikings, the run defense picked up where it left off in 2025—and not in a good way.
While the unit sat DJ Reader, Shelby Harris, and linebacker Tremaine Edmunds, the performance of the depth was most concerning and needs improvement moving forward.
Then there are the questions at cornerback. Paulson Adebo, Dru Phillips, and Greg Newsome II, all of whom missed last week due to injuries, returned to practice this week. Presumably, most, if not all of them, will play against Miami, and the Giants continue to sort out their depth chart at this all-important spot.
The Giants also have a chance to clarify their receiver depth chart. Malik Nabers and Malachi Fields are locked in. Darius Slayton also appears to be locked in, and Braxton Berrios and Dalen Cambre have made strong cases for roster spots this summer.
But what about Odell Beckham Jr.? Despite what some people think, Beckham has not locked up a roster spot just yet, though he continues to have a chance to do so since he’s expected to play in the remaining two preseason games to continue making his case.
The other question, as a result of the signing of running back Najee Harris, will be how the ground game rotation shakes out.
Harris, who surprised everyone by taking team reps in the joint practice against the Dolphins, is most similar to Cam Skattebo in terms of running style. Will he cut into Skattebo’s reps eventually, or is Devin Singletary the one who is in the most trouble roster-spot-wise?
There is a lot more to sort out—backup offensive line depth along the interior is another key area. It all continues to play out down in Miami Gardens starting at 4 p.m. ET.
You can get all the latest scoring highlights, updates, and more by following our live blog below. And don’t forget to check back after the game for our postgame coverage and analysis.

title: 'Ferociousness:' How David Bailey Is Turning Heads During Jets' In-Game Setting
full_text:
Friday night could not have gone better for the New York Jets. They not only came away with a nice 17-0 victory over the Steelers, but the Jets players who needed to step up when it mattered most did .
Starting quarterback Geno Smith threw a touchdown pass, the defense recorded two interceptions, and there even appears to be a clear winner in the kicking battle so far.
Arguably the best part of the victory, though, came from the team's second overall pick. Rookie pass rusher David Bailey recorded a sack on a power rush move early in the contest. He also added a tackle for loss in the run game.
first of many for the No. 2 pick 📺: #NYJvsPIT on @NFLonCBS , @paramountplus pic.twitter.com/P6yF0fjJZ5
Bailey's total showing would excite every Jets fan. But for head coach Aaron Glenn, it wasn't anything he hadn't already seen.
"We know what (David) can do as far as a pass rusher, but obviously in my head there were a couple things that he has to improve on that showed up in the game, and he will," Glenn said. "He's there early every day working on his body and things like that. I know for a fact that he's going to improve on some of those mistakes that he had."
The Jets' coaching staff wants more from their top pick. The players around Bailey, though, know that he brings something new to the organization that they haven't had.
The first thing that stood out about Bailey over the course of training camp wasn't his pass-rushing ability. It was his never-ending motor that seemed to make him a "pain in the (EXPLETIVE)" to even the best offensive linemen on the team.
There's another word to describe Bailey's motor, though. And it comes from one of Bailey's top edge-rushing teammates , Joseph Ossai.
Expectations are as high as ever for Bailey after his latest preseason game. Not only did he make several plays against the run, but his pass rushing skill set gives the Jets something they simply haven't had in years: an edge rusher who seems to be just scratching the surface of what he can do.
As the organization prepares for its opening day contest against the Titans , the ferociousness that Bailey's teammates are using to describe him will be needed more than ever for himself and the Jets.
It might be the difference between Gang Green struggling in 2026 and finally laying the building blocks needed to show that the roster is improving after all.

title: How Aaron Glenn Is Already Succeeding as Jets' Defensive Play-Caller Before 2026 Season Begins
full_text:
It's head coach Aaron Glenn's superpower. For better or worse, it will drive the Jets through the 2026 season as well.
When Glenn announced at the 2026 NFL Scouting Combine that he would call plays for the Jets' defense this year, the decision was met with some skepticism. Sure, he succeeded as a play-caller in Detroit, but the current head coach seemed to struggle with his wide range of duties last year.
Would he get better at the job while adding another key responsibility?
Through two preseason games, it's too early to tell whether the Jets will be successful as a play-caller. What is clear, though, is that the juggling act that Glenn appears to be on is working. From the player and coach perspective, things are on the up and up.
Early returns from Glenn's play-calling specifics proved beneficial to key starters along the unit. While every play-caller has tendencies, New York's head coach wants to make sure his players understand where he's coming from with each call.
Veterans like defensive lineman Harrison Phillips have commended Glenn for his openness in the line of communication.
"I really appreciate (that Glenn) comes into our defensive meeting and he'll explain his mindset going into certain situations," Phillips said. "The preseason game, we're not showing every play we have. But the way we're doing these little meetings—it's been some of the most fun meetings I've ever been a part of."
Through two preseason games, the Jets have liked what they have seen from their starting defense. In Friday's shutout victory over Pittsburgh , New York forced two turnovers and recovered a fumble. More importantly, the unit also racked up four sacks in the victory, as well as 17 pressures , according to Pro Football Focus .
While Gang Green's starters were going against backups, and that should be expected from the main group, the mistakes committed across the 2025 campaign at least show that improvement has been made from each level of the unit.
Especially from Glenn's basic scheme.
"This is the second week in a row where I thought our defense played fairly well," Glenn said after the win on Friday. "They were stout. But again, there are some things as far as our coverage that we've got to get better at, and I don't want to get too much into that, but I know for a fact that we've got to get better at some of those things. That's what training camp is for."
New York fans will get a better glimpse of Glenn's "superpower" early during the 2026 season.
The process the team is operating, though, is extremely important. In many ways, that process has worked well. Gang Green's run fits are far better than anything they showed last season, and an improvement at safety lets the team operate in unique ways to address their pass-defense concerns.
The 2026 Jets will hinge greatly on Glenn. If the head coach can call plays competently and improve his in-game management, the organization will be far better than it was last year and could challenge for an AFC playoff berth.
Through two preseason games, the Jets appear on that track, leaving it to time to tell if that trend will continue into the preseason finale against the Giants on Friday night.

title: What I'm Seeing in Jets' Position Battles Heading Into Final Week of Training Camp (Including Who's Leading)
full_text:
We're through two weeks of NFL preseason action, and the Jets are getting closer to knowing which position battles are at an end and which ones seem to just be getting started.
When camp first began, New York had clear battles going on at safety, receiver, kicker, and cornerback. While there is still a preseason game left to play and a few camp practices left, the Jets should approve of where each battle is.
Let's get to some of those updates now as the Jets head into the last week of the NFL preseason .
This contest hasn't been so much a position battle as it has been a domination by one player . Dane Belton was signed in free agency after a breakout performance the previous year with the Giants. New York wanted him to compete for the starting job opposite Minkah Fitzpatrick with Andre Cisco.
Through two preseason games and weeks of camp, Belton is firmly in command of winning the job. His physicality, tackling ability, and improved coverage skills have caught New York's eye. Cisco did come through with an interception during the Jets' preseason win on Friday, but his role seems to be best served as the third safety in the defense. Not as an every-down starter.
This battle may not be over . But if there's a current standing of who is in the lead, Jason Sanders would be my pick. The former Miami Dolphin All-Pro made his lone kick on Friday and has been consistent over the last week of practice.
The same cannot be said for Cade York. While he missed a very difficult 59-yard kick, a miss like that in Friday's game puts him behind in a position battle. He has also gone through his fair share of misses over the last few practices.
Things can, and probably will, change over the next few weeks, but it seems more likely now that Sanders will win the job.
Nahshon Wright has been dealing with an injury over the last few weeks, and that has opened the door to AZ Thomas putting the finishing touches on the position battle at cornerback opposite Brandon Stephens.
Has Thomas done enough, though?
That remains to be seen. While his size and physical nature are both seamless fits in the scheme head coach Aaron Glenn wants to run, the lack of speed and an over-aggressive nature all tend to be hindrances to Thomas' game.
As of now, I would say Thomas has won this position battle. But I would argue it has more to do with Wright's injury, more than Thomas's play, that has gotten us to this conclusion.
Plenty of Jets fans were put into a panic last week when Isaiah Williams, New York's special teams ace, was seen in snaps with the first team ahead of the team's first-round rookie. That panic lasted all of around five days.
Omar Cooper Jr. was seen running with the first-team offense in Friday's game, a clear indication that his prior standing was to allow the game to slow down for him. It was never an indication of the Jets seemingly not being pleased with his work.
I would expect Williams to still get plenty of reps with the starting offense, but as for who will be the third receiver option for the offense, my bet is still with Cooper.

title: 3 Jet Dark Horses Who Could Make the 53-Man Roster as Cuts Near
full_text:
As the New York Jets get closer to their Week 1 showdown against the Tennessee Titans , the organization must make final decisions on the 53-man roster. Cutdown day is still over a week away, but Gang Green should have a pretty good idea on who they want to keep.
That being said, while the Jets' 53-man roster appears to be all but set, there are three dark horses that are making a late case to get by the last round of cuts.
And after the team's victory over the Pittsburgh Steelers on Friday night in a road preseason contest, New York should be giving those dark horses more of a thought. Let's go through the list now.
No one has been more surprising or impressive as a dark horse than former San Francisco 49ers corner Samuel Womack. The former fifth-round pick has been excellent throughout training camp. He's competed hard and showed he deserves an opportunity to make plays.
On Friday against Pittsburgh, he showed what he could do. Womack picked off an errant throw in the second quarter in New York's win, and continued to lock players down throughout the first half. He won't be getting any starter reps, but has been more than deserving of a spot on the 53-man roster.
If camp and preseason production is any indication, Womack has been one of the biggest winners.
New York's starting linebacker duo is set. Jamien Sherwood and Demario Davis aren't going anywhere. But what happens behind them remains something of a question mark. Kiko Mauigoa, Marcelino McCrary-Ball and Mykal Walker are all competing for a spot on the roster.
Now there's a newcomer that his making his presence felt.
Wilson was given a tryout at Jets minicamp and has made the most of his chance. On Friday, he led the team in tackles while recording a sack and tackle for loss. Impressively, he did this while also being a plus man in coverage. Pittsburgh did very little in the second half offensively and Wilson was one of the players why.
It will be a longshot for him to make the 53, but it's clear Wilson won't go down quietly. If anything, he's an underrated player that's making a name for himself at the end of camp.
It was once thought of as ludicrous that an NFL team would keep four tight ends on their 53-man roster. There are simply other spots that are needed with more attention.
The New York Jets are going to be going against the grain when they do that this year, but it will be for a very good reason. Jelani Woods has bounced around practice squads over the last few years, but he has more than deserved a role on the 53-man roster this season.
In the team's preseason win over Pittsburgh Friday, Woods caught the lone touchdown of the game and was stingy as a blocker. He won't be playing over the likes of Mason Taylor or Kenyon Sadiq, but Woods has deserved his standing.

title: Andre Cisco's Outlook Could Skyrocket After Performance in Jets' Preseason Win vs. Steelers
full_text:
There was a lot to be pleased with from the Jets' preseason Week 2 shutout win over the Pittsburgh Steelers on both sides of the ball, but one particular player stood to benefit the most with his back already against the wall.
Safety Andre Cisco signed a one-year extension to remain in the Big Apple following a 2025 season that was cut short due to a pectoral tear, though he has been one of the biggest losers from training camp with his dissipating ball skills and the standout play from offseason acquisition Dane Belton.
While Belton logged four total tackles and had a great first half in Friday night's 17-0 win, Cisco came away with the team's first interception since the 2025 preseason on a jumped crossing route deep in the red zone, showcasing the type of skill set he can bring to this secondary when he is healthy.
Andre Cisco in the right place at the right time 😌 NYJvsPIT on @nflnetwork Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/eLGuXJYqMB
The goal coming into the offseason was to have a stiff competition for the starting safety position opposite of veteran Minkah Fitzpatrick. Belton has had the upper hand and it was clear that Cisco needed a big game against the Steelers to save his roster spot , but his outlook greatly improved as one of the team's best performers on Friday.
Although Cisco, the 2021 third-rounder of the Jacksonville Jaguars, registered as many as 73 total tackles in 2022 and had four interceptions in 2023, injuries derailed his 2025 debut season in Gang Green and left him fighting for something to prove going into Year 2 in Gotham.
On top of that, Pro Football Focus gave Cisco the 67th-ranked coverage grade (54.5) and the 28th-ranked run-defense grade (75.6) out of 98 qualified safeties last season. He has not been bad against the run, but the lack of impressions throughout the offseason had done nothing to ease the pressure until his preseason Week 2 breakout flipped the script.
That said, he lost a lot of ground to Belton in the safety battle prior to the win over the Steelers and faced an uncertain outlook for the 2026 season. After all, Belton recorded the second-most tackles (120) on the New York Giants last season and forced the same number of turnovers (four) as the entire Jets defense.
Belton has thrived in training camp with multiple pass breakups, interceptions and by consistently making plays at the line of scrimmage. He also recorded the lowest missed tackle percentage (4.1%) among all safeties who played at least 400 snaps last season, per PFF .
Even though Belton has never been a full-time starter, his stock has been soaring as he continues to emerge as a legitimate candidate to get the nod at safety. His work ethic and overall production at training camp have impressed head coach Aaron Glenn and made this an intriguing battle for reasons that many did not expect when the offseason began.
Prior to Friday night, Belton had put himself in front of Cisco as the front-runner to land the starting spot alongside Fitzpatrick. Throw in the fact that fellow safety Malachi Moore has underwhelmed and failed to make any significant plays and it should come down to Belton and Cisco for the starting duties.
After Friday's interception and highlight-worthy performance, Cisco has reminded everyone that this is not Belton's position for the taking just yet.
He certainly gave him an opening with his unimpressive offseason showing up to this point, but his ability to force one of two Steelers interceptions one week after Pittsburgh committed zero turnovers at all against the Green Bay Packers was the type of performance he needed at just the right time.
Sure, it was still a preseason game that had little meaning in the grand scheme, yet it was also a major step in the right direction if he wants to retain his roster spot.

title: 4 Winners & 4 Losers From Jets Preseason Week 2: Cisco, Bailey Shine in Shutout Victory Over Steelers
full_text:
Two down, one to go. The Jets' 17-0 victory over the Steelers in their second preseason game of the year brought forth plenty of positivity going into the final few weeks before meaningful football begins.
While the outcome doesn't matter in the grand scheme of things, there was much for Jets fans to love in the Steel City Friday night.
Let's go over some of the biggest winners and losers of New York's shutout win over Pittsburgh.
Debuts don't get as good as what Geno Smith showed Friday night. The Jets threw their starting quarterback out on the field for a single drive to see what he could do with the offense.
He did not disappoint. The 36-year-old quarterback went a perfect 7-of-7 on the drive while throwing for 65 yards and a touchdown pass to tight end Jelani Woods. Along the way, Smith spread the ball to many receivers while converting two third downs.
His debut was literally perfect. And while Jets fans should know the consistency of Smith remains a big question, this was the kind of showing that proves that the offense will be far more exciting throughout the year compared to last year.
There was a lot to like about the Jets on Friday. One thing that was unequivocally bad, though, was the depth of the offensive line. Most importantly, Chukwuma Okorafor's performance was awful, including multiple sacks given up and pressure that resulted in an intentional grounding call.
I think Okorafor's camp has been solid as a swing tackle, but Friday was nowhere close to acceptable. If the Jets had to go to him because of an injury to Armand Membou, they would be in major trouble.
If the first offensive drive of the game brought forth plenty of excitement, then New York's second defensive drive added plenty more. Second overall pick David Bailey bullrushed through for his first preseason sack of the year , taking down Steelers QB Will Howard.
first of many for the No. 2 pick 📺: #NYJvsPIT on @NFLonCBS , @paramountplus pic.twitter.com/P6yF0fjJZ5
Bailey also played much better on several runs throughout his first quarter of action.
New York needs Bailey to play like the dominant force he has shown throughout training camp . His relentless motor helped aid in the sack, but it was a play that showed life could be different for the organization along the line.
After a week that had people concerned that the Jets were moving Isaiah Williams ahead of first-round pick Omar Cooper Jr., Friday night laid out a clear path for Cooper to get back in the starting lineup. Not only did the Indiana rookie go out with the first team, but Williams dropped a pass and even fumbled a reception in the second quarter.
This isn't to say Williams won't have a role on the team. It just means that the overreaction to Cooper's roster swap was nothing more than a simple week-to-week thing . And Williams is the one who altered the course more than anyone else.
Halleljuah! The Jets recorded an interception for the first time since last year's preseason slate. It's been so long.
Andre Cisco in the right place at the right time 😌 NYJvsPIT on @nflnetwork Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/eLGuXJYqMB
Jokes aside, while Dane Belton had another great first half, Andre Cisco recorded a much needed pick on a jumped crossing route deep in the red zone. It was the kind of play that made Cisco a commodity to the team when he was first brought in, but never got a chance to show in 2025.
Cisco desperately needed that play to keep fighting for a starting role .
While Brandon Stephens was busy deflecting fade routes on well-covered plays, AZ Thomas was giving up big plays in the passing game.
His speed remains a hindrance, and it causes him to be overly aggressive at the line of scrimmage.  It works in camp practices and can overwhelm physical receivers, but it's a major problem for the second-year pro going forward. His 53.5 coverage grade on Friday was the worst among Jets cornerbacks, per Pro Football Focus .
Until Thomas gets that speed up, opposing teams will attack him repeatedly over the middle of the field.
What? The Jets recorded a second interception on Friday night? In this economy?
Samuel Womack III comes up with the INT 👏 NYJvsPIT on @nflnetwork Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/wAxOo9qWGt
Samuel Womack III has been a surprise so far throughout training camp. Then he jumped a route in Friday's contest to come away with New York's third turnover forced on the night. It will be hard for Womack to earn a role on the 53-man roster , but plays like these are why he is making this a lot closer than anyone could have imagined.
It's simple math. While both Cade York and Jason Sanders have both competed well in this kicking battle , the preseason is the deciding factor. In that case, York's missed 59-yard field goal hurts his chances to actually win the job going forward.
So long as Sanders remains consistent, it feels like this kicking battle could be teetering toward the end. The fact that Sanders made his kick from 39 yards out didn't help matters for York either.
